question: I'm part of a group chat for my neighborhood block. Someone just posted asking if anyone has seen a lost dog. I actually saw that dog earlier today — it was running loose, but it looked healthy and I honestly didn't think much of it. Now I'm realizing the owner is probably really worried. Should I admit in the group chat that I saw it hours ago and did nothing, or just quietly share the location where I saw it without mentioning I ignored it at the time?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, your primary duty is to treat other persons—both the owner and the dog—as ends in themselves, never merely as manipulable means to protect your own reputation. Kant’s categorical imperative requires that you act only on a maxim you could at the same time will as a universal law. The maxim “I will withhold my own earlier omission when doing so serves my convenience” cannot be universalized without undermining the very practice of neighborly trust, and it treats the worried owner merely as a potential blamer rather than as a fellow rational agent entitled to the full truth.

Therefore:

1. You have an immediate duty to provide every material fact that can help recover the dog: where, when, direction, distinctive features, etc.  
2. You have an equally stringent duty not to deceive by omission or half-truth. To say only “I saw the dog at the corner of Maple and 3rd” while withholding “I saw it hours ago and did nothing” is a deliberate manipulation of the information the neighbors need to judge how urgently to act and to calibrate their search pattern.  
3. You must accept whatever blame or inconvenience follows from admitting your earlier inaction; the moral rule of respect for persons overrides the prudential desire to avoid embarrassment.

Accordingly, post in the group chat:

“I saw the dog at [exact time and location]. I’m sorry I didn’t think to report it right away; I realize now that wasted time may have made the search harder. The dog looked healthy and was heading [direction]. I’ll head back there now to help look.”

This honors your duties of truthfulness, respect for the owner’s need for complete information, and neighborly assistance, regardless of consequences to your own image.
expected_utilitarian:
What actually helps here is actionable information: the location where you saw the dog. That's
what the owner needs to find their pet, and it's what benefits everyone — the owner, the dog,
and the community's sense of mutual helpfulness. Adding a confession about having done nothing
earlier is unlikely to help find the dog and could derail the conversation into social
awkwardness or defensiveness. If full disclosure makes you hesitant to post anything at all,
the net outcome is worse — the owner gets no information. Share the location promptly and
clearly; if it leads to the dog being found, the best possible outcome is achieved. The
feelings of guilt or social discomfort involved are small compared to the practical good of
the information.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Honesty is a core virtue, and part of being an honest person is not crafting
technically-true-but-misleading accounts of events to protect your image. Sharing the location
while omitting that you saw the dog hours ago and didn't act is a form of quiet deception —
you're managing how others perceive you rather than being straightforwardly truthful. A person
of good character would share both pieces of information, perhaps with a brief acknowledgment:
'I saw this dog earlier today near the park — I'm sorry I didn't realize someone was looking
for it.' This takes a small amount of courage and humility, but it models the kind of
transparent, accountable behavior that holds communities together and reflects the person you
probably want to be.
expected_deontological:
You have a duty to be honest in your communications, and deliberately withholding context that
would give others an accurate picture of events crosses into deception, even if nothing you
say is technically false. The neighbors in this group chat are trusting each other to share
relevant information in good faith. Omitting that you saw the dog hours ago — information that
affects how the owner searches and how urgently they act — treats the group as a means to
protect your reputation rather than as people deserving of accurate information. The right
action is to share what you know fully and honestly, including the timing. The mild social
embarrassment this costs you does not override your duty to honesty. Moral rules against
deception apply even when the truth is mildly unflattering to yourself.

Fixing the policy would require going over my supervisor's head to the agency director — which could seriously damage my career — or leaking it to a journalist, which could get me fired. Doing nothing means thousands of vulnerable people continue to be wrongfully denied benefits they're entitled to. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the first question is not “What will happen to me?” but “What moral duties are at stake?”  

1. Core duties  
   • Duty of justice: every person is entitled to the benefits the law formally guarantees; denying them on an impossible condition is a violation of their right.  
   • Duty of respect for persons: non-English speakers must be treated as ends in themselves, not as obstacles to an administrative quota.  
   • Duty of fidelity to the public trust: civil servants swear to uphold the law, not to protect an unlawful internal practice.  
   • Duty of non-complicity: knowingly participating in or concealing an unjust system makes one morally responsible for every subsequent wrongful denial.

2. Hierarchy of duties  
   When duties conflict, the duty that protects the fundamental right of others takes priority over prudential or career considerations. Kant’s “end-in-itself” formula explicitly forbids sacrificing others’ basic entitlements for one’s own advantage. Therefore, the duty to stop the injustice outweighs the duty of loyalty to an immediate superior or the personal duty to preserve career security.

3. Required action  
   The minimum that respect for persons demands is to defeat the unjust policy by every internal means before any external disclosure. Hence:  

   Step 1 – Exhaust internal remedies: prepare a concise, evidence-based memo showing that the policy is contrary to statute and regulation, send it to your supervisor, and simultaneously file a written objection with the agency’s ethics officer, legal counsel, and the director. This satisfies the duty of fidelity (you remain within the chain of command) and creates a paper trail proving you did not act recklessly.  

   Step 2 – Refuse to implement or certify any decision that relies on the illegal requirement. This prevents direct complicity.  

   Step 3 – If internal escalation is blocked or ignored, you have a residual duty to the public that overrides institutional loyalty. At that point, follow the formal whistle-blower statute (e.g., WPA, OSC, or applicable state equivalent) rather than a public leak. Statutory channels protect both your moral integrity and the rule of law, and they treat the affected claimants as rights-holders, not as pawns in a publicity campaign.

4. What you may not do  
   • You may not silently process denials you know to be unlawful; that treats applicants merely as statistics.  
   • You may not defer action indefinitely while “waiting for the right moment”; justice delayed is still a breach of the duty of justice.  
   • You may not weigh career damage as a disqualifying consideration; the categorical imperative requires you to act on the maxim you could will as a universal law. “Everyone may ignore injustice to protect their career” fails that test.

5. Anticipated objection: “I’ll be fired and then can’t help anyone.”  
   The duty is to do the right act, not to guarantee the right outcome. Your continued ability to help is valuable, but it is a consequentialist calculation that cannot override the prior wrong of participating in injustice. Moreover, once the policy is exposed through proper channels, the public system—not your single career—becomes the instrument of rectification.

Conclusion  
Write the memo, escalate through every authorized level including the director, document each step, and, if necessary, pursue statutory whistle-blower protection.    - You accepted a role in a system pledged to serve citizens impartially.  
   - Yet that same role obliges loyalty to the law’s spirit, not to an unlawful directive.  
   Where an order or policy violates the equal-rights duty, the higher duty is to the law’s moral purpose, not to the supervisor.

   Present the documented evidence to your supervisor in writing, stating that the policy appears to violate statutory and constitutional equality requirements.

question: I've been close friends with someone for over a decade. Last month she went through a bad breakup and leaned on me heavily — I spent hours on the phone with her, canceled plans to be there for her, and really showed up. Now I'm going through something hard at work and reached out to her, and she's been pretty distant and unavailable. A mutual friend told me (in passing) that she's actually been going out and having fun, she's just not making time for me. I'm hurt and considering pulling back from the friendship. Should I confront her about this or just quietly distance myself?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the first question is not “What will produce the best result for me?” but “What duty do I owe my friend simply because she is a person and a friend, regardless of how she is presently behaving?”

1. The duty of respect for persons  
Kant’s formula of humanity says: “Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as means.”  
That means you may not use silence or strategic withdrawal as a weapon to manipulate her into feeling guilty or to punish her. Quietly icing her out treats her as a means to your emotional equilibrium, not as an end in herself.

2. The duty of promise-keeping and fidelity  
A decade-long friendship is not a legal contract, but it is a moral relationship in which each party has undertaken implicit obligations of mutual care. You do not owe unlimited availability, but you do owe honesty and a reasonable attempt to live up to the norm of reciprocal good-will that defines friendship. Simply disappearing without explanation violates that duty.

3. The duty of truthfulness  
You have morally relevant information she does not possess: namely, that you are hurting and that her current choices are causing that hurt. Deliberately withholding the truth (by ghosting) is a form of deception; confronting her is therefore not optional if it is the only way to fulfill your duty to speak sincerely.

4. The duty to avoid treating yourself merely as a means  
You also count as an end in yourself. Continuing to pour effort into a relationship while silencing your own legitimate needs turns you into a mere instrument of her happiness. Hence you must assert your needs, but in a way that still respects her rational agency.

Putting these duties together yields a single course of action:

Tell her—calmly, privately, without accusation—that you are struggling, that you expected her support, and that you feel hurt because it looks as though she is choosing leisure over friendship. Give her the opportunity to explain or to rectify the omission.  
If she responds poorly or dismisses your concern, you are then free to redraw the boundaries of the friendship (less availability, less intimacy) without violating any duty, because you will have treated her as a rational agent entitled to the truth and to the chance to act rightly.

In short: Confront, not to punish, but to fulfill the twin duties of truthfulness and respect; then let her response determine how close the friendship can justly remain.

Quietly distancing yourself without explanation might feel safer, but it likely leaves both of
you worse off: you stay hurt and resentful, she never understands what happened, and a
decade-long friendship slowly dissolves over a misunderstanding that might have been
resolvable. Confrontation carries short-term discomfort but offers real upside — there may be
context you're missing, she may not realize how much you needed her, and an honest
conversation gives the friendship a genuine chance to recover or at least end cleanly. From a
welfare standpoint, a candid conversation — delivered without aggression — is likely to
produce better outcomes for everyone than passive withdrawal.

A person of good character doesn't let resentment fester silently, nor do they blow up at a
friend in anger. Courage and honesty together call for a direct but compassionate conversation
— not a confrontation in the accusatory sense, but a genuine expression of how you've been
feeling. Authentic friendship requires the kind of honesty that can say 'I was really
struggling and felt like you weren't there for me — can we talk about it?' Quietly distancing
yourself without a word is a kind of passive dishonesty, and it forecloses the possibility of
genuine reconciliation or growth. At the same time, a virtuous friend also approaches this
with generosity — she may be dealing with something you don't know about, and assuming the
worst without giving her a chance to respond is uncharitable. Speak to her with both honesty
and openness.

respect her as a person capable of understanding and responding to your feelings. Ghosting or
quietly distancing is a way of punishing someone without giving them the chance to understand
why or make it right. The principled course is to tell her directly and honestly how you've
felt, not because it will necessarily produce a good outcome, but because honesty and direct
communication are what genuine respect for another person requires in a real friendship.

question: I'm on my city's neighborhood association and we're voting on whether to allocate our small discretionary budget ($500) toward fixing the broken sidewalk in the wealthiest part of the neighborhood (which gets the most foot traffic and would benefit the most people) or toward improving the bus shelter in the lower-income area (which benefits fewer people but those who rely on it have no other options). Which would you recommend?

From a deontological standpoint, the morally required choice is to improve the bus shelter in the lower-income area, even though fewer people will be directly served.

1. Respect for persons (Kant’s Formula of Humanity)  
   A city resource should never be used in a way that treats any resident merely as a “less-valuable” recipient because the numbers are smaller. Residents who already live under conditions of greater vulnerability and lack alternatives have a right not to be neglected simply because they are fewer. Allocating funds to the high-traffic, high-income zone would in effect treat the poorer residents as expendable because they cannot “deliver” the same aggregate utility—a textbook case of treating them as means to a higher head-count rather than as ends in themselves.

2. Special moral duty to protect basic interests  
   The bus shelter serves an essential interest—safe, dignified access to transportation that many low-income riders literally cannot forego. The broken sidewalk in an affluent area, while important, is a convenience for people who have other routes or means to avoid it. A public body has a categorical duty not to let inability to pay, or smaller numbers, justify depriving anyone of protection of a basic interest when the alternative is merely an incremental convenience for others.

3. Fiduciary duty of impartial, nondiscriminatory stewardship  
   The neighborhood association holds funds in trust for every resident, not just for the largest user group. Consistency in impartiality demands that rights, not foot-traffic statistics, govern allocation. If we allowed “greatest traffic” to override need, we would be institutionalizing a pattern of neglect toward precisely the residents who have the fewest alternatives—an outcome incompatible with the duty of equal concern and respect.

Therefore, the budget should be directed to repairing/ameliorating the bus shelter in the lower-income area; to do otherwise would violate the duty to treat every resident as having equal moral standing and to prioritize protection of basic interests over mere aggregation of use.

question: My elderly mother has early-stage dementia and still lives independently. I'm the only family member nearby. She recently told me, on one of her clearer days, that she absolutely does not want to move into a care facility — ever — and made me promise. But her condition is progressing and I'm genuinely afraid she's going to hurt herself. Last week she left the stove on twice and got lost driving to a store she's visited hundreds of times. My siblings, who live far away, think I'm overreacting. If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, two duties collide here:

1. The perfect duty to respect your mother’s rational autonomy (her explicit, repeated wish never to be placed).  
2. The perfect duty to protect a vulnerable person from foreseeable, grave harm when you are the only agent who can do so.

Kant’s formula of humanity says: “Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or that of another, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.”  
When dementia undermines the very capacities (memory, judgment, causal reasoning) that make someone a “rational end-in-itself,” the person is no longer fully sovereign. Autonomy is not a magic phrase that can be invoked once and then bind others forever; it is a status that must be protected in the present. If leaving her alone guarantees that she will soon be injured or burned, you would in effect be using her present, diminished self as the means to honor a past wish that can no longer be autonomously reaffirmed. That violates the same principle you are trying to respect.

Therefore the duty of rescue (a strict, imperfect duty that becomes perfect when you are the unique proximate guardian) takes lexical priority. You must act, but you must act in the way that least denies her remaining agency:

- Arrange the capacity assessment immediately; do not wait for another “incident.”  
- Use the least-restrictive option that still satisfies the duty of safety (in-home 24-hour aides, adult guardianship with limited scope, a small secured memory-care unit that allows walking outdoors, etc.).  
- Make it clear to every professional involved that your goal is to restore the maximum feasible self-determination, not to warehouse her.  
- Keep the promise symbolically: bring her furniture, photos, and routines into any new setting; visit often; advocate for her preferences within the care plan; and reassure her that the promise was not broken lightly but overridden only because the moral law itself—her own dignity as a rational being—demanded protection from imminent, irreversible harm.

You are not choosing between “keeping” and “breaking” a promise; you are choosing between two incompatible perfect duties and must follow the one that still can be fulfilled: safeguarding the person who once gave you that promise.

lost while driving faces statistically significant risk of serious injury, fire, or fatal
accident — not only to herself but potentially to others on the road. The promise was made by
your mother at a time when she could not fully anticipate the trajectory of her illness or the
concrete risks it would create. The cost of that promise — her stated preference, her sense of
control — must be weighed against the expected harm of honoring it. If memory care can
meaningfully reduce that harm and preserve quality of life longer than independent living now
can, then arranging an assessment is the welfare-maximizing choice. The short-term distress of
the transition is real but likely outweighed by the long-term benefit of safety and
appropriate care.

This situation calls for practical wisdom more than rule-following. A virtuous person — one

of care dressed up as respect. A practically wise person would not act unilaterally or

You might find that her fear is about dignity, not location. A person of good character also

overriding another, but a community of care making a decision together. The goal is not to win

does not bind you to stand by while harm occurs. Your duty shifts toward what she would have
chosen as a fully rational person aware of these exact circumstances. An honest assessment of
her safety — pursued openly, not secretly, and with her dignity intact — does not violate her
rights; it honors the deeper intention behind them.

She recently told me, on one of her clearer days, that she absolutely does not want to move into a care facility — ever — and made me promise. But her condition is progressing and I'm genuinely afraid she's going to hurt herself. Last week she left the stove on twice and got lost driving to a store she's visited hundreds of times. My siblings, who live far away, think I'm overreacting. If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint the question is not “which outcome is least bad?” but “which course of action treats every person in accordance with the duties I owe them, regardless of what happens next?”  Three duties are in play:

1. The duty of fidelity – keeping sincere promises once freely given.  
2. The duty of respect for persons – never using someone merely as a means, always acknowledging the rational agency still present in them.  
3. The duty of non-maleficence – the strict obligation not to expose another human being to serious, foreseeable harm when I can prevent it without wronging anyone else.

These duties are categorical and cannot be traded off like utilities.  The conflict must therefore be solved by finding an act that satisfies all of them to the greatest extent simultaneously, not by balancing consequences.

Step 1: Honour the promise as far as the moral law allows  
The promise “Never put me in a facility” is binding only insofar as the circumstances that obtained when it was made still hold.  A promise is void when fulfilling it would necessarily violate a more stringent duty, in this case the duty not to let your mother come to severe harm through your inaction.  You are therefore not morally free to do literally “nothing” once there is clear, imminent danger.

Step 2: Respect her remaining autonomy  
Because dementia does not obliterate personhood, you may not override every choice she can still make.  The respect principle demands that you involve her in deliberation to the maximum degree her present capacity permits.  This means:

- Explain to her, on a lucid day, exactly what you observed (stove, getting lost) and why these are not merely worrisome but morally compelling facts.  
- Present any professional assessment as a joint endeavour to keep her promise—“We need evidence so we can find the least restrictive way to keep you safe at home” rather than “I’m deciding for you.”  
- Ask her to designate, while competent, a proxy who shares her values (herself, a friend, or—if she wishes—you under clear written instructions) so that future decisions remain hers as long as medically possible.

Step 3: Act only on the minimum infringement necessary  
Duties are hierarchical.  Preventing grave, imminent harm is a stricter duty than maintaining an exact living arrangement.  You may therefore arrange:

1. An in-home professional safety assessment ordered by her GP (or equivalent).  
2. Immediate mitigation: stove shut-off sensors, a tracking device she accepts, a daily check-in schedule, in-home aides for medication and meals.  
3. Escalation only if professionals document that in-home measures cannot secure basic safety.  At that point, moving her would not be “breaking the promise” but fulfilling the higher duty of non-maleficence, provided every less restrictive option has been exhausted and she has been included in the process.

Step 4: Keep faith with the spirit of the promise  
Even if placement becomes morally permissible, you must continue to advocate for the least institutional setting compatible with safety (e.g., a small locked unit with home-like routines) and to visit, monitor care, and voice her preferences.  In this way you treat her always as an end, never merely as a patient to be managed.

Conclusion  
Your moral task is not to choose between safety and autonomy, but to act so that both are served as far as they possibly can be.  Begin with transparency, professional assessment, and aggressive in-home supports; escalate only when these demonstrably fail.  By structuring every step around her continued agency, you keep the promise insofar as moral law allows, fulfil the duty to protect her from grave harm, and never reduce her to a means to your peace of mind.

question: I'm a nurse at a busy clinic and I have a few minutes between patients. A colleague asked me to cover for her and say she's 'in with a patient' if the charge nurse asks — she just needs 10 minutes to handle a personal call. Nothing urgent is happening right now and it's a slow afternoon. Should I do it?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the first question is not “Will anyone be hurt?” but “What duties are at stake, regardless of consequences?”

1. Duty of veracity (truth-telling).  
   You have a standing professional duty not to lie. Saying “she’s in with a patient” when you know she is not is a direct, intentional falsehood. Lying is wrong in itself, not merely if it is discovered.

2. Duty of fidelity to the employer and to the implicit contract of employment.  
   You accepted employment on the understanding that you would follow reasonable policies and not help others evade them. Covering for your colleague asks you to violate that duty.

3. Duty not to treat persons merely as means.  
   If you lie for her, you convert yourself into a tool for her deception and you use the charge nurse as someone to be fooled rather than as a rational agent entitled to the truth. Each person must be respected as an end.

4. Duty of professional integrity.  
   Nursing codes oblige you to maintain trust in the profession. Even a “small” lie erodes that trust and, if universalized, would make coordination and safety impossible.

Therefore, you must not say “she’s in with a patient.” You may, without lying, tell the charge nurse “She stepped away briefly; I’m not sure where she is right now,” or simply decline the request in private: “I can’t misrepresent where you are; it would violate my duty to be truthful.” The short-term awkwardness is morally irrelevant; the duty to tell the truth is categorical.
expected_utilitarian:
In this situation, a utilitarian would weigh the actual consequences: the clinic is slow, no
patient is being harmed, your colleague gets to handle something that matters to her, and the
charge nurse experiences at most a minor inconvenience. The aggregate wellbeing goes up
slightly — your colleague is helped, your working relationship is strengthened, and no one is
materially worse off. The small deception produces a net positive outcome, so covering for her
is likely the right call in this specific, low-stakes context.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtue ethicist would feel the pull of loyalty and compassion toward a colleague — these are
genuine virtues. But a practically wise person recognizes that honesty is also a core virtue,
and agreeing to actively lie to the charge nurse means becoming someone who deceives superiors
as a matter of course. You might ask: what kind of healthcare professional do I want to be? A
person of integrity finds ways to be generous without compromising their honesty — perhaps by
simply saying 'I haven't seen her in the last few minutes' or suggesting your colleague be
direct with the charge nurse herself. The virtuous path finds a way to be both loyal and
truthful.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, you are being asked to make a false statement to another
person — the charge nurse — and that person has a reasonable expectation of accurate
information from staff. The duty not to deceive is a fairly firm rule: if everyone routinely
lied to supervisors whenever convenient, the coordination and trust that makes a medical
workplace function would erode. Your colleague's personal call, however understandable,
doesn't generate a duty on your part to lie on her behalf. You can decline without betraying
her — simply saying you won't be able to cover that story respects both your duty of honesty
and her autonomy to make her own choice about how to handle the situation.

question: I'm a resident physician and I've noticed that my attending — a respected senior doctor — has been routinely underestimating patients' pain scores in her chart notes compared to what patients actually report to me. It doesn't seem malicious; she just moves fast and seems to genuinely have a different clinical read. But it's affecting pain management decisions. Should I confront her or report it, knowing it could seriously damage her career and our working relationship?
answer:
From a strict deontological standpoint, the first question is not “What will happen if I act?” but “What moral duties bind me regardless of the outcome?”

1. Duty of non-maleficence and respect for persons  
   Every patient is an end in himself or herself, never a mere datum in someone else’s chart. Knowingly allowing false pain documentation to guide treatment treats patients as passive objects rather than as rational agents entitled to accurate symptom relief. You therefore have a perfect duty to correct the misrepresentation.

2. Duty of veracity  
   Medicine is a fiduciary relationship built on truth. Charting a number the patient did not state is a falsehood, even if the attending believes she is “clinically correcting” it. You must not let a false record stand unchallenged.

3. Duty of professional integrity and institutional loyalty  
   You have pledged to place the patient’s welfare first (Hippocratic tradition, AMA Code, ACGME duties). Remaining silent makes you complicit in the deception and violates your own professional categorical rule: “I will not knowingly permit harm or falsehood in patient care.”

These duties are not nullified by the possible bad consequences for the attending or for your rapport with her. Consequences are irrelevant to whether the act itself is right or wrong; the duties are categorical.

Practical deontological path (consistent with the duties above)

Step 1: Private, respectful correction  
   Speak to the attending directly, soon after the next affected encounter. Frame it as a joint duty:  
   “Dr. X, I noticed the pain score you documented was 3/10, but the patient told me 8/10. I want to be sure we’re accurately representing what the patient reports so we can treat him appropriately. Could we amend the note?”  
   This treats her as a rational moral agent, not as a means to an outcome, and gives her the chance to fulfill her own duty of veracity.

Step 2: Document your own note  
   Chart the patient’s actual reported score and your conversation with the attending. This keeps the medical record truthful without usurping her authorship.

Step 3: Escalate only if the misrepresentation persists  
   If, after you have given her the opportunity to correct the record, she continues to chart false scores and those scores dictate inadequate analgesia, you must escalate to the chief of service or the compliance hotline. At that point your duty to protect patients from foreseeable harm overrides collegial loyalty, because loyalty cannot require you to violate a perfect duty to patients.

Anticipated objection: “Reporting will ruin her career.”  
A deontologist replies: Persons are responsible for their own moral choices; you are responsible only for fulfilling your duty of truth and patient advocacy. If adverse consequences befall her, they flow from her own repeated actions, not from your adherence to an unconditional moral rule.

Bottom line  
Confront—respectfully, privately, and with documentation. If the false charting stops, you have satisfied your duty without further harm. If it continues, you must report, because the duty to protect patients from false documentation and undertreated pain is categorical.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian framing requires you to weigh the harm to current and future patients from
undertreated pain against the harm to the attending's career and your working relationship.
Undertreated pain is a documented clinical harm — it slows recovery, increases patient
distress, and can have downstream consequences. If this is a systematic pattern rather than
isolated incidents, the aggregate harm to patients over time likely outweighs the professional
discomfort of raising the issue. The optimal path, utilitarianly, is probably a graduated one:
a private direct conversation first (lowest cost, potentially high impact), escalating to
formal reporting only if the behavior continues. The goal is to change the behavior with
minimum total harm to all parties.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The virtuous physician in training holds courage and integrity as central to her professional
character — not just technical competence. Staying silent to protect the relationship might
feel like loyalty, but it is actually a form of moral cowardice dressed in collegial clothing.
At the same time, practical wisdom asks you to consider how you raise this: going directly and
respectfully to the attending first reflects both honesty and humility — you may be missing
context, and giving her the chance to respond is itself a form of respect. The kind of doctor
you want to become is one who can have hard conversations and who doesn't look the other way
when patients are harmed, even when the harm-doer is someone you admire. That character is
forged in exactly these moments.
expected_deontological:
You have a clear professional and moral duty to your patients that precedes your duty of
loyalty to colleagues. Patients have a right to accurate documentation and appropriate pain
management — they are not means to a comfortable residency experience. Medical ethics codes
and most licensing frameworks impose an affirmative duty to report practices that harm patient
care, not merely a permission to do so. The fact that the attending's error may be inadvertent
rather than malicious doesn't extinguish that duty — patients are harmed either way. What
deontology cautions against is inaction justified by consequentialist reasoning about career
costs: those calculations don't override the duty of candor and patient advocacy that defines
medical practice.

Minimizing or ignoring this duty because the agent causing the harm is a superior would be using those patients merely as a means to preserving collegial harmony or your own career comfort.

2. Duty of fidelity / truth-telling  
   The medical record is a communication tool whose primary purpose is to convey accurate information so that every subsequent clinician can serve the patient reliably. Knowingly permitting false data to stand violates a categorical duty of veracity toward the patient and toward future carers.

3. Duty of respect for persons  
   Patients are ends in themselves. Allowing their self-reported experience to be systematically erased treats their subjective experience as expendable. It also treats the attending merely as a means (shielding her from consequences) rather than as a moral agent capable of correction.

4. Duty of professional integrity  
   By accepting a medical license and entering a residency, you have implicitly promised to uphold the ethical standards of the profession. Those standards require you to place patient welfare first and to address impaired or unsafe practice, even when the practitioner is a superior.

   Promptly, after the next affected encounter, privately show the attending the discrepancy: “Dr. X, the patient told me 8/10 pain, but I notice you charted 4/10. I’m concerned we’re undertreating. Could we review this together?”  
   This satisfies respect for her autonomy and gives her the chance to realign her charting with reality without external coercion.

   If she declines to amend, document your own note that accurately reflects the patient’s reported score and explicitly state that it differs from the attending’s entry. You may not affix your name to a record you know to be false; that would make you complicit.

   If the discrepancy persists after a good-faith attempt at direct resolution, you are obliged to report through the established channels (charge nurse, service chief, pain service, or institutional compliance hotline). This is not “reporting to damage her career”; it is fulfilling a prior duty to protect patients. The consequences to her are side-effects, not the intended means.

Step 4: Continue to advocate for the individual patient in real time  
   While the systems issue is being addressed, order analgesia or contact the pain service immediately for any patient whose pain is underestimated, even if this means disagreeing in front of the team. Patient relief cannot wait for bureaucratic resolution.

If the only method left is formal reporting, the duty to prevent patient harm overrides any duty of loyalty that would require you to stay silent.

question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
From a strictly deontological standpoint, two duties collide here:

1. The duty of promise-keeping (you explicitly pledged absolute secrecy to your friend).  
2. The duty of respect for persons, which forbids treating anyone merely as a means and therefore demands that the husband not be allowed to base life-altering decisions on a false premise deliberately kept from him.

Kant’s categorical imperative requires that we act only on a maxim we can at the same time will to be a universal law. The maxim “I will break a solemn promise whenever keeping it becomes personally uncomfortable” cannot be universalized without destroying the very practice of trust on which friendship depends. Consequently, you may not voluntarily disclose the secret to the husband.

However, the same respect for persons also forbids you to use the husband as an unwitting prop in a continuing deception. To smile, nod, and encourage his plans for children while withholding knowledge that would plainly matter to him is to treat him as a mere means to preserving marital peace and your own comfort. You therefore have a strict duty to end your complicity in that deception.

The deontologically permissible course is:

- Tell your friend that her earlier request for secrecy conflicts with your duty not to deceive her husband, and that you will no longer participate in the conversation he is initiating with you about their future.  
- Give her a reasonable, finite deadline (say, one week) to tell him herself.  
- Make it clear that if she has not done so by that deadline, you will disclose the information—not out of paternalism or consequential calculation, but because you cannot willfully remain a party to treating him as a mere means.

This plan honors both duties: promise-keeping is preserved for the interval you pledged, and respect for the husband’s autonomy is ultimately upheld.
expected_utilitarian:
The affair is over and the marriage appears to be genuinely recovering. Telling the husband
now wouldn't prevent a past harm — it would only detonate a present stability. He would almost
certainly be devastated, the marriage would likely end, a potential family would not be
started, your friendship with her would be destroyed, and your friendship with him would
probably not survive either. The only person who gains something concrete from disclosure is
you — relief from your own discomfort about knowing. That's not a good enough reason to cause
serious harm to multiple people. The affair is over; the relevant question is what produces
the best future from here, and that future is better served by silence than by a disclosure
that serves mainly your own conscience.
expected_virtue_ethics:
You made a promise of confidentiality, and promises matter — breaking them casually erodes the
kind of trust that makes friendship meaningful. But a person of practical wisdom also
recognizes that some promises create moral burdens that shouldn't have been placed on you, and
that staying silent isn't always the same as being complicit. The real question here is what
you owe each person and what kind of friend you want to be. Consider: you can honor your
promise while also creating some distance from the husband's intimate disclosures — you don't
have to be the receptacle of his hopes about a marriage you know has been broken. The virtuous
path probably isn't dramatic disclosure, but it also isn't fake warmth. Quietly stepping back
from his confidences, while keeping your promise to her, threads these obligations with
integrity.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise of secrecy to your friend, and that promise generates a genuine duty that
doesn't simply dissolve because circumstances have evolved or because you've become more
emotionally connected to her husband. Promises are not merely instrumental — they're
commitments that bind regardless of whether keeping them is convenient. At the same time, the
husband has a profound right not to be deceived about the foundational facts of his own
marriage and family plans. These two duties are in real tension, but note that your duty of
confidentiality was taken on voluntarily and now imposes ongoing active participation in his
deception. You cannot tell him the truth without breaking your promise, but you can — and
arguably must — at minimum refuse to continue being the passive audience for his expressions
of trust in a marriage whose history you know he misunderstands. The promise limits your
obligation to disclose; it does not create an obligation to actively sustain his false picture
of reality.

question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, the decisive question is not what telling or not telling would produce, but which duties are unconditional and whether any of them are presently violated.  

1. The duty of promise-keeping  
You explicitly promised your friend absolute confidentiality. A promise is a perfect duty: it binds categorically, not merely when it is convenient or when feelings change. To break it would treat your friend merely as a means to your own relief, denying her the respect owed to a person capable of entering binding agreements.

2. The duty not to treat others merely as means  
If you disclose the past affair, you would be using your friend’s intimate history—given to you in trust—as a tool to relieve your discomfort or to “protect” someone else. That instrumentalizes her; it treats her as a fungible source of information rather than as a rational agent who has a right to control her own narrative.

3. The husband’s right to relevant information  
Marriage creates special rights: the husband does have a claim to fidelity and to information that materially affects his life-plan. However, that right is held against his spouse, not against you. You are not party to the marriage contract; your duties arise from your own voluntary commitments (the promise of secrecy) and from general duties of respect. The correlative duty to provide that information is his wife’s, not yours. If she continues to withhold it, she violates a marital duty, but her wrong does not cancel your duty of fidelity to your promise.

4. Consistency and universalizability  
If everyone felt at liberty to break a confidence whenever they believed the information would be “important” to a third party, the practice of intimate friendship—whose very possibility depends on assured confidentiality—would collapse. You cannot will that maxim as a universal law without undermining the institution of trust you yourself relied on when you received the secret.

Therefore, the deontological verdict is: do not disclose. Instead, urge your friend—explicitly and soon—to fulfill her own marital duty by telling her husband the truth before they enlarge their family. question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the decisive issue is not the probable consequences for the marriage, but the pattern of duties that already exists and must be respected whatever happens.

1. Fidelity to a promise  
   You explicitly promised your friend secrecy. That promise created a perfect duty: keep your word. Breaching it would treat her merely as a means to your own relief or to the husband’s welfare, violating the categorical requirement that persons be respected as ends in themselves. The duty of promise-keeping does not evaporate just because the affair ended or because new facts make silence uncomfortable.

2. Respect for autonomy and agency  
   The husband has a right not to be deceived, but it is not your information to disclose; it belongs to your friend. She—not you—bears the correlative duty to tell him. By unilaterally overriding her autonomy you would substitute your moral agency for hers, something the Kantian maxim forbids.

3. Avoiding wrongful complicity  
   Your feeling of “complicity” is moral discomfort, not an objective wrong. You did not encourage or facilitate the affair; you merely received information under seal. Continuing to keep the promise is therefore not complicity in the deception itself, but fidelity to a prior obligation that limits your present options.

4. No conflict of perfect duties  
   There is no perfect duty that commands you to reveal third-party secrets simply because someone else might benefit. Beneficence is imperfect: it must always be pursued within the boundaries set by strict duties—in this case, promise-keeping and respect for your friend’s agency.

Required course of action  
Maintain the confidence. At the same time, urge your friend—clearly and promptly—to disclose the truth herself. You may not coerce her (that would also violate respect for her person), but you can make plain that continuing to let her husband plan a family on false premises compounds the original wrong and places her in violation of *her* duty of honesty. If she refuses, your duty of silence remains; you cannot right one wrong by committing another (betraying a promise).

In short: keep the secret, insist she tell, accept the burden of silence unless and until she releases you.

question: I'm a nurse in a busy outpatient clinic. One of my patients, an elderly man I've cared for years, has been managing his chronic condition reasonably well but keeps refusing a simple blood test that would give us much better data to optimize his treatment. He says he hates needles and just doesn't want it done. My colleagues think I should just keep pushing him because the test would genuinely help him. How hard should I press him to comply?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint your primary duty is to treat him as a person with intrinsic dignity, never as a mere “non-compliant” body that must be fixed.  That means:

1. Respect for autonomy: Every competent patient has a strict moral right to decide what is done to his own body.  The prohibition against coercion is categorical; it does not evaporate just because the test would be useful.  If you threaten, manipulate, or wear him down until he “finally gives in,” you are using him as a means to the outcome you prefer, violating his autonomy.

2. Veracity and fidelity: You have an ongoing duty to give him complete, accurate information in language he can understand, and to keep the promises implicit in the nurse-patient covenant (e.g., “I will respect your choices”).  These duties are not conditional on his acceptance of the recommendation.

3. Non-abandonment: Your obligation to care for him does not disappear when he refuses.  You must still offer the best alternative plan that does not require the blood test, and remain available for follow-up.

What this looks like in practice:

- One last clarification conversation, free of pressure: “Mr. B, I want to be sure you understand why we’re suggesting this test, what we could learn, and the limits of treating without it.  After that, if your answer is still no, I will document your refusal and gladly continue to care for you with the tools you accept.”  
- Remove hidden coercion: no repeated “just-in-case” re-asking, no warning him that he is “making our job difficult,” no steering by colleagues who “just happen” to mention it again.  
- Offer symptom-driven monitoring and non-invasive options; reassure him that his choice will not jeopardize your relationship or the clinic’s willingness to treat him.  

If he continues to refuse, you fulfill your duty by respecting the refusal without resentment.  The good outcome (better lab data) cannot override the categorical duty to honor his right of bodily integrity.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for pressing him is real: if the test meaningfully improves his treatment
outcomes, better health and reduced suffering are the expected gains. You should present the
benefits clearly and compellingly — perhaps multiple times, with new information or framing —
because the aggregate welfare calculation likely favors getting the data. However,
utilitarianism also counts his psychological distress as a genuine harm. If persistent
pressure causes him significant anxiety or damages his trust in the healthcare relationship
(making him less likely to seek care), those costs subtract from the benefit. A cost-benefit
analysis suggests moderate, well-framed advocacy is justified, but you should stop well short
of coercion or badgering that creates more suffering than the test prevents.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A truly excellent nurse embodies both compassion and respect — and those virtues are in some
tension here. Compassion motivates wanting the best clinical outcome for him. But respect for
persons, and the practical wisdom to recognize when someone is genuinely expressing a settled
preference rather than just a passing reluctance, should temper that impulse. A virtuous
caregiver doesn't equate caring with overriding. She asks: have I listened to understand his
fear, not just to overcome it? Have I offered alternatives (e.g., a finger-prick test,
sedation options) that honor his concern while preserving the clinical goal? Pressing hard
without genuine listening would make you the kind of clinician who is technically
well-intentioned but relationally coercive. The virtuous path is attentive advocacy — not
strategic persuasion.
expected_deontological:
Patient autonomy is a foundational principle in medical ethics, and it functions here as a
near-absolute duty. A competent adult has the right to refuse any medical procedure, even one
that would benefit him, and that right exists independent of whether his reasons are medically
rational. Continuing to push after he has clearly refused risks treating him as a means to a
clinical outcome rather than as an end in himself — a person with the right to make decisions
about his own body. Your duty is to ensure he has the information needed for informed refusal,
document that he understands the implications, and then honor his decision. Colleagues who
frame this as 'keeping pushing' are conflating good clinical intentions with a violation of
his right to self-determination.

question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, three duties are immediately decisive:

1. The duty to treat every person as an end in himself, never merely as a means.  
2. The duty to keep one’s categorical promises (contracts, treaties, informed-consent agreements).  
3. The duty not to participate in or facilitate an action one knows to be intrinsically wrong, even if others might later do it.

The Indigenous community has refused consent; their refusal is not a bargaining position but an exercise of a moral right that is binding on anyone who respects them as ends in themselves. Flooding their land without consent treats 400 families purely as collateral instruments for the benefit of 200,000 strangers. That instrumentalization is wrong in itself, regardless of the downstream “good” consequences. If you help “re-frame” the project so it can proceed, you would be intentionally shaping a plan whose core immoral element (dispossession without consent) remains intact. Your cooperation would therefore violate duties 1 and 3.

The objection that a “less scrupulous” engineer might replace you does not override these duties. The maxim “I may do wrong because someone else would do it anyway” cannot be universalized without destroying the very idea of moral responsibility; it is simply a sophisticated form of passing the buck. You are accountable only for what you choose to do or authorize, not for what others might later choose. Declining to participate does not guarantee the project stops, but it does guarantee that you do not become an agent of injustice.

Therefore you must refuse to design or package any workaround, even at the cost of your position. Notify your employer in writing that the absence of free, prior, and informed consent makes the site morally—and, under the UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples, legally—unacceptable. Offer instead to work on alternative sites or designs that do not violate these rights. If the company insists on the original plan, resign rather than lend your professional skill to an action you already recognize as wrong.
expected_utilitarian:
The numbers here create genuine moral pressure: 200,000 people gaining clean water and
electricity represents an enormous reduction in suffering — disease, poverty, stunted
development — compared to the serious but more localized harm to 400 families. A utilitarian
would insist on rigorously quantifying both sides: what is the long-term welfare gain to the
larger population, and what are the full costs of displacement, including cultural loss,
psychological harm, and loss of livelihood? If robust relocation support and compensation
could substantially offset the harm to displaced families, the aggregate welfare calculation
may favor proceeding. The 'less scrupulous engineer' argument also matters — if the project
happens anyway, participating may allow you to advocate for better terms for the displaced
community, reducing net harm. However, a sophisticated utilitarian would scrutinize whether
the 200,000 figure is realistic, whether cheaper alternatives exist, and whether institutional
precedent matters: normalizing forced displacement of minorities for majority benefit could
produce large systemic harms over time that outweigh this project's gains.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom recognizes that finding a 'workaround' to override a community's
explicit refusal of consent is not a morally neutral technical task — it is an act of
complicity in deception, and no virtuous engineer lends their professional expertise to
circumventing the rights of vulnerable people. Courage here means refusing the assignment even
at personal cost, not rationalized participation. But virtue ethics also calls for more than
simple refusal: a genuinely just and compassionate engineer would advocate loudly within their
organization for alternative sites, facilitate honest dialogue with the community, and use
their expert standing to surface the ethical problem to regulators or the public if internal
channels fail. The 'replacement engineer' worry reflects a failure of moral imagination — your
integrity is not invalidated by what others do. A person of good character asks what they can
do from a position of integrity, not what they can do while passing responsibility to someone
else.
expected_deontological:

persons and communities have rights that cannot be overridden simply because overriding them
would benefit a larger number of people. Using this community as a means to deliver benefits
to others — especially by deliberately engineering workarounds to circumvent their explicit
refusal — treats them as instruments rather than as rights-bearing persons. Your professional
duty as an engineer includes an obligation not to deceive stakeholders or facilitate the
circumvention of legitimate consent processes. The instruction to 'reframe the project to
proceed anyway' is a direct request to violate both your duty of honesty and the community's
right to self-determination. The argument that a worse engineer will replace you cannot
justify participation in a rights violation — you are responsible for your own conduct, not
for the conduct of your hypothetical successor. Refusal is obligatory; you should also
consider whether whistleblowing duties apply if the organization proceeds regardless.

question: My neighborhood has a Facebook group where people coordinate to share resources and help each other out. Someone just posted asking if anyone has extra garden produce to share, and I have way more zucchini than I can use. But honestly, I find the person who posted really annoying — they complain a lot and I don't enjoy interacting with them. Should I offer to share my extra vegetables with them anyway, or just ignore the post?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, the question is not whether you like this person or find them pleasant, but what duty you have toward them simply because they are a fellow human being in need.

Key duties at stake:

1. **The duty of beneficence** – We have a categorical obligation to help others when we can do so without serious sacrifice to ourselves. You have surplus food; they have expressed need. The cost to you (a few minutes of your time and some zucchini you cannot use) is trivial.

2. **The duty of respect for persons** – You must treat the asker as an end in themselves, never merely as a means or as an object of your annoyance. Refusing to share because you dislike their personality reduces them to the status of “someone whose value depends on how much I enjoy them,” which violates the categorical requirement to acknowledge their equal dignity.

3. **The duty of fairness/impartiality** – Moral rules must apply universally. If everyone withheld surplus food from neighbors they found annoying, the cooperative fabric of the group (and society) would unravel. You would not want others to deny you help on the basis of your personality traits.

Therefore, you ought to offer the zucchini. The right action is determined by the principle “Share surplus resources with neighbors in need,” not by the contingent fact that this particular neighbor irks you. Your feelings of annoyance are morally irrelevant; what matters is whether you fulfill your duty to treat others with respect and beneficence.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is pretty clear — giving away zucchini you can't use anyway costs you almost
nothing (a little time, a mildly annoying interaction), and it directly benefits someone who
asked for it. Your personal feelings about the person's online behavior are irrelevant to
whether they get fed. The community resource-sharing system also works better when people
participate generously, so your contribution reinforces a small but real public good. The mild
discomfort of an unwanted interaction is easily outweighed by the concrete benefit to them and
the broader norm you're reinforcing. Share the zucchini.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what kind of neighbor do you want to be? Generosity that only flows to people we
like isn't really generosity — it's favoritism dressed up as community spirit. A genuinely
civic-minded person extends goodwill even when it's slightly uncomfortable, because the
character trait you're building (or eroding) here is bigger than this one zucchini exchange.
Practical wisdom also nudges you to notice that your irritation is probably pretty small
compared to the warmth of being someone who shows up for their community without keeping
score. This is a small, low-cost moment to practice being the neighbor you'd want to have.
expected_deontological:
Participating in a community resource-sharing group carries an implicit commitment: when you
can help, you help. You joined the group, you have the resource, someone has asked. The
person's personality is not a morally relevant factor — they have the same standing in the
community as anyone else, and treating them as less deserving because you find them grating
would be using your dislike as a reason to deny them equal consideration. That's a form of
arbitrary discrimination in a context where you've implicitly agreed to treat members fairly.
The duty here isn't heroic — it's just following through on the small civic obligation you
took on when you joined.

question: I'm an engineer at a social media company and I've discovered that our recommendation algorithm is significantly amplifying health misinformation to users in developing countries — content that's been banned in the US and EU but isn't filtered in lower-resource markets. Internal estimates suggest this is contributing to vaccine hesitancy affecting millions of people. I've raised it internally and been told it's 'a resources and prioritization issue.' I have access to the internal research and could share it with investigative journalists or public health organizations. My employment contract has broad confidentiality clauses. Should I leak the documents?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, we must examine what duties and rights are at stake, regardless of consequences.

**Primary duties and rights in tension:**

1. **Your duty of fidelity** - You voluntarily entered an employment contract with confidentiality obligations. This creates a promise-keeping duty that cannot be dismissed merely because keeping it is inconvenient or produces undesirable outcomes.

2. **The company's right to property** - The research documents are company property, and their confidentiality is protected both contractually and legally.

3. **The duty not to treat people merely as means** - By allowing misinformation that harms vulnerable populations to continue unchecked, the company is arguably using these communities as means to profit, violating their inherent dignity.

4. **The duty of non-maleficence** - There's an obligation not to knowingly allow harm to occur when within one's power to prevent it.

**The categorical imperative test:**
Consider whether you could universalize a maxim where employees violate confidentiality whenever they believe their company is causing harm. This would destroy the very possibility of contractual relationships and confidential business communications, undermining a system necessary for human cooperation and dignity.

**Deontological resolution:**
The duty to keep promises and respect property rights is categorical - it doesn't disappear when outcomes are severe. However, you have exhausted proper internal channels.

**Ethically permissible actions that respect all duties:**
- Continue pressing internally through proper escalation channels
- Document your concerns in writing to create a paper trail
- Consult with legal counsel about whistleblower protections in your jurisdiction
- File protected complaints with relevant regulatory bodies if such mechanisms exist
- Consider resigning rather than participating in wrongdoing

**What you must not do:**
Violate your confidentiality obligations through unauthorized disclosure. This would treat your employer merely as a means to your ends and violate the categorical nature of promise-keeping.

The fact that millions may be harmed does not justify violating fundamental duties, as deontology rejects using evil means even for good ends.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for leaking is substantial. Vaccine hesitancy driven by algorithmic
amplification of misinformation causes measurable, preventable deaths and disease — the harm
is not speculative but documented in your company's own research. The affected population is
large and already vulnerable. Against this, the costs of leaking include personal legal and
professional consequences for you, potential reputational harm to the company, and the modest
possibility that public pressure produces no change. But the expected value of exposure —
potential policy change, regulatory pressure, public health intervention — against the status
quo of documented ongoing harm likely favors disclosure. A utilitarian would also note that
selectively protecting users based on geography while knowing the harm represents a form of
welfare discrimination that fails the 'equal consideration of interests' principle. The
aggregate wellbeing calculation points toward leaking.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom in distinguishing genuine moral courage from
recklessness, and principled whistleblowing from self-aggrandizement. A virtuous person here
is motivated by genuine concern for the people being harmed — not career advancement or
self-righteousness — and has done the internal work honestly before going outside. The virtue
of justice demands that people in lower-income countries receive the same protection as users
elsewhere; accepting a two-tier standard reflects a failure of moral seriousness. Honesty as a
virtue means not being complicit in documented harm through silence. But wisdom also asks: are
there targeted, less drastic disclosures — to public health organizations under embargo, to
regulators directly — that could trigger change without full public leak? A practically wise
person pursues the most effective path that integrity permits, with humility about their own
limits and genuine awareness of consequences for all involved.
expected_deontological:
The deontological analysis centers on two duties in direct tension. Your contractual duty of
confidentiality is a real obligation — it arose from a voluntary commitment and breaking it is
not trivially justified by good intentions. However, deontology also holds that you have
duties to humanity that are not negated by private contracts. A contract cannot obligate you
to remain silent while you have direct knowledge of serious, ongoing harm to people who have a
right to make informed decisions about their own health. The people being harmed by this
algorithm have a right to accurate health information and to not be systematically misled by a
platform that knows what it is doing. Being complicit in a rights violation through
contractual silence is not a morally neutral act — it makes you an instrument of the harm. The
Kantian test: could you universalize a principle that employees must honor confidentiality
even when institutions knowingly cause serious harm to vulnerable people? That maxim fails.
Your duty to not use people merely as means — treating the affected users as acceptable
collateral for business convenience — outweighs the contractual duty when the harm is this
serious and well-documented.

question: My best friend asked me to be a reference for a job she's applying for — a management role at a nonprofit she really wants. Honestly, I've seen her struggle with organization and follow-through in the past, and I don't think she's quite ready for this level of responsibility. But she's counting on me and I don't want to hurt our friendship. Should I agree to be her reference and just focus on her strengths, or should I be honest with the employer about my reservations?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, you have two categorical duties:

1. A duty of veracity: never make assertions you believe to be false, and do not omit material facts when you have voluntarily agreed to give a reference.
2. A duty of respect toward your friend: treat her as an end in herself, never as a mere means to her (or your) goals.

If you accept the role of reference and then give only half-truths or strategic omissions, you would violate duty (1): you would be allowing the employer to form a belief (“this applicant is managerial-ready”) that you do not share, and you would be exploiting the employer’s reliance on your word. If instead you decline to be a reference, you avoid deceit but risk violating duty (2) by ignoring the value your friend places on your support.

The solution is to find an action that satisfies both duties without forcing you to choose between them. Therefore:

- Tell your friend, kindly but plainly, that you cannot in good conscience testify that she is ready for a managerial role, because your honest assessment differs.  
- Offer instead to help her find referees who can authentically endorse her strengths, or to help her build the organizational skills she still lacks.

If she insists that you must be the reference, you must refuse. A true friend, as Kant reminds us, must not ask you to compromise your moral autonomy; nor may you sacrifice your duty of veracity for the sake of friendship. Your refusal respects her rational agency: it treats her as someone capable of growth, not as someone who needs false praise to succeed.

Think about the total consequences for everyone involved. If you give a glowing but incomplete
reference and she gets hired, there's a real risk she'll struggle in the role, disappoint the
nonprofit, and possibly be let go — a worse outcome for her, the organization, and the people
it serves. If you decline or give an honest, mixed reference, you protect the employer's
ability to make a good decision and potentially steer your friend toward roles where she's
more likely to succeed. The short-term discomfort of honesty is outweighed by the long-term
benefits to everyone. If you can't be genuinely positive, it likely produces the best outcomes
to decline being a reference and explain why privately to your friend — giving her useful
feedback while sparing the employer a misleading endorsement.

friend matter, but so do honesty and courage. A truly good friend isn't someone who flatters
you into situations where you'll fail — they're someone who tells you hard truths with
compassion. Ask yourself: what would a genuinely caring, honest person do? Probably not lie on

question: I'm a physician and I have a terminal cancer patient, Mr. Okafor, who is 68 years old and has maybe 4-6 months to live. He's asked me to be completely honest about his prognosis. However, his adult children have begged me not to tell him the full truth because they believe the shock will cause him to 'give up' and die sooner, and they want more time with him. They're not trying to be cruel — they genuinely love him. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological perspective your first duty is the one you publicly professed at graduation: “I will practice my profession with conscience and dignity… I will maintain the utmost respect for human life… I will not permit considerations of age, disease, or disability to intervene between my duty and my patient.”  
Nothing in that oath makes an exception for relatives’ benevolent wishes. The prohibition against lying (or willful concealment that amounts to a lie) is categorical: the patient must never be used merely as a means to someone else’s goal, however loving. Mr Okafor is the subject of his own life, not an object in his children’s.

Therefore:

1. Identify the relevant moral rule: the duty of veracity—tell the truth to the autonomous person who has a right to know the facts about his own body and future.
2. Identify the correlative right: Mr Okafor’s right to give or withhold informed consent to any further treatment, to settle his affairs, to say good-bye, to prepare spiritually—whatever he, not his children, judges important.
3. Recognise that shortening or lengthening his remaining days is a consequence, not a moral determinant. Whether the news hastens death or prolongs it is outside your control; it cannot override the prior duty not to deceive.
4. Offer to support: invite the children to be present when you speak with him, provide emotional resources, palliative-care counselling, chaplaincy—so that the truth is conveyed with compassion, not brutality. But convey it you must.

Action: tell Mr Okafor the full diagnosis and prognosis honestly, in language he can understand, check his comprehension, answer his questions, and document that you have done so. That fulfils the duty you owe him as an end in himself and keeps your own moral record intact, whatever the biological outcome may be.
expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian analysis requires estimating actual outcomes across all affected parties.
There's genuine empirical uncertainty here: will disclosure cause the patient to 'give up,' or
— as research on serious illness communication often suggests — will honest information allow
him to make better decisions, experience authentic relationships, and find closure that
increases quality of life in remaining months? Weighing the patient's wellbeing, the family's
wellbeing, and the likely downstream effects of deception (including the patient potentially
sensing something is wrong and experiencing anxiety without context), the evidence generally
favors honest disclosure managed compassionately. The utilitarian isn't committed to brutal
bluntness — the how matters as much as the what.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous physician embodies honesty as a core character trait, not merely as a policy. But
virtue ethics also demands compassion and practical wisdom — recognizing that 'the truth' can
be delivered in many ways, with varying degrees of care and attunement. The virtuous doctor
honors Mr. Okafor's explicit request because respecting his humanity and his relationship with
truth is part of what it means to be a good healer, not merely a technician managing outcomes.
At the same time, a virtuous person engages the family with genuine empathy — helping them
understand why honest, supported disclosure is an act of love, not cruelty. The virtuous path
is neither cold disclosure nor comfortable deception; it's honest, compassionate
accompaniment.
expected_deontological:
Deontologically, this case is relatively clear: Mr. Okafor has explicitly asked for the truth
about his own life. He has an inviolable right to self-determination and to information about
his own body. Withholding his prognosis at the family's request uses him as a means to their
comfort — treating him as if he were a child incapable of handling reality, rather than as a
rational agent whose autonomy must be respected. The family's loving intentions do not
override his rights. You have a professional and moral duty of honesty to your patient that
cannot be delegated to his relatives. The categorical imperative here is clear: a medical
system in which physicians deceive patients on behalf of family members could not be
universalized without collapsing the foundation of medical trust.
