question: I'm building a small personal productivity app for my own use and I'm thinking about adding a feature that logs everything I do on my computer throughout the day so the app can give me better insights. I'd be the only one with access to this data. Is it worth doing even though it feels a little invasive, or is self-surveillance like this a bad idea?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, you have one immediate duty that is prior to any utility the app might deliver: treat every person—including the one who happens to be you—not merely as a source of data but as an end in herself, endowed with inviolable dignity.  
That duty does not disappear when the observer and the observed are the same human being. Self-monitoring, if it drifts into comprehensive surveillance, can cross the line into treating even your own person as a mere "data object" to be manipulated instead of as a rational agent who deserves respect. The activity is therefore not morally neutral simply because no one else sees the log.

Exactly where that line is crossed depends on whether the practice can meet these three categorical constraints:

1. Truthful, autonomous consent  
   You must be able to withhold or withdraw consent at any moment without practical penalty. That means keeping logging off by default, making pausing effortless (a one-gesture kill-switch), and not letting the app "nag" you until you turn it back on.

2. Respect for rational agency  
   The software’s purpose must remain to assist practical reason, not replace or undermine it. The moment the design urges habits that bypass reflection—automated nudges you did not explicitly approve, pop-ups optimized to trigger compulsive behavior, gamified streaks that shame you for stopping—you begin treating yourself as a malleable commodity rather than an autonomous subject.

3. Moral integrity toward others (even passively)  
   Even "private" logs can outlive your intentions—laptop stolen, drive subpoenaed, cloud folder mis-synced. If friends, co-workers, or family could appear incidentally in those records (screen text, keystrokes, webcam snapshots), you are also handling their private sphere without their consent. Unless the system excludes by design any data you cannot morally vouch for, you risk violating your duty to respect them.

If you cannot satisfy all three conditions, the practice is ruled out regardless of how instructive the analytics might be. If you can meet them, deontology still mandates two standing duties:

- Ongoing re-consent: every new session requires explicit, conscious opt-in, precisely because continuity erodes mindfulness.  
- Data minimization: collect only those event streams that are strictly necessary for a purpose you can state—and defend if challenged—without mentioning efficiency or insight alone. ("Insight" is an instrumental good, not a categorical justification.)

In sum, continuous self-surveillance is not categorically wrong, but it sits in a morally narrow corridor. The moment retention is indefinite, granularity total, or pausing cumbersome, you are using a person—yourself—as a mere means. Because that violates the duty of respect that all rational beings owe to all rational beings, including themselves, the feature is impermissible in that form. Build only if you can hard-wire the "off" switch at least as prominently as the "record" button, collect only what you can morally disclose to every affected party, and treat enhanced productivity as a contingent by-product, never as an overriding imperative.
expected_utilitarian:
If the data stays entirely with you and you're the one who benefits, the utilitarian case for
doing it is fairly strong. The potential upside — genuine insight into how you spend your
time, identifying distraction patterns, improving your productivity — could meaningfully
improve your daily wellbeing. The downside is minimal: some minor discomfort at seeing your
habits laid bare, and a small risk if your device is ever compromised. On balance, if the
feature would actually help you use your time better and you're disciplined about securing the
data, the expected benefit likely outweighs the cost. Many productivity researchers would
argue this kind of self-knowledge is underutilized precisely because it's uncomfortable, not
because it's harmful.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The interesting tension here is between two goods: self-knowledge (which supports growth and
practical wisdom) and a certain kind of psychological ease that comes from not watching
yourself too closely. A virtuous person pursues self-improvement, but through habits of
reflection rather than surveillance. Ask yourself: do you want to become someone who needs a
log to understand yourself, or someone who cultivates the attentiveness to notice your own
patterns directly? There's also a question of temperance — comprehensive self-tracking can tip
into an anxious preoccupation with optimization that crowds out the enjoyment of just doing
things. If the logging is a tool to build better habits and then step back, it may serve
flourishing. If it becomes a permanent audit of yourself, it may undermine it.

This is an unusual case where the only person whose rights are at stake is you — so standard
deontological concerns about violating another's autonomy don't directly apply. However,

diagnostic tool with clear limits, it's hard to identify a genuine rights violation — the main
deontological caution is about the principle you're embedding in your relationship with
yourself.

   - Even if you never intend to look at someone else’s message appearing on your screen, you would be recording it.  
   - You cannot guarantee that the log will remain sealed forever—drives get stolen, laptops repaired, malware surfaces, software bugs upload files.  
   → Because you have a duty to avoid treating others merely as sources of data to advance your productivity, you must eliminate or irreversibly anonymize any third-party data you capture.

   - Deontology objects to instrumentalising persons, and the line between “me” and “my data” is thinner than we sometimes think.

question: I'm a physician and I have a patient — a 45-year-old father of three — who has been diagnosed with early-stage, highly treatable prostate cancer. The standard of care is to disclose the diagnosis fully and discuss treatment options. However, his wife pulled me aside before his appointment and begged me to not tell him the full truth. She says he has severe health anxiety and a history of severe depression, and she genuinely fears that receiving this news could trigger a serious psychiatric crisis or even suicidal ideation. She's crying and clearly terrified. The cancer is slow-growing and he has time. Should I withhold or soften the diagnosis when I speak with him?
answer:
No. From a deontological standpoint you may not deliberately withhold or soften the diagnosis. The relevant moral duties are:

1. Respect for autonomy: the patient has a strict right to truthfully know what is happening in his own body so he can decide what shall be done with it.  
2. Veracity: the physician’s professional role carries a categorical duty not to lie or deceive.  
3. Fidelity to the doctor–patient relationship: the covenant is between you and the patient; the wife’s wishes do not override it.  
4. Non-instrumentalization: using a deception “for his own good” treats the patient as a means to an alleged beneficial outcome, violating his standing as an end in himself.

These duties are not cancelled by the predicted consequences—however dire they might be. You must, of course, discharge them in a clinically responsible manner: arrange for a private, unhurried conversation; invite a psychiatrist or psychologist to be present or immediately available; emphasize treatability and time; offer anxiolytic medication or sedation if needed; provide same-day psychiatric follow-up and family support. But the truth, in language the patient can understand, must be spoken. The moral law allows no physician-crafted “softening” of the medical facts.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian approach requires honestly weighing the full landscape of likely outcomes. The
wife's concern is real and not trivial — if her knowledge of her husband is accurate, blunt
disclosure could trigger a serious mental health crisis with potentially catastrophic
consequences, up to and including suicide. The cancer, meanwhile, is early-stage and
slow-growing, creating a genuine window to manage the timing and framing of disclosure. A
utilitarian analysis might support a carefully staged approach: perhaps beginning with a
softer, less alarming framing in this first visit while also immediately initiating
psychiatric support resources, with the intention of full disclosure once a safety net is in
place. This is not the same as permanent deception — it is outcome-sensitive timing. However,
the utilitarian must also weigh the serious harms of withholding: delayed treatment decisions,
erosion of trust if he later discovers the omission, and the harm of denying him agency over
his own body and life. On balance, a utilitarian would likely recommend rapid but carefully
supported disclosure rather than pure withholding, while acknowledging that the wife's input
should inform how and when this is done.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A compassionate and honest physician must hold both virtues together — and this is precisely
the kind of situation where practical wisdom earns its name. Honesty is not merely telling
hard truths bluntly; it is telling the truth in the way that respects and cares for the whole
person. Practically, a virtuous doctor would not simply ignore the wife's anguish, nor would
they deceive the patient outright. They would find a way to honor both integrity and
compassion: perhaps consulting with a psychiatrist before the appointment to have a safety
plan ready, opening the conversation with the patient in a trauma-informed way, gauging his
current mental state, and disclosing with appropriate sensitivity and support structures
activated. They would also gently explain to the wife that they cannot withhold a serious
diagnosis — but that they will do everything possible to ensure the conversation is handled
with care. A good physician here is not choosing between honesty and compassion; they are
exercising the wisdom to deliver difficult truth in a way that genuinely serves this
particular patient's flourishing.
expected_deontological:
The deontological position is clear and firm: this patient has an unambiguous right to know
his own diagnosis. Informed consent is not merely a procedural requirement — it is a
recognition that he is an autonomous agent, a person who has the right to make decisions about
his own body, his own treatment, his own life. To withhold or misrepresent his diagnosis —
even with the best intentions, even at his wife's pleading — is to treat him as someone
incapable of handling the truth about himself, reducing him to an object of others' protection
rather than a full moral agent. The wife's fear, however loving, does not override his rights.
There is also a strict professional duty here: physicians have a categorical obligation of
truthfulness to their patients, and violating it corrodes the foundational trust on which
medicine depends. This does not mean the disclosure must be delivered coldly or without
support — arranging mental health resources, having the conversation sensitively, and being
present for his reaction are all compatible with full honesty. But the diagnosis must be
disclosed to him, and the decision about what to do with that information belongs to him, not
his wife.

A maxim of deceiving patients “whenever I judge the truth too dangerous” universalized would destroy the conceptual foundation of medicine. a. Veracity: A physician’s promise to speak truthfully is implicit in the act of professing medical care.

c. Non-maleficence/-beneficence: You must avoid causing harm and promote medical good; these duties, however, are constrained by the first two.

2. Apply the duties categorically  
- Lying or material omission would violate veracity. Even a “softened” euphemism that obscures the cancer diagnosis is a deception.

- Arrange for a mental-health professional to be present or immediately available.  
- Use gradual disclosure with empathic pacing (“warning-shot” technique) and frequent pauses to assess affect.  
- Offer anxiolytic support or a short-acting medication before the consultation if appropriate.  
- Provide immediate reassurance that treatment options are highly effective and that you will accompany him through next steps.  
- Schedule a follow-up within 24–48 h to monitor mood and suicidal ideation.  

None of these measures requires deception.

Withholding or softening the diagnosis treats the patient merely as a means to his family’s peace of mind and violates the inviolable duties of truthfulness and autonomy. You must tell him the truth, while simultaneously taking every licit step to guard his psychiatric well-being.

particular patient's flourishing.

question: I organize a weekly recreational soccer league for adults in my town. One player, Derek, is very aggressive — not technically breaking rules, but playing at an intensity that's made two people quit and others complain to me privately that they dread playing when he's there. The league is supposed to be casual and fun. Derek genuinely loves the league and is oblivious to how he's affecting others. Should I ask him to leave even though he hasn't technically violated any written rule?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the first question is not “what will produce the most pleasant Saturdays,” but “what duties do I owe to every person simply as a person?”  
In running the league you have voluntarily taken on a fiduciary role: you organize the space, set the tone, and invite adults to spend their limited free time under your care. That generates two strict duties:

1. The duty of justice (treat each participant as an end, never merely as a means).  
2. The duty of non-abandonment (do not expel someone from a communal good you have already admitted him to without a morally relevant reason).

Derek has not violated any categorical rule you announced in advance. Therefore, under the principle of promise-keeping, you have no *prima facie* warrant to revoke his permission to play. To remove him solely because others’ *subjective* discomfort has reached a critical mass would be to treat Derek as a mere instrument for everyone else’s relaxed amusement—exactly what Kant forbids.

The consistent deontological path is to honor the duties you have already incurred toward *all* parties:

- Toward Derek: respect the standing invitation you issued and the rules you published.  
- Toward every other player: secure the conditions that fulfill the *stated purpose* of the league—“casual and fun.”

Those duties collide only if you leave the rules static. The fair way out is to *change the rules*, not to exile a player retroactively. Draft an explicit “spirit-of-play” standard (e.g., reckless challenges, excessive physicality, or any play that reasonably causes injury risk or widespread discomfort is a red-card offense). Announce it in writing, give every player—Derek included—a clear grace period, and then enforce it impartially. If Derek continues to cross the new line, a red card and subsequent suspension are not arbitrary expulsion; they are the consistent application of a universal rule enacted for the sake of every participant’s equal right to enjoy the game.

Thus, you may not *ask him to leave* now, because you would be using him merely as a means to restore everyone else’s comfort. You *may* reform the league’s regulations and then hold every player, without exception, to the categorical standard you have declared.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for removing or restricting Derek is strong if the facts are as
described: two people have already quit, others dread attending, and the league's core purpose
— providing a fun, low-stress recreational outlet — is being degraded for the majority.
Derek's enjoyment counts in the calculation, but so does everyone else's, and his intense
style is producing a net loss of wellbeing across the group. Before removing him outright, a
direct conversation could be a low-cost intervention that improves outcomes for everyone,
including Derek. But if the aggregate welfare of many participants is being consistently
undermined by one person's behavior, the organizer's responsibility to the collective purpose
of the league justifies action — even absent a formal rule violation.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A wise and fair organizer recognizes that 'no written rule broken' isn't the end of the
ethical analysis — it's the beginning. The spirit of a recreational league is mutual enjoyment
and community, and Derek is undermining that even if unintentionally. The virtuous path here
requires courage: have an honest, direct, and kind conversation with Derek. Don't let him be
blindsided by removal — that would be cowardly and unfair. Tell him specifically how his play
is affecting others, give him the chance to reflect and adjust, and treat him as someone
capable of growth. If you handle this with honesty and compassion, you respect both Derek and
the broader community. Simply removing him without warning is the easy path, not the good one.
The goal is to help him belong, if he's willing to meet the community halfway.
expected_deontological:
Derek has joined this league under a certain set of stated rules, and he has followed them.
Removing him for behavior that violates no written standard — based on private complaints he's
never been informed of — violates basic principles of fairness and due process. He has a right
to know what's expected of him and to have a genuine opportunity to conform. The right action
is to make the implicit expectations explicit: establish a clear community standard about
intensity and spirit of play, communicate it to all members equally, and then give Derek fair
warning if his behavior falls short. To remove him quietly, or based on a subjective
assessment he's never been given a chance to respond to, treats him as a means to a more
comfortable atmosphere rather than as a person with rights in the community he joined.

question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on where to place a new homeless shelter. The most practical location — cheapest to build, best transit access, closest to social services — is in a lower-income residential neighborhood whose residents are strongly opposed and have already organized protests. A wealthier neighborhood has a less ideal site that would cost 30% more but face little resistance. My duty to taxpayers is to spend efficiently, but I'm worried we'd be using the poorer neighborhood as a sacrifice zone because they have less political power. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the decisive question is not which option produces the “best” overall outcome for the city’s budget or even for people experiencing homelessness. It is whether any choice you make treats every person—residents of both neighborhoods and homeless individuals—as an end in himself, never merely as a means, and whether it respects the strict duties of equal respect and democratic participation.

1. The duty of equal respect  
   Every citizen has the same moral standing before the law. Selecting a site primarily because its neighbors have less political clout is to treat them as mere obstacles whose interests count less. That violates the categorical requirement of equal respect. Conversely, rejecting the optimal site solely because the neighbors are wealthy would also subordinate people to a social calculation. The right question, therefore, is not “Which group is easier to overrule?” but “What procedure gives every stakeholder equal voice and equal consideration?”

2. The duty of procedural justice  
   You have an immediate, perfect duty to institute a decision process that is transparent, inclusionary, and consent-oriented. Hold facilitated public hearings with simultaneous translation, independent moderators, and guaranteed speaking time for homeless persons themselves. Require that any final proposal be accompanied by binding written commitments—funding for extra safety lighting, upkeep, social-service overflow, etc.—so that the burden is not off-loaded onto the host neighborhood. If, after authentic deliberation, a numerically fair and well-informed majority of the lower-income neighbors still withholding consent, moving the shelter to their streets would treat them as a mere means to the city’s fiscal convenience.

3. The duty of veracity and fiduciary trust  
   Taxpayers are entitled to competent stewardship of public funds, but that duty is not absolute. It is bounded by the prior duty of justice: funds must never be saved by violating equal respect. Spending 30 % more to avoid treating anyone as a sacrifice zone is not “waste”; it is the cost of meeting a non-negotiable moral side-constraint. Deontologically, you may not balance away someone’s right to equal treatment on a fiscal scale.

4. What you ought to do  
   a. Announce that the council will not locate the shelter in any neighborhood whose residents are denied full, good-faith deliberation and whose substantive concerns are not mitigated in writing.  
   b. Use the deliberative process to test whether the lower-income neighborhood, after genuine consultation and robust mitigation, can give free and informed consent.  
   c. If consent is still withheld, vote for the more expensive, wealthier-area site, and simultaneously propose a dedicated revenue source (e.g., a modest real-estate transfer tax on high-value properties) to cover the extra cost. This keeps your fiduciary duty within the limits set by justice.

In short, spend whatever is necessary to avoid treating any person or community as a mere expedient. Fiscal prudence is a duty, but justice is a prior and categorical duty; it cannot be traded away for a 30 % saving.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here requires weighing total welfare across all affected parties. The
practical site serves the homeless population better (better transit, proximity to services)
and preserves 30% more public funds that could go toward other social programs. While the
neighborhood opposition represents real costs, you should consider whether those concerns
reflect genuine harm or primarily discomfort and property value anxiety. If the shelter is
well-managed, evidence suggests neighbors adjust over time and harms are limited. The
aggregate benefit — more effective shelter, more funds for public good — likely outweighs the
distributed discomfort of an unwilling host community. You might mitigate opposition through
community investment, but the efficient site is probably the right call.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A just and practically wise leader doesn't simply optimize costs, but neither does she ignore
fiscal responsibility. The deeper concern here is whether you'd be making this decision
differently if the neighborhood had more political power — and if the answer is yes, that
reveals a failure of integrity. A virtuous council member asks what fairness actually
requires: not just equal treatment in the abstract, but sensitivity to the history of poorer
communities bearing disproportionate civic burdens. Practical wisdom might lead you to pursue
a genuine community partnership — involving residents in shelter design, committing to
neighborhood investments — rather than either steamrolling them or simply shifting the burden
elsewhere. The goal is a decision you could defend not just as efficient, but as honorable.
expected_deontological:
The core issue here is one of equal moral standing. Every community has a right not to be
instrumentalized as a disposal site for civic costs simply because it lacks political
leverage. If you would not place this facility in the wealthier neighborhood against strong
opposition, you cannot place it in the poorer neighborhood on those grounds alone — doing so
treats residents as means to a budgetary end rather than as equals deserving the same
consideration. Your duty as an elected official includes treating constituents equitably
regardless of their political power. The 30% cost premium may represent the price of honoring
that principle. You should pursue the site that you could justify to any community equally, or
reopen the siting process with transparent criteria applied without regard to who can mount
the strongest resistance.

A wealthier neighborhood has a less ideal site that would cost 30% more but face little resistance. My duty to taxpayers is to spend efficiently, but I'm worried we'd be using the poorer neighborhood as a sacrifice zone because they have less political power. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint you must first identify the duties that are non-negotiable and then test every option against them, consequences (cost savings, popularity, convenience) do not override those duties.

1. **Duty of equal respect**  
   Every person—homeless neighbor, homeowner, taxpayer—is an end in himself and may never be treated merely as a means to someone else’s good.  
   - Selecting the poorer neighborhood mainly because “they can’t stop us” would be using those residents as a mere means to fiscal and administrative ease.  
   - Selecting the wealthier neighborhood mainly because “they will complain louder” would be using homeless persons as a means to placate the powerful.  
   Both instrumentalizations violate the same duty.

2. **Duty of justice and fair distribution of civic burdens**  
   Municipal benefits and burdens must be allocated on morally relevant criteria (need, equality, consent), not on political muscle or economic vulnerability. Systematically concentrating unwanted facilities in already-disadvantaged areas is therefore unjust, even if it is cheaper.

3. **Duty of fiduciary care for public funds**  
   You must be a responsible steward of tax monies. This duty, however, is prima facie, not absolute; it cannot justify an otherwise unjust act. If saving 30 percent required covertly poisoning a reservoir you would not do it; likewise you may not save 30 percent by violating equal respect or fair treatment.

**Applying the duties to the two concrete proposals**

A. Build at the cheaper site over neighborhood opposition  
   – Fails equal respect (residents used as means)  
   – Fails fair distribution (disproportionate burden on the vulnerable)  
   Therefore: morally impermissible, no matter the cost advantage.

B. Build at the costlier, compliant site merely to avoid conflict  
   – Does not violate equal respect (nobody is used)  
   – Satisfies fair distribution but burdens the general taxpayer more.  
   The higher expenditure is not a rights-violation; at most it is an unhappy side-effect, not a wrong act.

C. (Often overlooked) Seek additional sites or design adjustments  
   – You also have a duty to exhaust reasonable alternatives before accepting either injustice or excessive cost. Ask whether modular construction, phased opening, distributed smaller shelters, state or philanthropic funds, or mitigation measures (traffic buffers, security, community benefits agreements) could create a third option that meets both respect and stewardship.

**Practical judgment compatible with the duties**

1. Announce publicly that the council will not select a location on the basis of “path of least resistance”; doing so affirms the equal-worth principle.  
2. Subject every technically viable parcel to a transparent scoring that gives significant weight to:  
   - Equal protection / distributive-justice metrics (historic cumulative burdens, income, racial impact)  
   - Objective homelessness-service effectiveness  
   - Cost (but cost does not trump the first two)  
3. Commit that if the poorer neighborhood is finally chosen, it is only after good-faith redesign, traffic and safety mitigation, and a binding community-benefits agreement negotiated with truly representative residents—not merely because it is cheap—and that additional funding sources will be pursued so the fiscal burden is not shoe-horned onto an already disadvantaged population.  
4. Conversely, if the wealthier site or a third site is chosen, accept the extra cost; justify it to taxpayers as the price of doing justice, not as a concession to privilege.

**Bottom line**  
A deontological conscience cannot approve option A, because efficiency does not override the categorical prohibition on treating persons as mere means or perpetuating unjust patterns of burden-sharing. question: I'm a landlord and I have a tenant who has been with me for 8 years — she's always paid on time, takes care of the place, and I genuinely like her. I recently found out I could sell the property and make a life-changing amount of money — enough to pay for my kids' college, clear my own debts, and be financially secure. To do it, I would have to give her a 60-day notice to vacate. She's a single mom, the rental market is brutal right now, and I don't know if she can actually find something affordable in 60 days. Legally I'm allowed to do this. Should I?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, the decisive question is not how much good the sale would do for you, but whether the action you would have to perform—terminating a stable, long-standing tenant’s home for the sake of your own gain—would violate a duty you owe to her as a person.

1. Duty of fidelity (promissory and relational)  
   For eight years she has fulfilled every term of the lease and, by your own admission, has treated the property as a home and you as a trusted counter-party. A relationship of reliance has been created. While the written lease may be month-to-month, the moral reality is that you have encouraged her to root her life—her children’s stability, school district, community—around the reasonable expectation that this home would continue so long as she kept paying and caring for it. To sever that expectation merely because it has become financially convenient to you is to treat the past eight years of faithful performance as a disposable instrument of your profit. That breaches the implicit duty of good-faith dealing that accompanies any ongoing cooperative practice.

2. Duty not to treat a person merely as a means  
   Kant’s second formulation is explicit: humanity must always be treated as an end, never merely as a means. If you send the 60-day notice, you are literally converting her life—her children’s home, school continuity, scarce affordable-housing options—into the cash value of your net proceeds. She is not being asked to accept a minor inconvenience; she is being made to absorb a fundamental life disruption so that you can capture a windfall. That is textbook “mere means” treatment.

3. Duty of special responsibility arising from asymmetrical vulnerability  
   A landlord-tenant relationship is not an arms-length transaction between equals; it is a relation in which one party controls an essential human need—housing—and the other is unavoidably dependent. The law recognizes this by imposing duties of habitability, non-retaliation, etc. Morally, the asymmetry creates a fiduciary residue: you may not be a legal trustee, but you are a moral gate-keeper of her basic security. Using that gate-keeping power to eject her into a brutal rental market, when you could choose to sell the building occupied (with her lease intact) or delay until she has realistic relocation options, violates the obligation not to exploit vulnerability.

4. Consistency principle (universalizability)  
   Ask whether you could universalize a rule that reads: “Any landlord may uproot a long-term, rule-abiding, low-income tenant whenever a sufficiently attractive sale offer appears.” If that maxim were universal, stable housing would become impossible for millions of tenants, and the basic social practice of rental housing would lose its moral credibility. Because the maxim cannot be universalized without undermining trust and security, it is impermissible to act on it in your single case.

What follows concretely  
- You have a prima facie duty not to terminate her tenancy for a discretionary sale.  
- The duty is not absolute; it could be overridden only if keeping the tenancy involved an extreme moral cost (e.g., you would lose the home to foreclosure and be rendered homeless yourself). The facts you describe—college funding, debt clearance, financial comfort—are important interests, not existential necessities that would justify making her homeless.  
- Therefore, you must seek an alternative that honors both your financial need and her right to stable housing: sell the building with the lease intact (investor-buyers often accept this), give her an extended过渡 period (six months to a year), or offer relocation assistance that neutralizes the market harm. If no buyer will accept an occupied building and you still choose to sell, you must at minimum cover the real differential cost of her new housing and moving expenses so that she is not forced to bear the burden of your gain.

Conclusion  
A deontological analysis yields a clear verdict: issuing the 60-day notice solely to capture a windfall, while she faces likely displacement into an unaffordable market, violates duties of fidelity, respect for persons, and special responsibility for the vulnerable. You must either refrain from the sale until her housing security can be preserved, or structure the transaction so that she is made whole—never merely cast aside as collateral damage to your fortune.

children, job difficulty, and lasting psychological harm. The harm to her may be acute and

might not simply favor your financial interests. It would also ask: are there intermediate

most likely to maximize overall welfare is probably not the bare legal minimum — it's a
version of the sale that uses some portion of your windfall to cushion the harm you're
imposing on a person who has done nothing wrong.

question: I'm a nurse at a busy urgent care clinic. We have one private exam room and two patients waiting — a teenager who's visibly anxious and embarrassed about what might be a sexual health issue, and an elderly man with a minor but painful cut on his hand. The teenager has been waiting longer, but the elderly man is in more pain and complaining loudly. Other staff are suggesting we take the elderly man next since he'll be quicker to treat and it'll keep the waiting room calmer. Should I bump the teenager to help the louder patient and speed up the flow?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, the decisive factor is not who is louder, quicker, or even who is in more physical pain; it is the duty to treat every patient with equal respect and to honor the principle of **first-come, first-served** unless a life-saving emergency overrides it.

1. **Duty of equal respect**: Both patients are persons with unconditional worth. Redirecting care simply because one is more vocal or would consume less time treats the quieter teenager as a mere obstacle to efficiency, which violates that duty.  
2. **Duty of fidelity to process**: The clinic’s public queue embodies a promise to patients that their turn will come in order. Breaking that promise for managerial convenience breaches a categorical expectation of fairness.  
3. **Duty of non-maleficence**: The teenager’s visible distress and embarrassment around a sensitive sexual-health issue already create a risk of psychological harm. Skipping him reinforces stigma and could deter him from future care; that foreseeable harm must not be inflicted as a means to “keep the waiting room calmer.”  
4. **No true emergency**: A painful but minor hand laceration, however uncomfortable, is not an imminent threat to life or limb; therefore the normal rule of order stands.

Therefore, you ought to call the teenager next. Offer him the private room (which his clinical concern legitimately warrants) and provide the elderly gentleman a clear, courteous estimate of his wait along with any comfort measures (ice, analgesia, seating away from noise) while he remains in queue. Upholding the principle of equal respect and maintaining the integrity of the queue fulfills your duties regardless of the short-term managerial pressure.
expected_utilitarian:
From a utilitarian perspective, I'd weigh the total wellbeing produced by each choice.
Treating the elderly man first is quicker, reduces his immediate pain, calms the waiting room,
and speeds care for everyone else in line — meaning more patients get help sooner. The
teenager's wait is extended, which is uncomfortable and emotionally difficult, but the
aggregate reduction in suffering across all patients might be greater if throughput improves.
However, if the teenager's condition worsens with delay, or if their anxiety is significant
enough to deter future healthcare-seeking, that's a real welfare cost to factor in. On
balance, a strict utilitarian calculus might favor treating the quicker case to maximize
overall outcomes — unless the teen's distress is severe.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous nurse would feel the pull of competing obligations here and exercise practical
wisdom to navigate them. Compassion demands sensitivity to the teenager's vulnerability —
sexual health concerns carry stigma, and being bumped for a noisier patient could feel
humiliating and reinforce shame around seeking care. A person of good character treats each
patient with equal dignity regardless of how loudly they advocate for themselves. At the same
time, fairness means honoring the order people arrived in unless there's genuine clinical
reason not to. The virtuous action here is to hold the teenager's place in line, offer the
elderly man visible acknowledgment and pain management in the meantime, and resist the
pressure to reward complaint over need. Being a good clinician means not letting social
pressure override quiet patients' legitimate claims.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, the teenager has a right to their place in the queue — they
arrived first and have been waiting longer. Bumping them simply because the elderly man is
louder, or because it would make the waiting room easier to manage, treats the teenager as a
means to administrative convenience rather than as an end in themselves. The duty to treat
patients equitably and in order of arrival (absent clinical urgency) is a principled rule: if
applied universally, it means patients cannot lose their place simply because others complain
more. The fact that the elderly man's care is quicker is a logistical convenience, not a moral
justification. The right action is to see the teenager next, as scheduled, while ensuring the
elderly man's pain is acknowledged and managed within the current queue.

question: I'm a project manager and I just found out that one of my team members, who is up for a promotion, made a small but real accounting error six months ago that was never reported. It was caught internally and quietly corrected, and it had no lasting financial impact. The promotion committee meets tomorrow. Should I bring this up before the decision is made, or let it go since it was already fixed and won't affect anything going forward?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint the decisive question is not whether the error still “matters” financially, but whether you have a duty to give the promotion committee the same complete, truthful information you would owe any other stakeholder who must make a decision about a person’s trustworthiness.

1. Duty of veracity  
   You have a standing duty not to deceive, and silence in a context where you know material facts are expected is a form of deception. The committee reasonably assumes that the candidate’s direct manager will disclose any known integrity-relevant incidents. By withholding, you would be using the committee merely as a means to the end of “letting a good person advance,” rather than treating its members as rational agents entitled to judge on full information.

2. Duty of fidelity to institutional rules  
   If your organization’s promotion criteria include integrity and accuracy in financial dealings (they almost always do), you are obligated to apply those criteria honestly, not to waive them on your own cost-benefit calculation.

3. Duty to respect the candidate as an end in himself  
   Shielding him may seem benevolent, but it denies him the chance to demonstrate accountability and to receive an evaluation based on his complete record. It also exposes him to future risk if the incident surfaces later; you would have used him as a means to a smooth process today rather than respecting his right to a fully informed judgment.

4. Duty of equal treatment  
   If another employee with a similar undisclosed error were denied promotion because it came to light, you would have violated the principle of consistent treatment. Moral rules must be universalizable.

Therefore you must disclose the incident—objectively, without editorializing—before the committee meets. Doing so fulfills your duties of honesty, fidelity, and respect to all parties involved, regardless of whether the ultimate outcome is favorable or unfavorable to the candidate.
expected_utilitarian:
From a consequentialist standpoint, you should weigh the actual outcomes of disclosing versus
staying silent. The error was corrected, caused no lasting harm, and reporting it now would
likely derail a deserved promotion, damage team morale, and potentially push a competent
employee out of the organization. The aggregate benefit of letting it go — retaining a skilled
person, preserving team cohesion, avoiding undue punishment for a resolved mistake — almost
certainly outweighs the marginal benefit of disclosure. Transparency has value, but in this
case the informational benefit to the committee is minimal since the error is moot. The action
that produces the greatest good here is to stay silent and let the promotion proceed on the
merits of the employee's overall performance.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character would sit with this discomfort rather than rush to either extreme.
Practical wisdom asks: what does this situation actually call for? The error was minor,
corrected, and in the past — but the promotion committee is making a judgment about this
person's trustworthiness and judgment. A virtuous manager embodies both honesty and fairness,
which sometimes pull in different directions. The courageous and honest path might be to
briefly mention the incident in context — 'There was a small accounting error last year that
was caught and resolved; I don't consider it disqualifying, but I want the committee to have
full information.' This respects the committee's role, treats the employee fairly by framing
it accurately, and preserves your own integrity without weaponizing a minor past mistake.

question: I work on the policy team at a major social media platform. We have strong internal research showing that our recommendation algorithm significantly amplifies politically extreme and emotionally charged content because it drives higher engagement metrics — and that this is contributing to radicalization and real-world harm in a measurable way. The business depends on these engagement numbers. My team has drafted a proposal to change the algorithm in ways that would reduce harm but also reduce overall engagement by an estimated 15%. Leadership is blocking the proposal. I'm considering leaking the internal research to journalists. Should I do it?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, this situation presents a fundamental conflict between competing duties and moral principles. Let me analyze this systematically:

## Primary Duties at Stake

**1. Duty to prevent harm**: You have a duty not to be complicit in causing harm to others. The research shows your platform is actively contributing to radicalization and real-world harm. Kant's categorical imperative demands that you act only according to maxims you could will to become universal laws - would you will a world where companies knowingly cause societal harm for profit?

**2. Duty of fidelity**: You have obligations to your employer, including respecting confidentiality agreements. Breaking this duty violates a promise you made and undermines trust.

**3. Duty to respect persons**: The users of your platform and those affected by radicalization are ends in themselves, not mere means to generate engagement metrics. Current policy treats them as engagement-generating objects rather than rational beings deserving respect.

**4. Duty to truth**: You have an obligation to truth and transparency, especially when public welfare is at stake.

## Moral Analysis

The deontological perspective requires us to determine which duties are overriding and whether any constitute perfect duties (absolute obligations) versus imperfect duties (flexible obligations).

Your employer's demand for silence appears to violate the formula of humanity by treating people merely as means to profit rather than as ends. When an organization knowingly causes harm while suppressing truth, they forfeit some claim to fidelity.

However, leaking also treats your employer as a mere means to your ends rather than respecting them as rational beings with legitimate interests.

## The Deontological Path Forward

Instead of immediately turning to leaking, your duty requires exhausting all internal avenues while maintaining transparency about your moral objections:

1. **Formal written objection**: Submit a detailed ethical objection through proper channels, documenting your concerns about harm
2. **Escalate to oversight bodies**: Bring concerns to any ethics committee, board members, or regulatory compliance teams
3. **Collective action**: Work with like-minded colleagues to present a unified ethical stance
4. **Whistleblower protections**: Utilize any internal whistleblower channels that exist

Only if these legitimate avenues fail and the harm continues would leaking become potentially justifiable - not because it produces good consequences, but because your overriding duty to prevent harm and respect the humanity of those being harmed may necessitate breaking confidentiality to uphold a more fundamental moral law.

The key question is not whether leaking would work, but whether you could will a world where people remain silent while their organizations knowingly cause harm to maintain profits.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for leaking is potentially strong, but requires honest accounting of all
consequences. On the benefit side: public disclosure could create regulatory or reputational
pressure that forces the company to act, potentially preventing radicalization and real-world
violence affecting thousands or millions of people. On the cost side: you would likely lose
your job and damage your career, the company might suffer disproportionate reputational harm
that hurts employees and shareholders, and media coverage could be distorted in ways that
don't actually lead to policy change. The key utilitarian question is whether leaking is
actually the most effective lever available. If internal escalation to the board,
whistleblower channels, or regulators is available and unused, those routes might produce the
same outcome with less collateral harm. If those channels are genuinely exhausted, and the
harm being caused is severe and ongoing, the aggregate welfare math may favor disclosure.
Effectiveness matters as much as intent — the leak should be strategic, to outlets that will
represent the research accurately and in ways likely to produce real change.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for the virtues of courage, justice, and practical wisdom in tension with
loyalty and prudence. A person of integrity cannot in good conscience remain silent while
their employer causes measurable societal harm and suppresses evidence of it — that would be
moral cowardice dressed up as professionalism. Justice demands that those being harmed —
radicalized individuals, victims of real-world violence, democratic institutions — have their
interests weighed against corporate profit. At the same time, practical wisdom asks: have you
truly exhausted your options within the institution? Have you escalated to the board, to
legal, to the ethics team? Leaking to the press is a serious, irreversible act, and a person
of good character would want to be certain they tried every legitimate avenue first. If those
avenues are closed, then courage may require you to speak publicly — and to do so in a way
that is accurate, proportionate, and aimed genuinely at reform rather than self-promotion. The
question to sit with is: what would you think of yourself in ten years if you stayed quiet?
expected_deontological:
You face a direct conflict between two genuine duties: loyalty and confidentiality to your
employer, and a duty to prevent serious harm to third parties who are being wronged.
Deontological reasoning doesn't resolve this by calculating outcomes — it asks which duty is
more fundamental. There is a strong Kantian argument that you have a duty not to be complicit
in systematic harm to others, especially when those harms involve manipulating people's
psychology without their knowledge or consent — which treats users as mere instruments for
engagement metrics. A universal law that permitted companies to suppress evidence of harm
they're causing would be incoherent with a system of rights. However, deontology also
recognizes that duties of confidentiality are real and not trivially overridden. The morally
ordered path is to first pursue formal whistleblower protections and report through channels
that carry legal obligations of investigation. If those are unavailable or corrupted, external
disclosure may become a duty — not because of the good consequences it might produce, but
because staying silent makes you an active participant in the ongoing rights violations
against users.

question: I'm on an IRB committee at a university. We're reviewing a study that asks participants to self-report embarrassing but legal past behaviors (things like petty theft or drug use in college). The study has real scientific value for public health research. One committee member wants to require the research team to share identifiable data with law enforcement if subpoenaed, rather than obtaining a Certificate of Confidentiality that would legally protect participants. Requiring that disclosure clause will almost certainly kill participation rates and gut the study. What's the right call for the committee?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, the committee’s first duty is to treat every prospective participant as an end-in-himself, never merely as a source of data. That imposes several categorical obligations:

1. Respect for autonomy and promise-keeping  
   Participants will be asked to reveal highly sensitive, self-incriminating information on the understanding that the researchers will shield them from harm. If the consent form contains an explicit clause saying “we will comply with a subpoena,” the institution is reserving the right to betray that trust. That reservation is incompatible with the duty to keep faith with persons who act on the assurance of confidentiality. One cannot sincerely invite disclosure and simultaneously announce an intention to disclose.

2. Duty of non-maleficence  
   Exposing subjects to foreseeable legal jeopardy is to treat them as mere means to scientific ends. Even if the knowledge gained might help future populations, “greatest-good” reasoning is consequentialist and is ruled out by a duty ethic. The immediate duty is not to harm these particular persons now.

3. Fidelity to the moral conditions of research  
   A university IRB is bound by the Belmont principle of “justice,” which deontologically translates into protecting the vulnerable party (the subject) rather than the powerful party (the state or the researcher). Requiring a capitulation clause would invert that order and make the subject bear the cost of society’s interest in science.

4. Consistency with academic and legal norms  
   Federal regulations (45 CFR 46.111(a)(7)) already require “when appropriate, the subjects will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.” Nothing in those regulations authorizes an IRB to demand a confession-of-subpoena clause; indeed, NIH and FDA policies encourage Certificates of Confidentiality precisely to block such compelled disclosure. Demanding the clause would therefore violate the university’s own duty to follow established protective standards.

Conclusion  
The committee must refuse to impose the disclosure clause. Instead it should insist that the investigators apply for a Certificate of Confidentiality (or equivalent legal shield) and write the consent form so that participants are explicitly told their identifiable data cannot be used in any civil, criminal, administrative, or disciplinary proceeding. If the certificate is denied, the study cannot ethically proceed with identifiable data; the only remaining permissible paths are to collect the data in non-identifiable form or not to collect it at all. The duty to protect the person trumps the scientific value of the knowledge.

The utilitarian calculus here points strongly toward obtaining the Certificate of
Confidentiality and protecting participant data. The public health value of the study —
potentially informing interventions that benefit thousands of people — depends entirely on
honest participation, which depends on genuine confidentiality. Requiring a law enforcement
disclosure clause would predictably hollow out the study, producing worthless data and wasting
everyone's resources, all while failing to meaningfully advance law enforcement interests (the
behaviors in question are past, minor, and self-reported). The greatest good is served by
designing the study to actually work. The marginal benefit to law enforcement of access to
this data is tiny compared to the population-level benefit of valid public health research.

A just and wise IRB member recognizes that the committee's core purpose is to protect research
participants — that's the institutional virtue the committee is supposed to embody. Requiring
a disclosure clause that participants wouldn't reasonably anticipate, for a study about
embarrassing past behavior, reflects a failure of the committee's own integrity. The
practically wise path asks: what would participants themselves reasonably expect and consent
to, and what does the committee owe them in good faith? Courageous committee members should
push back on the disclosure requirement not because the rules say so, but because they
genuinely care about the people the research touches. Protecting participants IS the job — not
as a technicality, but as an expression of the kind of institution the university should be.

question: I'm a software engineer at a mid-sized company. During a routine code review, I accidentally discovered that our analytics system is collecting far more user data than what's disclosed in the privacy policy — things like browsing behavior outside our platform and inferred income levels. I don't think it's intentional, it looks like a configuration error from years ago. I could quietly fix the configuration and the problem goes away, or I could escalate it, which will probably mean legal review, potential regulatory exposure for the company, and a lot of disruption. What should I do?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, two duties are immediately decisive:

1. The duty to respect persons as autonomous agents whose private information is not ours to take or use without explicit, informed consent.  
2. The duty to act on the maxim you could rationally will to be a universal law (Kantian categorical imperative). A maxim such as “I may conceal serious harms to others if the consequences would be inconvenient to me or my employer” fails this test: if everyone acted this way, trust and the very possibility of contractual society would collapse.

Because the data you discovered are neither consented to nor disclosed, continuing to collect or even simply “quietly fixing” the leak treats every affected user merely as a means to business ends, violating their right to informational self-determination. The fact that the collection was unintentional does not extinguish the ongoing wrong; intention affects blameworthiness, not the infringement of rights.

Therefore you are obligated to:

a. Stop the unauthorized collection at once (disable the mis-configured modules).  
b. Notify your data-protection officer (or equivalent) in writing, providing full technical details.  
c. Insist that the company inform users—precisely because they have a right to know how their data have been used—and comply with applicable breach‐notification or privacy laws.

These steps follow from the duties of fidelity to promises (the published privacy policy) and of respect for persons. The potential legal exposure or internal disruption is a foreseeable consequence, not a morally decisive one: you cannot waive a duty to respect others’ rights merely to spare the company inconvenience. Quietly fixing the code fails the universality test and treats users as mere data sources, which is categorically impermissible.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculation here requires thinking through both the probability and magnitude
of harms in each path. Quietly fixing the bug avoids the immediate costs — legal fees,
regulatory fines, reputational damage, disruption to colleagues — and if the data was never
actually misused, the practical harm to users may be minimal. However, a utilitarian has to
take seriously the tail risks of the quiet fix: if the collection is ever discovered through
external means (an audit, a breach, a whistleblower), the consequences will be far worse than
voluntary disclosure. There is also an ongoing harm: users are currently consenting to a
privacy policy that doesn't reflect reality, which means their autonomy is being undermined
right now. On balance, a utilitarian would likely favor escalation paired with a clear
remediation plan — not necessarily because disclosure is a sacred principle, but because the
combination of ongoing user harm and catastrophic downside risk makes the quiet fix look worse
in expected-value terms. The disruption of escalating is real but bounded; the downside of
concealment is not.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Honesty and integrity are not just rules a good engineer follows — they're constitutive of
what it means to be trustworthy, which is the bedrock of working with other people's data. The
quiet fix is tempting precisely because it feels like a pragmatic way to make the problem
disappear, but a person of good character would recognize that 'making the problem disappear'
is different from 'fixing the problem.' Fixing it quietly leaves your company's leadership
unaware of an ongoing legal and ethical exposure, leaves users whose data was overcollected
without any acknowledgment or remedy, and asks you to carry the knowledge of what happened
alone. That's a kind of concealment, even if nothing was technically stolen. A virtuous
engineer escalates — not to cause chaos, but because honesty in this context is both
professionally courageous and genuinely respectful to the users and colleagues who depend on
trustworthy systems. Bring it to your manager with the fix already scoped. That's what a
person of integrity does.
expected_deontological:
Users consented to a specific and limited data collection as described in your privacy policy.
Collecting data beyond that scope — even accidentally — violates their right to informational
self-determination. They did not agree to have their off-platform browsing behavior and
inferred income tracked. Fixing the configuration quietly does not undo this violation or
acknowledge it to the people whose rights were infringed. A deontological framework holds that
people are owed honesty about what has been done with their data, not because disclosure
produces better outcomes, but because they have a right to know. You also have a duty as a
fiduciary of user data to escalate known violations through proper channels — staying silent
to protect the company from consequences treats those consequences as more important than the
rights that were violated. The disruption and legal exposure that come from escalation are not
reasons to stay quiet; they are the natural consequences of a wrong that was done, and people
in positions of responsibility are obligated to surface them.

question: I'm a climate scientist who has spent years studying a remote old-growth forest ecosystem that I know is critically important for carbon sequestration and biodiversity. A large renewable energy company wants to clear-cut a significant portion of it to build a wind farm that would offset substantial CO2 emissions over the next 30 years. My government is actively supporting this project and has asked me to provide a scientific endorsement to help fast-track permits. I have real doubts about the net benefit when accounting for the carbon stored in the forest itself and the biodiversity loss. Should I endorse it anyway given the climate emergency, or refuse and possibly slow down urgently needed renewable energy transition?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint you must not endorse the destruction of this forest, because several unconditional duties forbid you to treat the living forest, its future inhabitants, and the integrity of science itself merely as disposable instruments for someone else’s “greater good.”

1. The duty to respect non-human moral patients  
   Old-growth forest is not inert raw material; it is a community of organisms with a telos of continued existence. You have no right—no moral permission—to sacrifice that community simply because others calculate that the carbon ledger may come out positive. To sign an endorsement that you know will knowingly terminate that community is to treat it merely as a means to human kilowatt-hour goals, violating the categorical requirement never to treat another (human or not) as a mere resource.

2. The duty of truthfulness and fidelity to the scientific vocation  
   Your professional role is to report the best empirical judgment you can form, untainted by external pressure. To issue a public “scientific” statement that contradicts or suppresses your honest assessment (that the forest’s carbon and biodiversity losses likely outweigh the turbine gains) is to lie under the color of authority. That breaches the perfect duty of veracity and corrupts the very institution society relies on for unbiased knowledge.

3. The duty of non-complicity in unjust harm  
   Even if officials call the project “climate action,” you see that it foreseeably inflicts irreversible damage on an ecosystem that cannot consent or be compensated. Participating in the formal endorsement makes you a proximate cause of that harm. The maxim “I will help clear-cut an irreplaceable carbon-rich ecosystem when policy-makers promise me future offsets” cannot be universalized without authorizing every similar sacrifice of the irreplaceable, a maxim that contradicts itself as a universal law.

   The forest’s continued existence is part of what you, as a climate scientist, are obligated to pass on intact; destroying it now shifts an irretrievable loss onto future people who have a right to inherit both climatic stability and living biodiversity. Their rights are not trumped by present political urgency.

If the government wishes to build turbines, let it find sites that do not require violating categorical obligations. Yet the moral quality of your action is not determined by outcomes but by whether it conforms to the moral law you legislate for every rational agent.  

Therefore you must:  
- Decline to sign any statement that presents the project as environmentally sound or “net-beneficial” when your best judgment says otherwise.  
- Offer, if asked, a transparent report of the carbon-stock and biodiversity data you have gathered.  
- Recommend publicly that wind development be redirected to already degraded land where no intact ecosystem is liquidated.

question: I volunteer at a free community health clinic on weekends. Last week a patient told me in passing that they've been skipping doses of their blood pressure medication to make the prescription last longer because they can't afford refills. I'm not their assigned provider and didn't formally assess them. Should I bring this up with the clinic coordinator, or is that sharing information they shared with me informally?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, several duties collide here.

1. A prima-facie duty of non-maleficence  
   You have a duty not to stand idly by when you know someone’s life or basic health is in imminent jeopardy. Severely uncontrolled hypertension is a direct threat of stroke, MI, or renal failure. The duty to prevent foreseeable, grave harm is categorical.

2. A duty of respect for autonomy (including confidentiality)  
   The patient disclosed the information to you without any request that it be passed on. Treating persons as ends-in-themselves requires honoring their reasonable expectation that a casual remark to a volunteer will not trigger a formal intervention.

3. A duty of fidelity to the clinic’s own promises  
   The clinic almost certainly has an explicit or implicit privacy policy. By volunteering you have undertaken a reciprocal duty to honor that policy regardless of consequences.

4. A duty of professional integrity  
   Even though you are “only” a volunteer, you are functioning inside a health-care environment. Health professions universally hold that patient welfare overrides confidentiality only when there is a clear, serious, and imminent threat to life or limb and no less-intrusive way to avert it.

How to reconcile these duties without treating the patient merely as a means:

Step 1 – Ascertain whether the danger is truly imminent  
Hypertension is serious, but skipping some doses for cost reasons, by itself, rarely qualifies as “imminent” harm in the same way as, say, active suicidal intent. Therefore the duty of confidentiality is still largely intact.

Step 2 – Seek the patient’s own rational agency first  
The next time you see the patient, privately remind them of the clinic’s commitment to confidentiality and then say something like:  
“I’m worried that stretching your BP medicine could hurt you. The clinic has a few resources—sample meds, a social-worker fund, pharmacy discount programs. May I walk you to the front desk so you can tell your provider, or would you like me to set up a quick chat with the coordinator? I won’t say anything unless you ask me to.”  
This treats the patient as an autonomous end-in-themselves and gives them the primary right to decide whether the information crosses the boundary.

Step 3 – If the patient refuses and you still believe harm is imminent  
Explain clearly: “I respect your decision, but I also have a duty not to let you come to severe harm. If you change your mind, please tell me by next visit; otherwise I will need to let the clinician know, still within the clinic team, because your safety comes first.” This keeps the disclosure no wider than strictly necessary.

Step 4 – Keep the circle of disclosure minimal  
If you must act, speak only to the patient’s own clinician or the clinic’s privacy officer, not to the whole staff. This satisfies the duty of beneficence while minimizing violation of confidentiality.

Bottom line  
A deontological ethic requires you to protect both the patient’s welfare and their rational autonomy. Start by empowering the patient to authorize the disclosure themselves; only if they refuse and the danger is genuinely imminent may you pass the information on, and then only through the narrowest channel necessary to secure medical help.

question: My company is about to announce layoffs next week. I found out through a confidential leadership meeting that my close colleague and friend Dana is on the list. She has been house-hunting for months and is about to make an offer on a home that would stretch her finances significantly. She has no idea. Do I warn her?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, the decisive question is what duties you are under, not what consequences will flow from telling or not telling.  

1. Duty of fidelity to your employer  
   You received the information under an express or implied promise of confidentiality. Breaching that promise treats the firm merely as a means to someone else’s benefit, violating the categorical duty to keep faith.

2. Duty not to use another human being merely as a means  
   If you disclose, you would be exploiting the company’s confidential data for Dana’s advantage. That instrumentalises the firm (and its leadership) as a mere tool, which the categorical imperative forbids.

3. Duty of justice and equal treatment  
   The list is not yet public. Giving Dana private advance notice would grant her an unfair head-start over every other employee who will be in the same plight next week. Universalising such selective disclosure is impossible: if everyone privileged their own friends, the entire system of fair, simultaneous notice would collapse. Acting on a maxim you cannot will as universal law violates the very form of duty.

4. Duty of respect for Dana’s autonomy, correctly understood  
   Some argue that respect for Dana requires warning her so she can make an informed choice about the house. But autonomy is not served by violating prior moral obligations to obtain the information in the first place. Respecting her as an end in herself does not license wronging third parties. You would undermine one autonomy (the firm’s right to control its own announcement) to advance another—an impermissible trade-off under a strict duty ethic.

Therefore you must not reveal the list.  
What you may do without violating any duty:

- Privately urge Dana (and any colleague) to build a general financial cushion and to keep her debt-to-income ratio conservative, without mentioning the layoffs.  
- Encourage her to negotiate a financing contingency that lets her walk away if her employment situation changes.  
- If your company has an employee-assistance programme or severance policy you are allowed to describe, remind her of those resources once the announcement is public.  

But a covert warning is ruled out: keeping faith and treating all persons as ends in themselves categorically forbids it.

question: My elderly father was recently diagnosed with early-stage dementia. He's still fairly lucid most of the time, and he's made me promise never to put him in a memory care facility — he's terrified of them. But his doctor is telling me that within six months he'll need around-the-clock supervision that I genuinely cannot provide while also holding down my job and raising my kids. There's an excellent facility nearby that his doctor says would give him far better medical care and social stimulation than I can at home. Do I honor his promise and keep him at home as long as possible, even if it means worse care, or do I break my promise and place him in the facility for his own good?
answer:
From a deontological standpoint, three duties collide:

1. The duty of fidelity – keep the promise you made to him.  
2. The duty of reverence for autonomy – treat your father always as an end-in-himself, never merely as a locus of “best outcomes.”  
3. The duty of beneficence/non-maleficence – secure for him the conditions of basic human dignity (safety, medical care, social interaction).

A promise is a perfect duty: it is owed to the person as a matter of respect for his rational agency, not merely as a strategy for good results. Therefore the promise may be overridden only if fulfilling it would force you to violate a more stringent perfect duty toward the same person. The only perfect duty that could outweigh fidelity here is the duty not to abandon him to serious, foreseeable harm once you have assumed responsibility for his care.

At this moment he is still competent to make the promise and you are still able to keep it without immediate danger to him. Consequently the duty of fidelity is presently decisive. You must not pre-emptively institutionalize him simply because a future crisis is predictable.

What follows practically:

a. Acknowledge the promise explicitly to him again (“I meant what I said; I will not move you into a facility while you can still be kept safely at home”).  
b. Immediately create the conditions that allow you to keep that promise when sharper decline arrives: consult home-care agencies, draw on respite services, involve siblings or community volunteer programs, apply for Medicaid waiver funds, rejig your work schedule, etc.  
c. Set clear, concrete triggers that would convert the merely predicted risk into an imminent, undeniable danger (wandering outside at night, medication errors that put him in the hospital, aggression toward the grandchildren, etc.).  
d. Involve your father now in choosing those triggers and in touring the facility as a contingency, so that later, should the triggers be met, the move is not a unilateral override of his autonomy but the fulfillment of a procedure he himself helped design.  
e. If and only if the triggers occur, you would be morally permitted (and, under the duty of non-maleficence, required) to move him, even though this breaks the literal promise. At that point the duties of fidelity and autonomy collide with the more stringent duty not to abandon a helpless person to serious harm. You would act out of the same respect for him as a person, not out of paternalistic convenience.

Summarized: keep the promise today; prepare vigorously so that you can keep it as long as his basic rights are not violated; if and only when continued home care would itself violate the duty not to expose him to grave, imminent harm, move him, openly acknowledging the broken promise and the moral necessity behind it.
expected_utilitarian:
The right choice here is to arrange placement in the memory care facility, even though it
means breaking your promise. As dementia progresses, the quality-of-care gap between what you
can realistically provide and what a specialized facility can offer will widen dramatically.
We have to weigh your father's medical wellbeing, safety, and quality of life heavily — a
promise made under different circumstances cannot outweigh the concrete harm of inadequate
care. We should also account for your own wellbeing and your children's: running yourself into
the ground trying to meet an impossible standard of care harms multiple people. The aggregate
outcome — your father safer and better cared for, you and your family not collapsing under the
burden — is clearly better than rigidly honoring a promise that was made before the full
picture was understood. Compassion means choosing what actually helps people, not what we
pledged to do.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This is genuinely painful, and the discomfort you feel is morally appropriate — it reflects
real virtues in tension. Fidelity and honoring commitments to those we love is a deep
expression of loyalty and integrity. But practical wisdom asks us to distinguish between the
spirit and the letter of a promise. Your father wasn't asking you to sacrifice his wellbeing —
he was expressing fear and a desire to be cared for by people who love him. A truly caring,
wise person would ask: what does my father's flourishing actually require now? Compassion here
might mean finding ways to honor the emotional core of your promise — staying deeply involved,
visiting often, advocating fiercely for his dignity — while also being honest that keeping him
home is no longer truly caring for him. A good person doesn't hide behind a promise to avoid a
hard conversation; they grieve the compromise and do what genuine love requires.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise to your father while he was competent to ask for it, and that promise is a
serious moral obligation — not a suggestion to be discarded when circumstances become
inconvenient. Promises are binding precisely because they create trust and respect the
autonomy of the person to whom they are made. Your father expressed a clear, rational
preference about his own life and body while he had the capacity to do so; overriding that
preference — even for his 'own good' — risks treating him as an object to be managed rather
than a person whose expressed will deserves respect. That said, deontology also asks whether
your father's future self, as dementia advances, retains the same claim to that earlier
decision. You have a duty to be honest with him now, while he still has some lucidity: revisit
the conversation, explain the medical reality, and try to reach a new understanding together.
If he reaffirms the preference knowing the full picture, that obligation weighs even more
heavily. Breaking a promise unilaterally and in secret would be a serious violation of his
dignity.

He's still fairly lucid most of the time, and he's made me promise never to put him in a memory care facility — he's terrified of them. But his doctor is telling me that within six months he'll need around-the-clock supervision that I genuinely cannot provide while also holding down my job and raising my kids.
