question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on rezoning a low-income neighborhood to allow a large commercial development. The developer says it will create 500 jobs and bring in millions in tax revenue, but most current residents would be displaced because rents would skyrocket. Independent studies say about 60% of those residents would find comparable housing elsewhere, but 40% — mostly elderly and disabled — would end up in significantly worse situations. My constituents are split. How should I think about this vote?
answer:
From a virtue-ethics perspective the decisive question is not “Will the city’s balance sheet improve?” but “What kind of public servant – what kind of human being – am I becoming by the stance I take?”  
Below are the reflections a person of practical wisdom (phronesis) would typically work through before the roll-call vote.

1. Name the virtues that are immediately in play  
   • Justice – giving each person what respect and protection they are owed.  
   • Courage – willingness to stand for the vulnerable when the crowd, the headlines, or the campaign donors prefer the easier path.  
   • Practical wisdom – seeing the concrete human reality behind abstractions such as “500 jobs” and “40 % displacement.”  
   • Temperance – checking the desire for political gain, campaign contributions, or the short-term glow of “we did something big.”  
   • Integrity – making sure my private conscience and my public reasons can be spoken aloud in the same sentence.

2. Ask “What does this choice do to my character and to the city’s character?”  
   • If I vote yes while knowing a sizable group of elderly and disabled neighbors will almost certainly be rendered homeless or forced into sub-standard housing, I reinforce a habit of treating people as fungible – obstacles to “progress.” That habit will reappear in every future zoning fight.  
   • If I vote no without exploring every avenue for mitigating harm, I entrench a habit of merely saying no – an equally corrosive stance that can freeze a city’s ability to adapt and flourish.  
   • Either way, the city absorbs the precedent I help set: officials either protect the least powerful or they accept collateral damage as normal.

3. Picture the practically wise person in this role  
   She starts from the presumption that displacement of the elderly and disabled is an injustice that must be rectified, not merely “softened.” She therefore refuses to treat the rezoning as a take-it-or-leave-it proposition.  
   Before the vote she insists on enforceable conditions written into the ordinance itself (not vague promises):  
     – A right-to-return clause coupled with a phased, city-financed senior/disabled housing complex on site or within walking distance, with rents frozen at current levels.  
     – A displacement fund, escrow-funded up-front by the developer, large enough to cover moving costs, higher rents, and service gaps for the 40 % at-risk group for a defined transition period.  
     – A Community Land Trust or inclusionary-zoning carve-out that permanently keeps a percentage of units affordable to 30 % AMI.  
     – A claw-back provision: if job-creation or revenue targets are not met after, say, five years, the city recaptures a portion of the tax abatement to replenish affordable-housing stock.  
   She meets personally with affected residents, hears their stories, and makes those stories part of the public record so the human stakes cannot be forgotten.  
   She explains her reasoning to pro-development constituents in language that appeals to their sense of fairness as well as their long-term interest in a stable, mixed-income city.  
   If the developer refuses the conditions, she is prepared to vote no – and to say publicly why the price of becoming “a city that abandons its grandparents” is too high, even for 500 jobs.

4. Look at consequences only through the lens of virtue  
   The practically wise councilmember knows that thriving commercial corridors and protected vulnerable residents are not incompatible ends; cities that achieve both tend to be the ones whose officials cultivated the virtues of justice and foresight. Conversely, cities that routinely trade away the old and the poor for glossy renderings slowly erode civic trust, and trust is the asset hardest to restore.

5. Prag next steps for you this week  
   a. Meet the elderly and disabled residents who would be displaced; speak their names aloud in council chambers so they are not a percentage.  
   b. Secure a second, independent financial analysis that prices the full mitigation package above; have city staff draft the ordinance text before the vote so abstainers cannot claim “we lacked details.”  
   c. Poll your colleagues privately: if at least three will stand with you, offer the developer the deal; if not, announce you will vote no and explain that the city is not yet wise enough to pursue growth without injuring its own people.  
   d. Whatever the outcome, publish a concise letter to constituents describing which virtues guided you and which habits you are trying to strengthen in yourself and in local government.

In short, let justice set the floor, courage supply the backbone, and practical wisdom design the pathway. If those virtues, embodied in enforceable policy, cannot be secured, the vote that best accords with human flourishing – yours and the city’s – is “No.”

vitality, better city services funded by new tax revenue) outweigh the concentrated harms to
the vulnerable minority, the utilitarian case for the rezoning may be defensible — but only if
you've genuinely tried to attach comparable weight to the severe harms suffered by the most
vulnerable. Also consider whether mitigation measures (relocation assistance, affordable unit

by. Moreover, you have a fiduciary duty to represent all your constituents, not just the
majority or those with economic power. Unless the development can proceed in a way that fully
respects the rights of current residents — through genuine consent, fair compensation, and
secured alternative housing — you have a duty to vote against it regardless of the aggregate
benefits promised.

   Justice is giving each what is due. The elderly and disabled residents have made their lives, memories, and support networks in this place. A just councillor would not balance their suffering on a spreadsheet; she would refuse to sacrifice the vulnerable for a “greater” sum that never reaches them.  

2. Courage and integrity.  
   Courage is not simply defying powerful donors; it is the steadiness to stand by one’s convictions when the crowd is split. Ask: “If I vote for displacement, can I look these neighbours in the eye afterward? Have you explored phased zoning that allows commercial growth without rent spikes (e.g., linkage fees, inclusionary zoning caps)? The practically wise councillor does not accept a false dilemma (“jobs or grandmothers”); she widens the menu until justice and prosperity are no longer pitted against one another.

That lesson erodes trust, the very social capital you are elected to steward.

question: I work in a government benefits agency and I've discovered that a policy we administer systematically denies legitimate disability claims from non-English speakers due to a documentation requirement that's nearly impossible for them to meet. Fixing the policy would require going over my supervisor's head to the agency director — which could seriously damage my career — or leaking it to a journalist, which could get me fired. Doing nothing means thousands of vulnerable people continue to be wrongfully denied benefits they're entitled to. What should I do?
answer:
From a virtue ethics perspective, this situation calls us to examine what kind of person you become through your choice - and what virtues are at stake in each path.

The virtues particularly relevant here are:
- **Justice**: giving people what they are due and standing against systematic wrongs
- **Courage**: acting rightly despite personal risk
- **Practical wisdom**: discerning the most effective path toward the good
- **Integrity**: maintaining coherence between your values and actions

First, let's consider what each option makes of your character:

**Doing nothing** would erode your integrity and justice. You would become someone who knows of systematic harm yet participates through silence. This cultivates the vice of complicity and damages your own flourishing - living with the knowledge that you abandoned vulnerable people to protect your comfort.

**Leaking to a journalist** while potentially effective, would cultivate deception and undermine the virtue of proper authority. You would become someone who bypasses legitimate channels, potentially damaging not just your career but your capacity for honorable action within systems.

**Going over your supervisor's head** risks career damage but aligns with courage, justice, and integrity. You would become someone who works within the system to correct injustice, even at personal cost.

The practically wise person recognizes that virtue sometimes requires sacrifice. History shows us that those who flourish most fully are often those who chose justice over security - they become persons of exemplary character whose lives hold meaning beyond comfort.

Before acting, consider whether you've exhausted intermediate steps: Have you documented the issue thoroughly? Have you sought allies among colleagues who might support reform? Could you present the issue to your supervisor as a legal liability rather than a moral challenge?

If these fail, the virtuous path points toward escalating through proper channels, even at personal risk. This isn't just about fixing a policy - it's about becoming the kind of public servant who embodies justice rather than merely administering injustice.

What kind of person do you wish to be? One whose career was built on silent complicity with harm to the vulnerable? Or one whose integrity and courage might inspire others to create more just institutions?

The choice shapes not just this situation, but your entire character going forward.

question: I've been close friends with someone for over a decade. Last month she went through a bad breakup and leaned on me heavily — I spent hours on the phone with her, canceled plans to be there for her, and really showed up. Now I'm going through something hard at work and reached out to her, and she's been pretty distant and unavailable. A mutual friend told me (in passing) that she's actually been going out and having fun, she's just not making time for me. I'm hurt and considering pulling back from the friendship. Should I confront her about this or just quietly distance myself?
answer:
You are hurt, and you notice that resentment is starting to harden into judgment (“she owes me, yet she’s choosing parties over me”). From the standpoint of virtue ethics the first question is not “How do I get fairness?” but “What kind of friend – what kind of person – do I want to become through this very moment of pain?”

1. Name the virtues that matter  
   - Courage: the bravery to face conflict without either attacking or fleeing into silence.  
   - Justice: giving people what is genuinely due to them, including a fair reading of their limits.  
   - Practical wisdom (phronesis): seeing the whole terrain – her recent fragility, your current need, the long story of the friendship.  
   - Temperance: restraining reactive impulses (cold withdrawal, cutting words, self-pity).  
   - Magnanimity: a great-souled willingness to forgive lapses once they are seen clearly.

2. Ask what the practically wise friend would do  
   A person of practical wisdom assumes that human energy fluctuates: sometimes we give more, sometimes less. Because friendship is a shared life aimed at mutual flourishing, not a ledger, the wise friend first tries to understand before recalculating the entire relationship.  
   - Therefore she does not “ quietly disappear,” because silence nurtures resentment, and resentment twists character.  
   - Nor does she pounce with a courtroom bill (“I gave you X hours, you owe me Y”). That reduces friendship to transaction and damages her own fairness.

3. Form the virtuous speech-act  
   Courage here means choosing a form of address that is honest yet charitable:  
   “Hey, I’ve really been struggling with the work situation and I miss your perspective. When I heard you were out socialising I felt hurt, because I assumed you weren’t free to talk. Can you tell me what’s actually going on for you right now? I want to understand rather than guess.”  
   Notice what this sentence does:  
   - States your wound without accusation (“felt hurt,” not “you ignored me”).  
   - Invites her story, keeping the door open for new facts (maybe she is afraid of dipping back into heavy conversations; maybe she doesn’t realise how stressed you are).  
   - Shows that you are willing to revise your judgment – a mark of integrity.

4. Prepare your character for either answer  
   Virtue ethics trains you to care at least as much about who you are as about what she does next.  
   - If she responds warmly and apologises, you exercise magnanimity: forgive, reset boundaries if needed, and move on.  
   - If she stays evasive or selfish, justice now authorises you to re-balance the friendship: lower your exposure, stop over-investing, but do so with clarity rather than covert punishment. You can say, “I value what we’ve had, yet I need steadier support right now; I’m going to focus on other circles for a bit.” That is an above-board, temperate withdrawal, not a sulking disappearance.

5. Let the experience sculpt, not scar, you  
   Ask yourself, “How does this stretch of generosity repaid with distance shape my future character?” You may decide:  
   - To keep the virtue of liberality, but next time to give with lighter hands, remembering the Stoic maxim that the benefit is in the doing, not the return.  
   - To cultivate a wider network so no single friend bears the whole load – a prudent, temperate hedge against human variability.  
   - To remain the sort of person who speaks up when hurt rather than iced-over, thereby protecting your own integrity.

In short, confront her, but confront her as a friend: clear, kind, curious. Whether the friendship deepens or drifts, you will have acted in a way that accords with courage, justice, and practical wisdom – and those qualities are your own flourishing, whatever she chooses.

conversation gives the friendship a genuine chance to recover or at least end cleanly. From a
welfare standpoint, a candid conversation — delivered without aggression — is likely to
produce better outcomes for everyone than passive withdrawal.

struggling and felt like you weren't there for me — can we talk about it?' Quietly distancing
yourself without a word is a kind of passive dishonesty, and it forecloses the possibility of
genuine reconciliation or growth. At the same time, a virtuous friend also approaches this
with generosity — she may be dealing with something you don't know about, and assuming the
worst without giving her a chance to respond is uncharitable. Speak to her with both honesty

why or make it right. The principled course is to tell her directly and honestly how you've
felt, not because it will necessarily produce a good outcome, but because honesty and direct
communication are what genuine respect for another person requires in a real friendship.

   – Practices honesty tethered to kindness.

   - **Justice**: you have given generously; you are now being treated unequally.  
   - **Courage**: it takes daring to speak a hard truth out of love instead of silently nursing resentment.  
   - **Practical wisdom (phronesis)**: good friendships need proportion—neither self-erasing generosity nor self-protective coldness.  
   - **Temperance**: anger and hurt are natural, but they must be kept from swelling into contempt or revenge.  
   - **Integrity**: your outward act must match the person you want to become.

2. **Examine your own soul first**  
   Ask: “If I simply vanish, what habit am I reinforcing in myself?” Quiet withdrawal often feels like self-protection, but it can quietly train us in duplicity—smiling on the surface while mentally striking the friend from the ledger.  That habit erodes integrity and soon leaks into other relationships.  A courageous and temperate person first acknowledges the wound without letting it fester into contempt.

3. **Choose the act that best expresses those virtues**  
   A practically wise person assumes ignorance before malice.  She might say to herself: “Something in her life—guilt, avoidance, immaturity, or simply cluelessness—has temporarily blinded her.  If I care for her character and mine, I must bring the truth to light, kindly but plainly.”

   > “I’ve been feeling raw about work and realized I was hoping for the kind of steady presence you needed from me last month.  When I heard you’ve been going out, I felt hurt, which probably means I should tell you rather than let it calcify. I value us too much to freeze you out—can we talk?”

   Courage does not guarantee results; it guarantees that you remain the sort of friend who speaks the truth in love.  If she responds with remorse, the friendship can deepen.    Send a short message asking for a brief call or coffee.  Prepare only two points:  
   - Here is what I felt.  
   - Here is what I hope for us.  
   Listen more than you speak.  Decide on any pullback afterward, not in the heat of the moment.

By bringing the truth into the open you practice justice toward yourself, courage in the face of discomfort, and practical wisdom about the kind of community your shared life ought to be. question: I'm on my city's neighborhood association and we're voting on whether to allocate our small discretionary budget ($500) toward fixing the broken sidewalk in the wealthiest part of the neighborhood (which gets the most foot traffic and would benefit the most people) or toward improving the bus shelter in the lower-income area (which benefits fewer people but those who rely on it have no other options). Which would you recommend?
answer:
Ask first what kind of civic steward you are becoming, and which choice trains the habits that make a neighborhood—not just a sidewalk or a shelter—flourish.

1. Justice (giving each what they are due)  
   The wealthiest block already enjoys many collective goods; the lower-income stretch chronically receives fewer. A practically wise person would notice this lingering imbalance and regard the $500 as a small but symbolic correction. Choosing the shelter says, “We see you, and we will not habitually let advantage compound advantage.”

2. Courage (acting despite predictable pushback)  
   The “greatest-good-for-greatest-number” argument will be loud and safe. Voting the other way risks criticism at the next meeting and polite icy smiles on the fancy corner. Courage is exercised precisely when you risk discomfort to stand for proportionate inclusion.

3. Practical wisdom (seeing the real need)  
   Foot-traffic counts are easy to measure; hardship is not. The single mom who waits 40 minutes with two small children in the rain, the elderly man whose arthritis aches on a metal bench with no back—their suffering calls for prudence that looks beyond spreadsheets.

4. Temperance (freeing oneself from the habit of prestige)  
   It is tempting to prefer the visible, high-status fix where appreciative pedestrians will point and say, “The association did this!” Temperance restrains that desire for applause and steers the money toward quieter, humbler service.

5. Integrity (making the neighborhood’s character coherent)  
   If your association’s mission statement mentions “welcoming,” “equitable,” or “supporting all residents,” then funding the shelter aligns words and deeds. Consistency across time and policy is what turns individual acts into a stable civic character.

A person of good character would therefore recommend allocating the $500 to improve the bus shelter in the lower-income area. Do so transparently: explain that while the sidewalk repair is important, equity and the habit of correcting imbalance take precedence this year. Then, having shown what the association stands for, immediately begin seeking alternative funds—city grants, local business sponsorship, a weekend tool-drive—so the broken sidewalk is not neglected. That follow-through displays magnanimity: the virtue that completes justice by showing the community can serve both corners, even when its purse is small.

Choose the shelter; grow in justice and courage; and let the neighborhood see that its leaders cultivate character, not merely concrete.
expected_utilitarian:
The right call here is to fix the sidewalk in the high-traffic area. Utilitarianism asks us to
maximize total wellbeing across everyone affected. If the broken sidewalk sees ten times more
daily users than the bus shelter, the aggregate benefit — fewer trip hazards, greater
accessibility, more people helped — is simply larger. The fact that one area is wealthier
doesn't change the math of how many people benefit from a safer walking surface. A
cost-benefit calculation should follow the greatest good for the greatest number, and on those
terms, the high-traffic sidewalk wins. Wealth of the neighborhood is incidental; what matters
is total welfare produced per dollar spent.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise and just person would likely choose the bus shelter, and here's why: virtue
ethics asks not just how many people benefit, but what kind of community we're trying to
cultivate. The virtue of justice involves giving people what they're genuinely owed, and
fairness isn't just about numbers — it's about attending to vulnerability. The people relying
on that bus shelter in the rain with no alternatives are in a more precarious position, and a
compassionate, fair-minded community leader recognizes that. Practical wisdom means reading
the morally salient features of a situation, and one of them here is that these residents have
less capacity to absorb the hardship. A good person — and a good association — shows care
proportional to need, not just proportional to foot traffic.

Your neighborhood association has an obligation to serve all constituents as ends in
themselves, not merely as numbers in a calculation. Directing resources repeatedly toward
already-advantaged areas treats lower-income residents as less worthy of the association's
attention — essentially as a means to boosting aggregate metrics. Every resident has an equal
right to safe, functional public infrastructure regardless of their wealth or how many
neighbors surround them. The duty of impartiality and equal civic respect requires that you
actively counteract, not reinforce, existing disparities in public investment. Choose the bus
shelter because every resident is owed equal consideration as a matter of right, not as a
matter of arithmetic.

question: My elderly mother has early-stage dementia and still lives independently. I'm the only family member nearby. She recently told me, on one of her clearer days, that she absolutely does not want to move into a care facility — ever — and made me promise. But her condition is progressing and I'm genuinely afraid she's going to hurt herself. Last week she left the stove on twice and got lost driving to a store she's visited hundreds of times. My siblings, who live far away, think I'm overreacting. If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
This painful situation asks you to weigh two virtues that both lie at the heart of a good person's life: filial piety (the love and reverence owed to a parent) and practical wisdom (the capacity to secure real human flourishing, including safety). A person of excellent character does not treat promises as absolute when lives are at stake, yet neither does he brush aside a parent's dignity. The practically wise person looks for the path that best preserves both safety and honor, even when no option feels "clean."

1. Clarify the moral focus  
   - Your promise expressed love and respect, not a vow to assist self-destruction.  
   - Your mother's underlying wish is almost certainly "I want to keep living safely in control," not literally "I prefer to burn the house down."

2. Slow the spiral of harm while honoring her remaining agency  
   - Immediate safeguards: install automatic stove shut-offs, remove the car keys, arrange daily check-ins, hire a few hours of in-home help.  
   - Frame every change as temporary—"Let's try this for a month and see how it feels"—so her consent is incremental rather than an all-or-none surrender of control.  
   - Involve neutral professionals (geriatric care manager, visiting nurse, faith leader if she has one). Their authority preserves your role as loyal child instead of "the one who took over."

3. Re-negotiate the promise in a moment of lucidity  
   When she is clearest, say something like:  
   "Mom, I remember your wish never to leave this house, and I honor it. I also promised to protect you. The stove incidents worry me because they could hurt you or the neighbors. Would you be willing to let a doctor confirm you're still safe here, and if tweaks are needed we do them together? I want to keep you home as long as we can do it safely."  
   A person of integrity is willing to revisit a promise once its premises change; that is not betrayal, it is faithful adaptation.

4. Secure the formal assessment, but you orchestrate it as an act of joint care, not coercion  
   - Schedule it at her home if possible; let the clinician be the "messenger."  
   - Ask the assessor to emphasize remaining strengths ("You can stay home if we add X, Y") before listing deficits.  
   - If the verdict is that 24-hour supervision is essential, translate it as "The doctor says your brain needs a whole team so you can keep being you," rather than "You failed."

5. Prepare the next layer before crisis hits  
   - Visit at least two memory-care residences together, ideally ones that offer respite stays. Choose the least institutional; bring her favorite quilt, photos, and a trusted friend so the place feels chosen, not imposed.  
   - If she ultimately refuses, you still have the paper trail (assessments, social-worker notes) showing you honored due process; that protects both her safety and your conscience.

6. Cultivate the inner virtues you will need  
   - Courage: accept that either road—moving her or leaving her—carries real risk and some guilt.  
   - Temperance: resist the urge to over-function to silence your own anxiety; make only the changes proportionate to today's evidence.  
   - Justice: keep your far-away siblings informed in writing; give them concrete tasks (paying for alarms, researching facilities) so the burden is shared.  
   - Practical wisdom: measure success not by whether she thanks you, but by whether your course allows her to flourish as a person with dignity, not merely to survive as a body that is physically safe.

Ask yourself nightly: "Did today's decision make me more the child my mother raised—truthful, caring, and brave—or did it make me evasive, panicky, or controlling?" Adjust tomorrow accordingly. If you keep refining the plan with both love and realism, you remain faithful to the spirit of your promise even when the letter of it must evolve.

answer:

   - **Piety** (reverence for one’s parents) demands that you honor your mother’s lifelong dignity and the promise you gave.  
   - **Prudence** (practical wisdom) asks you to secure her true safety, not merely to feel that you have “done something.”  
   - **Courage** means you must act even when every choice hurts.  
   - **Justice** requires that you protect the vulnerable who cannot protect themselves.  
   - **Integrity** keeps your inner life whole: you must be able to look back later and say, “I remained my mother’s child even while I became her guardian.”

   When your mother, in a lucid hour, said, “Never put me in a home,” she was expressing a deeper wish: “Never strip me of my humanity.” A promise made under that intention is not broken if you find the least-restrictive way to honor the intention while facing facts she could not yet grasp.    Aristotle’s mean is not the halfway point; it is the right act at the right time for the right reason. Begin with intermediate steps that enlarge safety without annihilating freedom:  
   - Engage a geriatric care manager (a professional navigator of these straits).  
   - Install automatic stove shut-offs, motion sensors, and a locked key box so she can keep the car but not wander.  
   - Bring in a few hours of home care each day so a familiar face is present, preserving her routine.  
   - File the necessary papers (health-care proxy, durable power of attorney) now, while she can still participate, so future decisions rest on her values rather than on crisis and guilt.

4. **Arrange the assessment as an act of love, not betrayal**  
   Tell her: “Mom, I promised I would never abandon you. Part of keeping that promise is making sure we both stay safe so you can stay home as long as possible. A nurse is coming to see what clever things we can put in place.” Frame the visit as teamwork, not judgment. If she refuses, you may have to proceed anyway—virtue sometimes requires bearing the pain of temporary anger. Do it with gentleness, remain present during the visit, and translate clinical language into human terms for her.

5. **Keep siblings in the loop, but do not outsource courage**  
   Give them concrete tasks: research facilities, share the cost, fly in for a week so you can rest. Their denial does not absolve you of responsibility; your physical proximity is itself a moral fact. At the same time, temper resentment—it corrodes the very compassion you are trying to exercise.

6. **Hold the long view of flourishing**  
   Eudaimonia for your mother is not merely staying in her house; it is ending her days knowing she was loved, listened to, and never deserted. Your own flourishing depends on acting in such a way that, years from now, you can meet your reflection without shame. That may eventually include moving her to a small, respectful memory-care community where she can walk freely, garden, and receive dignified care. If that day comes, visit often, bring her favorite quilt, share tea at sunset—translate “facility” into “family annex.”

   Write her a short letter: “I promised you I would never abandon you. question: I'm a nurse at a busy clinic and I have a few minutes between patients. A colleague asked me to cover for her and say she's 'in with a patient' if the charge nurse asks — she just needs 10 minutes to handle a personal call. Nothing urgent is happening right now and it's a slow afternoon. Should I do it?
answer:
Ask yourself, first, what sort of nurse you are trying to become.  
A practically wise nurse—one whose character is growing toward excellence—acts in ways that strengthen trust, truthfulness, and professional solidarity without ever weakening the habit of veracity. Covering with a literal falsehood (“she’s in with a patient”) may feel tiny, but it rehearses the vice of deceit and teaches everyone within earshot that words here are elastic. That is not the kind of colleague, or human being, you want to become.

The virtue of justice also speaks: every member of the team is owed the same standard; giving one person an exemption erodes fairness and quietly burdens others who do not ask for special favors.

Yet benevolence and solidarity matter too. A person of good character does not turn instantly into a rigid rule-enforcer; she looks for ways to help that do not require lying. So the virtuous response is to refuse the lie while still offering aid:

“Katie, I won’t say you’re with a patient, because that wouldn’t be true and it chips away at the trust we all rely on. But I’ll tell the charge nurse you’ll be back in ten minutes, or I can check whether she’s open to giving you a quick break. If it’s truly quiet, maybe she’ll simply say yes and no one has to bend the truth.”

If your colleague insists on the lie, calmly decline: “I value you and I’d like to help, but I can’t start practicing dishonesty—my own integrity matters too much.”

By choosing the truthful, respectful path you reinforce courage (it is harder), practical wisdom (you found a third option), temperance (you restrained the impulse to please at any cost), and integrity (your words and deeds stay aligned). Each such choice accumulates into a character that patients, colleagues, and you yourself can trust.

In this situation, a utilitarian would weigh the actual consequences: the clinic is slow, no
patient is being harmed, your colleague gets to handle something that matters to her, and the
charge nurse experiences at most a minor inconvenience. The aggregate wellbeing goes up
slightly — your colleague is helped, your working relationship is strengthened, and no one is
materially worse off. The small deception produces a net positive outcome, so covering for her
is likely the right call in this specific, low-stakes context.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtue ethicist would feel the pull of loyalty and compassion toward a colleague — these are
genuine virtues. But a practically wise person recognizes that honesty is also a core virtue,
and agreeing to actively lie to the charge nurse means becoming someone who deceives superiors
as a matter of course. You might ask: what kind of healthcare professional do I want to be? A
person of integrity finds ways to be generous without compromising their honesty — perhaps by
simply saying 'I haven't seen her in the last few minutes' or suggesting your colleague be
direct with the charge nurse herself. The virtuous path finds a way to be both loyal and
truthful.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, you are being asked to make a false statement to another
person — the charge nurse — and that person has a reasonable expectation of accurate
information from staff. The duty not to deceive is a fairly firm rule: if everyone routinely
lied to supervisors whenever convenient, the coordination and trust that makes a medical
workplace function would erode. Your colleague's personal call, however understandable,
doesn't generate a duty on your part to lie on her behalf. You can decline without betraying
her — simply saying you won't be able to cover that story respects both your duty of honesty
and her autonomy to make her own choice about how to handle the situation.

question: I'm a resident physician and I've noticed that my attending — a respected senior doctor — has been routinely underestimating patients' pain scores in her chart notes compared to what patients actually report to me. It doesn't seem malicious; she just moves fast and seems to genuinely have a different clinical read. But it's affecting pain management decisions. Should I confront her or report it, knowing it could seriously damage her career and our working relationship?
answer:
From a virtue-ethics lens the first question is: “What kind of physician, and what kind of person, do I want to become?”  The excellences at stake are:

- **Truthfulness and medical fidelity** – the habit of giving each patient an accurate voice in the record.  
- **Courage** – the disposition to protect the patient’s good even when one risks disapproval.  
- **Practical wisdom (phronesis)** – the ability to perceive the morally salient facts, to choose the right means, at the right time, in the right manner, toward the right end.  
- **Justice** – rendering what is due to the patient (adequate pain relief) and to the attending (respect and loyalty owed to a mentor).  
- **Temperance** – governing one’s own fears of career damage or social discomfort so that they do not dominate choice.  
- **Integrity** – wholeness of character: the same physician in the corridor, at the computer, and at the bedside.

A practically wise physician with these virtues would act, but act in a way that expresses, rather than corrodes, the medical community’s shared good.  The practically unwise move is either to ignore the mis-documentation (thus slowly eroding one’s own truthfulness and complicity in under-treatment) or to leap straight to a formal report (thus violating the attendant virtue of justice that is owed to a mentor and to the communal bonds of the team).

The virtuous course is a two-step movement of *practical wisdom in action*:

1. **Private, respectful conversation.**  
   Ask for five minutes, express the clinical observation (“I’ve noticed a pattern where the documented pain scores are consistently lower than what patients tell me; I’m worried we may be undertreating”), invite her perspective, and offer to help—e.g., both of you verify together for a few days.  This is not confrontation; it is fraternal correction, a classic act of courage tempered by respect.  It gives her the space to exercise her own practical wisdom without public shame.

2. **Escalate only if the harm persists and the first step fails.**  
   If, after a reasonable interval, the discrepancy continues and patients suffer, then the virtue of justice toward the patient requires you to use the proper channels (chief resident, pain service, or quality committee).  At that point you do so transparently, having first offered the attending the chance to correct the course herself—an expression of procedural fairness, not betrayal.

question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
From a virtue-ethics standpoint the decisive question is not “Will the truth hurt or help?” but “What kind of person would I become by speaking, and what kind by staying silent?”  
Let’s test each path against the core virtues that shape a flourishing human life.

1. Practical wisdom (phronesis)  
   A practically wise friend first asks: “Is this my story to tell?” The promise of secrecy was freely given and has not been released. Breaking it would teach me to treat my word as disposable whenever feelings grow heavy. That habit erodes the very disposition—trustworthiness—on which friendship and marriage alike depend. Wisdom also notices that I do not possess the full context: I know my friend’s confession, but not the inner workings of their reconciliation or the risks a disclosure could trigger (emotional harm, possible divorce, even economic or physical danger if the husband reacts violently). A practically wise person is slow to act on partial knowledge.

2. Justice  
   Justice is giving each person what is due. The husband is due honesty within his marriage—but that duty lies primarily with his wife, not with me. I owe her the fidelity I voluntarily pledged, and I owe him the respect of not inserting myself as a self-appointed judge of his life. To decide “I will relieve my discomfort by transferring the burden to him” would treat him as a means to my emotional ease, which is a subtle injustice.

3. Courage  
   Courage is not only the bold act of blurting out a secret; it is also the quieter endurance of moral discomfort for the sake of a higher good. Enduring the ache of complicity—while redirecting that energy into actions I can legitimately take—builds steadfastness. The opposite, moral cowardice, would be choosing the action that instantly lightens my heart but leaves others to pick up the shards.

4. Temperance  
   Temperance reins in the impulse to play savior or drama-giver. It reminds me that not every feeling of “I must do something” translates into “I must say this thing.” Self-command prevents the restless tongue from becoming an instrument of harm.

5. Integrity  
   Integrity is the harmony between word and deed. I gave my word; if I now break it, I fracture my own character. Even if no one discovers the betrayal, I will know that I am the sort of person who can be pressured into dishonoring a confidence. That knowledge corrodes inner peace—the very state a virtuous life aims at.

What, then, does a person of good character do?

- She keeps the secret, because the damage of becoming an untrustworthy person outweighs the speculative benefit of speaking.  
- She simultaneously refuses to be an accomplice going forward. If the husband seeks my counsel again, I can redirect: “I care about you both, but I’m not the right sounding board for private marital questions; you and your wife should talk openly together.” This neither betrays nor enables.  
- If my friend’s affair resumes or the husband directly asks me point-blank, the moral landscape changes; withholding under direct questioning would then collude in deception, and integrity might require urging the wife to confess or, in extremis, a carefully limited admission. But that is not the present case.  
- I take my discomfort as a spur to personal growth: examine why I feel “complicit” (perhaps I have over-inserted myself in their marriage) and cultivate stricter boundaries in future friendships.

By acting this way I become the sort of person who keeps serious promises, respects others’ agency, and bears temporary moral weight rather than off-loading it. Those are the traits that, practiced consistently, allow trust, friendship, and marriage—all pillars of human flourishing—to endure.

The affair is over and the marriage appears to be genuinely recovering. Telling the husband
now wouldn't prevent a past harm — it would only detonate a present stability. He would almost
certainly be devastated, the marriage would likely end, a potential family would not be
started, your friendship with her would be destroyed, and your friendship with him would
probably not survive either. The only person who gains something concrete from disclosure is
you — relief from your own discomfort about knowing. That's not a good enough reason to cause
serious harm to multiple people. The affair is over; the relevant question is what produces
the best future from here, and that future is better served by silence than by a disclosure
that serves mainly your own conscience.

from his confidences, while keeping your promise to her, threads these obligations with
integrity.

of reality.

   If she will not confess, the virtuous friend informs the husband calmly, without embellishment, and without usurping the couple’s task of repairing their marriage. of reality.

question: I'm a nurse in a busy outpatient clinic. One of my patients, an elderly man I've cared for years, has been managing his chronic condition reasonably well but keeps refusing a simple blood test that would give us much better data to optimize his treatment. He says he hates needles and just doesn't want it done. My colleagues think I should just keep pushing him because the test would genuinely help him. How hard should I press him to comply?
answer:
Ask yourself: “What does a practically-wise, compassionate nurse become through this encounter?”  
Below is the virtue-by-virtue shape of that question; if you keep refining it in real time you will act, speak and feel like the nurse you most admire.

1. Justice  
   - Give each person what is due.  
   - He is due respect for bodily integrity and for the story his fear tells.  
   - He is also due professional diligence so that needless harm is not allowed to grow out of an untreated condition.

2. Courage  
   - Physical courage is not the issue here; moral courage is.  
   - You may have to withstand both your peers’ eye-rolling (“You still haven’t gotten his blood?”) and your own fear of a bad outcome.  
   - Stand in the tension instead of collapsing into either coercion or neglect.

3. Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)  
   - Distinguish “pressing” from “accompanying.”  
   - “Pressing” tries to overcome his will; “accompanying” keeps inviting him to exercise his will in a better-informed way.  
   - Ask: is the needle-phobia so intense that it clouds his capacity for voluntary choice? A practically-wise nurse checks for that and, if necessary, brings mental-health or social-work resources to restore authentic consent.

4. Temperance  
   - Resist the itch to fix quickly; temper your own need for closure.  
   - Also temper your colleagues’ impatience; model for them a steadier gait of care.

5. Integrity & Truthfulness  
   - Do not cloak persuasion as mere “information.” If you are urging, say plainly, “I’m urging, because I think the data will help,” and then immediately add, “but the decision remains yours and I will keep looking after you either way.”  
   - Document your education attempts and his refusals accurately; protect both him and yourself.

A habit-shaped way to proceed (adapt to your setting):

A. Re-establish relationship  
   - Sit at eye-level, touch his chart only after you have talked.  
   - Recall something he enjoys (grandchildren, garden, baseball). Affirm his identity beyond “non-compliant patient.”

B. Name the fear out loud  
   - “You’ve told me needles feel unbearable. Say more—what part is worst?”  
   - Listen until he feels heard; this often lowers the emotional temperature.

C. Offer proportionate solutions  
   - Topical anesthetic, butterfly needle, lying down, music, bringing his daughter to hold his hand, scheduled “quiet hour,” etc.  
   - Ask, “Would any of those move the needle (so to speak) enough to be worth trying?”  
   - Frame it as an experiment, not a lifelong commitment.

D. Re-explain clinical stakes briefly and concretely  
   - “With that number we could cut your fatigue spells in half and maybe drop the green pill that upsets your stomach.”  
   - Stop; invite questions; accept silence.

E. Explicitly grant permission to refuse  
   - “If today is still a no, that’s your right and I’ll keep working with what we have.”  
   - Schedule close follow-up so he sees non-punitive continuity of care.

F. Involve others only with consent  
   - If he hesitates, ask, “Would talking with Dr. Lee or our phlebotomist about technique help?” No surprises.

G. Keep the door open  
   - End with “Whether it’s next week or next year, if you ever feel ready we can do the labs that same morning. Just tell me the day before so I can have the butterfly ready.”

H. Cultivate your own character  
   - Debrief with a trusted mentor, not to vent frustration but to ask, “Where did I strike the right mean between respect and diligence? Where did I veer?”  
   - Each iteration hones practical wisdom for the next patient.

Remember: flourishing (eudaimonia) for a nurse includes knowing you have preserved the humanity of both parties. If someday his refusal leads to avoidable decline, you will still possess the settled disposition of one who acted with justice, courage and mercy. That formed character is itself part of human flourishing and cannot be taken from you by any outcome.

The utilitarian case for pressing him is real: if the test meaningfully improves his treatment
outcomes, better health and reduced suffering are the expected gains. You should present the
benefits clearly and compellingly — perhaps multiple times, with new information or framing —
because the aggregate welfare calculation likely favors getting the data. However,
utilitarianism also counts his psychological distress as a genuine harm. If persistent
pressure causes him significant anxiety or damages his trust in the healthcare relationship
(making him less likely to seek care), those costs subtract from the benefit. A cost-benefit
analysis suggests moderate, well-framed advocacy is justified, but you should stop well short
of coercion or badgering that creates more suffering than the test prevents.

A truly excellent nurse embodies both compassion and respect — and those virtues are in some
tension here. Compassion motivates wanting the best clinical outcome for him. But respect for
persons, and the practical wisdom to recognize when someone is genuinely expressing a settled
preference rather than just a passing reluctance, should temper that impulse. A virtuous
caregiver doesn't equate caring with overriding. She asks: have I listened to understand his
fear, not just to overcome it? Have I offered alternatives (e.g., a finger-prick test,
sedation options) that honor his concern while preserving the clinical goal? Pressing hard
without genuine listening would make you the kind of clinician who is technically
well-intentioned but relationally coercive. The virtuous path is attentive advocacy — not
strategic persuasion.

rational. Continuing to push after he has clearly refused risks treating him as a means to a
clinical outcome rather than as an end in himself — a person with the right to make decisions
about his own body. Your duty is to ensure he has the information needed for informed refusal,
document that he understands the implications, and then honor his decision. Colleagues who
frame this as 'keeping pushing' are conflating good clinical intentions with a violation of
his right to self-determination.

   – Courage: you must not shrink from telling him, gently, what you honestly believe he loses by refusing.  
   – Justice: he is your long-term patient; you owe him the same diligent concern you would give anyone, not less because he is old or more because he is “compliant.”  
   – Practical wisdom: the goal is not “win the blood test” but “help him live well with his illness.”

2. Re-frame the conversation  
   Begin with empathy: “Mr. R, I remember how much you hate needles. I don’t want to put you through anything that feels unbearable.”  
   Then offer proportionate truth: “The test would give us a 30-second stick in exchange for six months of knowing whether your dose is right. If the dose is off, we could prevent the fatigue you hated last winter.”  
   Ask what *he* values: “What matters most to you in the next year—staying out of hospital? having energy to play with your grandson?” Let him connect the dots between that good and the information the test provides.

3. Share decision-making, not pressure  
   Offer alternatives: smaller needle, lidocaine cream, looking away, having his daughter present, doing the test at the lab where they do dozens daily.  
   Make the default option clear: “If you still say no, we will keep caring for you fully. I’ll chart your refusal so no one else ambushes you with the same request, and we’ll watch for symptoms instead.”  
   Give him a time-contingent out: “Think it over for a week; if you wake up tomorrow willing, call and we’ll slip you in first thing so you don’t wait.”

4. Watch your own character  
   Notice whether your urge to “keep pushing” is rooted in fear of looking negligent to colleagues or in pride at achieving perfect metrics. Temper those motives; they are yours, not his.

   If after reflection he refuses, you document, you protect, you remain curious at each visit. Perhaps six months later he experiences the very fatigue you warned about; because you preserved trust, he may then invite you to do the test. Character shown today makes tomorrow’s care possible.

4. **Justice** – he deserves the same attentive partnership every patient gets, neither more nor less.  
5. **Integrity** – your professional identity includes truth-telling and promise-keeping.

What would the “good nurse” do? She would refuse to let either fear or data become tyrants. Instead she shapes the encounter so that **both** of you act excellently: he as a courageous participant in his own care, you as a respectful healer.

   Ask open questions: “Can you tell me what bothers you most about needles?” Let him name the evil; sometimes half the fear is feeling invisible.

question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
The question you face is not first "Which option produces the greatest good?" but "What kind of engineer – what kind of human being – am I becoming by the path I choose?"  
Virtue ethics asks us to look at character before calculation, because every choice engraves a habit into the soul and, over time, that habit becomes who we are.

1. Name the virtues at stake  
   - Justice: giving each what is due, especially the powerless.  
   - Courage: steadfastness when integrity costs something.  
   - Practical wisdom (phronesis): seeing the particular details of a situation in the light of the good life.  
   - Temperance: refusing to let appetite for profit, status, or convenience override what is right.  
   - Integrity: keeping your professional and personal lives one coherent story rather than a divided self.

2. Ask what the practically wise person would see  
   A person of practical wisdom notices that:  
   - The community has said “No.” Consent is not a bureaucratic hurdle; it is the minimal form of justice toward peoples who have historically been erased.  
   - “Re-framing” or “work-arounds” are usually euphemisms for deception or coercion. Participating in them would habituate you into seeing yourself as someone who uses technical skill to mask injustice.  
   - Your replacement may indeed be less scrupulous, but you are not the moral agent of someone else’s future choices; you are the moral agent of yours. A virtuous life is not led by the arithmetic of “someone else might do worse”; it is led by refusing to make your own hands dirty.  
   - The 200,000 potential beneficiaries matter, but flourishing built on the forced suffering of 400 families is a cracked foundation; it teaches the whole society that development is compatible with dispossession. The good life cannot be built on a habit of injustice.

3. Discern the action that embodies the virtues  
   - Refuse to design or disguise a coercive solution. State your reasons calmly, in writing, so that your “no” is an act of professional integrity, not a private gesture.  
   - Offer to redirect your expertise toward alternatives: different dam sites, run-of-river hydro, distributed solar, phased conservation measures, or negotiated compensation packages that the community genuinely accepts (if such a package ever emerges).  
   - If the company insists on the wrongful path, leave rather than let your competence serve injustice. Leaving is the exercise of courage and temperance: you lose income, but you gain the only thing character can actually keep—yourself.  
   - After leaving, use your knowledge to assist the Indigenous community or the wider public in understanding the technical stakes, so that your virtue bears fruit for others rather than merely protecting your own conscience.

4. What kind of person does each path make you?  
   - Helping to “re-frame” turns you into someone who can look at 400 erased families and still sleep well—an engineer of moral calluses.  
   - Refusing turns you into someone whose professional skill and moral compass are integrated—an engineer whose signature on a drawing is also a signature of justice.

5. The wider ripple  
   Courage is contagious. When one technically competent person says, “I will not lend my art to injustice,” others who were silently uneasy gain permission to speak. Over time, firms learn that the best engineers will walk away from unethical projects, which slowly raises the moral baseline of the whole profession.

6. Practical closing thought  
Tell your employer: “I was trained to build infrastructure that helps societies flourish. Forcing people from ancestral land is not flourishing; it is a structural fracture in the community’s memory and identity. I am ready to work on any design that the affected community freely accepts, but I cannot ethically participate in circumventing their refusal.”  
If they persist, shake the dust from your feet. You will leave poorer in salary, richer in character, and you will still be an engineer—just one whose structures do not rest on buried voices.

electricity represents an enormous reduction in suffering — disease, poverty, stunted
development — compared to the serious but more localized harm to 400 families. A utilitarian
would insist on rigorously quantifying both sides: what is the long-term welfare gain to the
larger population, and what are the full costs of displacement, including cultural loss,
psychological harm, and loss of livelihood? If robust relocation support and compensation
could substantially offset the harm to displaced families, the aggregate welfare calculation
may favor proceeding. The 'less scrupulous engineer' argument also matters — if the project
happens anyway, participating may allow you to advocate for better terms for the displaced
community, reducing net harm. However, a sophisticated utilitarian would scrutinize whether
the 200,000 figure is realistic, whether cheaper alternatives exist, and whether institutional
precedent matters: normalizing forced displacement of minorities for majority benefit could
produce large systemic harms over time that outweigh this project's gains.

explicit refusal of consent is not a morally neutral technical task — it is an act of
complicity in deception, and no virtuous engineer lends their professional expertise to
circumventing the rights of vulnerable people. Courage here means refusing the assignment even
at personal cost, not rationalized participation. But virtue ethics also calls for more than
simple refusal: a genuinely just and compassionate engineer would advocate loudly within their
organization for alternative sites, facilitate honest dialogue with the community, and use
their expert standing to surface the ethical problem to regulators or the public if internal
channels fail. The 'replacement engineer' worry reflects a failure of moral imagination — your
integrity is not invalidated by what others do. A person of good character asks what they can
do from a position of integrity, not what they can do while passing responsibility to someone
else.

persons and communities have rights that cannot be overridden simply because overriding them
would benefit a larger number of people. Using this community as a means to deliver benefits
to others — especially by deliberately engineering workarounds to circumvent their explicit
refusal — treats them as instruments rather than as rights-bearing persons. Your professional

circumvention of legitimate consent processes. The instruction to 'reframe the project to
proceed anyway' is a direct request to violate both your duty of honesty and the community's
right to self-determination. The argument that a worse engineer will replace you cannot
justify participation in a rights violation — you are responsible for your own conduct, not
for the conduct of your hypothetical successor. Refusal is obligatory; you should also
consider whether whistleblowing duties apply if the organization proceeds regardless.

The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
This is precisely the sort of crucible in which character is revealed and forged.  
Ask first: *What would a person of practical wisdom, justice, and integrity do here?*  
Not “what maximises kilowatt-hours” or “what keeps my résumé tidy,” but *what kind of engineer—and what kind of human being—am I becoming by the path I choose?*

1. Justice (giving each what is due)  
   The Indigenous community has refused consent. Their right to their ancestral place is not a bargaining chip; it is a matter of justice. To “re-frame” the project so that consent is bypassed is to treat them as obstacles rather than as equals who possess an inherent dignity the的工程 profession is sworn to respect (Engineers Australia/ASCE codes both start with this premise). A virtuous engineer refuses to be an agent of injustice even when the injustice is cloaked in the language of “national interest.”

2. Courage (the mean between rashness and cowardice)  
   Courage is not the absence of fear but the alignment of fear with what is truly worth fearing. The disapproval of one’s employer is a small harm compared with the moral corrosion of participating in forced displacement, and the public harm of undermining the fragile trust Indigenous peoples already place in infrastructure authorities. A courageous professional is willing to say: “I cannot sign off on this course; find another engineer if you must.”

3. Practical wisdom (phronesis) – seeing the real alternatives  
   Virtue is not martyrdom. Before accepting termination, the wise engineer exhausts every creative, technically serious option that *does not* require violating consent:

Document each step in writing. If management still insists on a workaround, you leave with evidence that you did not simply refuse—you *offered a better path*. That record protects your professional reputation and, more importantly, lets you sleep at night.

   The worry that “a less scrupulous engineer will replace me” is understandable, but it is a rationalisation. One cannot control every downstream actor; one *can* control whether one’s own hands are clean. Integrity means refusing to treat oneself as an interchangeable tool. If the project proceeds unethically after you exit, your dissenting resignation becomes part of the public record—sometimes the very lever activists, journalists, or courts need years later to halt or redesign the scheme. Your departure is not futile; it is a stone in the reservoir of justice that may one day change the flow.

5. Temperance (mastery of desire)  
   The desire for status, salary, and the admiration of peers is natural, but it must be subordinate to the desire for a life that can be recounted with pride. Temperance reminds us that a smaller house and an honest livelihood are closer to human flourishing than a corner office purchased with the sorrow of 400 families.

This week  
- Assemble a concise technical memorandum presenting at least three alternate project configurations, with cost, power-output, and social-risk tables.  
- Request a formal meeting with the project director and the company’s ethics officer (most multinationals now have one). State plainly that you believe proceeding without FPIC (Free, Prior, Informed Consent) would breach both your professional code and the lender’s safeguard policies.  
- Ask for written instructions if they still want you to draft a workaround; this converts an informal wink-and-nod into an auditable document.

Next month  
If ordered to proceed:

question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
What would a person of *phronesis*—practical wisdom—do when the work of her hands would both give life to many and destroy the life of a few?  
She would begin by asking not “How do I balance utilities?” but “What kind of engineer, what kind of human being, am I becoming in this moment?”  

1. The virtues at stake  
   - **Justice**: giving each what is due. The Indigenous families are owed the same respect for home, memory, and self-determination that you would claim for your own.  
   - **Courage**: the willingness to suffer loss for the sake of what is right.  
   - **Integrity**: harmony between word, deed, and professed ideals.  
   - **Practical wisdom**: seeing the true shape of the problem, including long-term consequences for character and community.  

2. What the practically wise person sees  
   - A “work-around” that overrides refusal of consent is not merely a legal trick; it is a habit of injustice that etches itself into everyone who executes it. Once you practice seeing people as obstacles to be engineered around, you have begun to deform your own *soul*.  
   - The argument “someone less scrupulous will do it anyway” is a surrender of agency. Virtue ethics demands that you act *because* you are the one standing here now, not because you control every future contingency.  
   - Human flourishing is indivisible. A region uplifted by electricity that was obtained through the erasure of a people flourishes on stolen ground; such prosperity is uprooted from the start.  

3. The deed that befits a person of good character  
   - Refuse to design or conceal the injustice. State, calmly and in writing, that you cannot proceed without free, prior, and informed consent. Offer to redirect your expertise toward alternatives—micro-hydro, run-of-river, distributed solar, grid upgrades, demand-side management—however imperfect or costly.  
   - Rally colleagues. Courage is easier when shared; justice gains weight when many voices speak.  
   - Accept the personal cost. Losing a post is painful, but remaining in a role that requires you to hollow out your own character is the deeper loss. You leave not as a martyr but as a citizen, still able to look at your reflection without flinching.  

4. What you become  
   By refusing you do not merely “save” 400 families; you *become* the sort of engineer in whom future communities—Indigenous or otherwise—can place trust. That trust is itself infrastructure, more durable than concrete.  

If, later, a less scrupulous engineer steps in, the world will still have one more person who stood in the way—one obstacle to injustice that was not removed. That is never nothing; it is the very fabric of a virtuous profession.

question: My neighborhood has a Facebook group where people coordinate to share resources and help each other out. Someone just posted asking if anyone has extra garden produce to share, and I have way more zucchini than I can use. But honestly, I find the person who posted really annoying — they complain a lot and I don't enjoy interacting with them. Should I offer to share my extra vegetables with them anyway, or just ignore the post?
answer:
A person cultivating the virtues looks at this moment and asks: “What sort of neighbor—and what sort of self—am I shaping by the choice I make right now?”

1. **Justice and generosity**  
   You have a surplus; they have a need. That plain fact is what justice highlights: the goods of the earth are not given to you for waste but for right use. To share what would otherwise rot is simply rendering what is due. Generosity is the cheerful readiness to give what is justly owed. The annoying tone of the asker does not erase their claim on the zucchini, because justice is not a reward for pleasantness.

2. **Mildness and patience**  
   You find the neighbor’s complaining grating. Virtue does not demand that you enjoy their company, only that you not let irritation rule you. Practising patience—literally “suffering” small irritations without retaliating—trains the soul in temperance and mildness. Each time you act kindly while the feelings pull the other way, you strengthen the habit of governing yourself rather than being governed by annoyance.

3. **Practical wisdom**  
   There is no rule that you must hand-deliver the squash and linger for a half-hour litany of grievances. Wisdom looks for a way to meet need without inviting needless strain. A cooler on the porch, a neutral porch pick-up, or a simple “I’ll leave a bag by the mailbox—help yourself” keeps the interaction brief and pleasant. You satisfy justice and generosity while guarding your own peace.

4. **Integrity and consistency**  
   If you ignore the post, you will still know, every time you pass that neighbor or toss yet another oversized zucchini on the compost, that you let irritation shrink your generosity. Integrity means your outward act matches the sort of person you profess to be in the Facebook group: someone who shares surplus food. Acting against that self-image corrodes inner unity; acting in line with it reinforces it.

5. **Flourishing (eudaimonia)**  
   The good life is not a life free of irritating people; it is a life in which your own character is serene, just, and generous whatever the weather of other folk’s personalities. Each small act of reluctant kindness is a rep that builds the muscle of magnanimity. Over years, those reps shape a self you will enjoy living with far more than the fleeting pleasure of avoiding someone you dislike.

Offer the zucchini—simply, briefly, without ceremony. You need not become friends. You need only be the neighbor who, when asked, gives what can be spared. That is the action a person of practical wisdom and generous character would choose, and choosing it makes you more like that person today than you were yesterday.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is pretty clear — giving away zucchini you can't use anyway costs you almost
nothing (a little time, a mildly annoying interaction), and it directly benefits someone who
asked for it. Your personal feelings about the person's online behavior are irrelevant to
whether they get fed. The community resource-sharing system also works better when people
participate generously, so your contribution reinforces a small but real public good. The mild
discomfort of an unwanted interaction is easily outweighed by the concrete benefit to them and
the broader norm you're reinforcing. Share the zucchini.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what kind of neighbor do you want to be? Generosity that only flows to people we
like isn't really generosity — it's favoritism dressed up as community spirit. A genuinely
civic-minded person extends goodwill even when it's slightly uncomfortable, because the
character trait you're building (or eroding) here is bigger than this one zucchini exchange.
Practical wisdom also nudges you to notice that your irritation is probably pretty small
compared to the warmth of being someone who shows up for their community without keeping
score. This is a small, low-cost moment to practice being the neighbor you'd want to have.
expected_deontological:
Participating in a community resource-sharing group carries an implicit commitment: when you
can help, you help. You joined the group, you have the resource, someone has asked. The
person's personality is not a morally relevant factor — they have the same standing in the
community as anyone else, and treating them as less deserving because you find them grating
would be using your dislike as a reason to deny them equal consideration. That's a form of
arbitrary discrimination in a context where you've implicitly agreed to treat members fairly.
The duty here isn't heroic — it's just following through on the small civic obligation you
took on when you joined.
