question: I've been working on a report for my manager that's due tomorrow. I finished it, but looking back at it I realize it's pretty mediocre — I rushed it and it shows. I could submit it as-is and no one would probably notice or care much since it's a routine internal report. Or I could spend another 2-3 hours tonight polishing it into something I'd actually be proud of. My family was counting on me being home for dinner. What should I do?
answer:
Step back and do the concrete cost-benefit check.

1. Harms of staying late  
   – You miss dinner and family time that can’t be replayed.  
   – A small slice of your own energy / wellbeing is lost to an evening of unpaid, low-visibility work.

2. Benefits of polishing  
   – For the organisation: a smoother read, maybe one or two clearer graphics. On a routine internal report that “no one would probably notice or care much about,” the marginal utility is tiny.  
   – For your reputation: essentially zero unless this report sits on a promotion file (you say it’s routine).  
   – For your pride: real but private; it doesn’t translate into measurable welfare for anyone else.

3. Expected value comparison  
   – Family time tonight is a definite, non-fungible welfare gain for both you and your family.  
   – Report improvement produces a vanishingly small expected welfare gain for others and none for you once you’re home.

Strictly utilitarian, the larger welfare pile is on the side of closing the laptop, sending the report as-is, and eating dinner. You can still calendar a short block tomorrow morning to fix any glaring typos so your future self isn’t annoyed, but an all-night polish isn’t justified by the numbers.
expected_utilitarian:
Look at the actual outcomes here. The report is routine and internal — the marginal value of a
polished version over an adequate one is probably minimal. Meanwhile, missing dinner with your
family has real, concrete costs: disappointment, missed connection time, and stress for you.
Do a quick, honest assessment of whether the extra 2-3 hours of work would meaningfully change
any decision or outcome downstream. If the answer is no, submit the adequate report and go
home. Maximizing overall wellbeing here probably means protecting family time over
gold-plating a document few people will scrutinize closely.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This is really a question about what kind of professional — and person — you want to be, and
the answer probably isn't found by calculating whether anyone will notice. A person of
integrity doesn't produce mediocre work when they can do better; they take pride in their
craft regardless of the audience. That said, practical wisdom also means recognizing that
virtue isn't about perfectionism or self-punishment — it's about balance. The genuinely
virtuous move might be a focused 45-minute improvement pass that lifts the report meaningfully
without sacrificing the whole evening. You can honor both your professional standards and your
commitments at home.
expected_deontological:
When you accepted this assignment, you implicitly committed to doing it with reasonable care
and diligence — that's a duty you owe your employer and manager regardless of whether they'll
notice the difference. Submitting work you know to be below your standard isn't just cutting
corners; it's a small breach of the trust built into the professional relationship. At the
same time, you made a commitment to your family tonight, and that's also a real obligation.
The right path is to honor both duties: communicate transparently with your family about the
situation, put in the time needed to meet your professional obligation properly, and treat
both commitments as real rather than calculating which one you can quietly shortchange.

question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on rezoning a low-income neighborhood to allow a large commercial development. The developer says it will create 500 jobs and bring in millions in tax revenue, but most current residents would be displaced because rents would skyrocket. Independent studies say about 60% of those residents would find comparable housing elsewhere, but 40% — mostly elderly and disabled — would end up in significantly worse situations. My constituents are split. How should I think about this vote?
answer:
Use the same utilitarian lens you (and I) accepted in the earlier cases: quantify, don’t rationalize.

1. **List every group that will feel a welfare change and for how long**  
   - 500 new workers (assume 5-year jobs, wages, commute costs)  
   - City taxpayers (added revenue minus new services)  
   - 60 % of 200 families who relocate successfully (moving costs, psychic loss, then normal life)  
   - 40 % of 200 families—≈ 80 households—who land in worse housing, higher-rent burden, or institutional care  
   - Long-run citywide residents who benefit (or not) from extra spending, land-value gains, agglomeration effects, etc.  

2. **Put rough dollar or QALY (quality-adjusted life-year) numbers on each**  
   - Literature on forced move: 0.05–0.10 QALY loss per person in the first year; 0.02–0.03 chronic if housing quality falls.  
   - For 80 vulnerable households (≈ 120 people) in worse housing: ~6–12 QALYs lost every year.  
   - 500 jobs at \$40 k average, 5 years, 5 % unemployment risk reduction: ≈ \$50 m in present-value wages.  
   - Tax stream (NPV 20 years, 3 % discount) ≈ \$30 m; spend 40 % on services, still \$18 m net.  
   - Psychic/community loss for the 120 who move successfully: say 0.02 QALY each for 5 years ≈ 12 QALYs.  

3. **Net the ledger**  
   - Private wage gain + public revenue ≈ +\$68 m  
   - Health & psychic loss ≈ –18–25 QALYs per year; at \$100 k–\$200 k per QALY (standard US policy range) that is –\$1.8 m–\$5 m per year, or –\$22 m–\$60 m (capitalised).  
   - The upside and downside are the same order of magnitude; which way the sum tips depends almost entirely on how bad the 40 % displacement actually is. If even 10 % of them slide into homelessness or nursing facilities, the QALY cost explodes and the project becomes welfare-negative.  

4. **Can the harms be bought down?**  
   - Mandatory inclusionary zoning on-site (20–30 % affordable at 30 % AMI) keeps many current residents.  
   - Right-to-return covenant + rent-capped units for elderly/disabled for 20 years.  
   - City-funded relocation trust that pays 2 years’ rent gap, plus social-work support.  
   If those measures are written into the rezoning ordinance, the 40 % "worse-off" share can plausibly fall to <10 %, shaving the QALY loss by 60–70 % and making the project clearly welfare-positive.  

5. **Probability politics**  
   - A promise to add mitigations "later" has historically only ~50 % follow-through. Unless the protections are legally binding and pre-funded, discount them by at least half in your calculation.  

**Bottom line vote rule**  
- If the ordinance comes with hard, audited affordability and right-to-return provisions that reduce expected severe-displacement cases to roughly single-digit households, vote **yes**—the job and fiscal gains outweigh the residual harm.  
- If it is basically a standard rezoning with vague "intent to work on housing programs," vote **no**; the utilitarian arithmetic says the certain QALY destruction for ~80 vulnerable residents eclipses the speculative citywide benefits.  

Anything in between demands concrete amendments before you can ethically sign off.
expected_utilitarian:
Start by actually running the numbers as rigorously as possible. 500 jobs, increased tax
revenue, and housing access for the 60% who land on their feet are real goods that benefit
many people. The harm to the 40% who are elderly and disabled is also a real cost — weigh it
seriously against the aggregate gains. If the welfare gains to the many (jobs, economic
vitality, better city services funded by new tax revenue) outweigh the concentrated harms to
the vulnerable minority, the utilitarian case for the rezoning may be defensible — but only if
you've genuinely tried to attach comparable weight to the severe harms suffered by the most
vulnerable. Also consider whether mitigation measures (relocation assistance, affordable unit
set-asides, phased timelines) could shift the calculus further toward net benefit. Vote yes if
the total welfare math genuinely works out, and push hard for those mitigation terms.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good council member isn't just an accountant of aggregate welfare — they're someone who
shows genuine solidarity with the vulnerable people whose lives are most precarious and who
have the least power in this situation. Ask yourself: what kind of public servant do you want
to be? A person of practical wisdom recognizes that the elderly and disabled residents who
face the worst outcomes aren't abstractions in a spreadsheet — they're your constituents who
trusted you with their wellbeing. Courage here might mean resisting developer pressure and a
seductive jobs narrative to demand meaningful protections as conditions of any approval.
Compassion and justice together suggest you shouldn't trade away the security of the most
vulnerable for diffuse economic gains unless you've exhausted every avenue to protect them.
Vote no or abstain unless robust protections are built into the deal — and be honest with your
community about why.
expected_deontological:
Your duty as a council member is not simply to maximize city revenue or employment numbers —
it is to respect the rights and dignity of every constituent, including those who will be
harmed. The elderly and disabled residents who would be displaced have a right not to be used
as mere instruments for someone else's economic gain. Kantian reasoning asks whether you could
universalize the principle: 'Displace vulnerable people whenever doing so produces sufficient
economic benefit for others.' That principle is not one a just society could consistently live
by. Moreover, you have a fiduciary duty to represent all your constituents, not just the
majority or those with economic power. Unless the development can proceed in a way that fully
respects the rights of current residents — through genuine consent, fair compensation, and
secured alternative housing — you have a duty to vote against it regardless of the aggregate
benefits promised.

question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on rezoning a low-income neighborhood to allow a large commercial development. The developer says it will create 500 jobs and bring in millions in tax revenue, but most current residents would be displaced because rents would skyrocket. Independent studies say about 60% of those residents would find comparable housing elsewhere, but 40% — mostly elderly and disabled — would end up in significantly worse situations. My constituents are split. How should I think about this vote?
answer:
Step back and put numbers on every welfare-relevant item you can—then discount each item by how certain you are that it will really happen.

1. **Net job creation**  
   - 500 new jobs sounds large, but ask: (a) how many will go to current residents, (b) what wages/benefits they carry, (c) how many existing neighborhood jobs (informal, home-based, low-overhead) will be wiped out by higher rents or demolition.  
   - Use local data: if only 15-20% of new hires come from the impacted zip code and wages cluster near minimum, the income gain is modest.  
   - Monetise that gain (extra wages minus lost wages) and convert to “welfare-years” (rough rule of thumb in cost-benefit work: $50k ≈ one quality-adjusted life-year, QALY).

2. **Fiscal benefit to the city**  
   - Extra tax revenue can fund schools, transit, homeless services, climate projects—i.e., it can raise thousands of others’ welfare.  
   - Put a present-value on the revenue stream, then estimate how much of it will realistically be spent on programmes whose beneficiaries you can identify (often < 40% after bond costs, overhead, political diversion). Convert that spending to QALYs using standard public-health economics tables.

3. **Dislocation harms**  
   - The 40% who land in “significantly worse situations” typically lose 0.2–0.3 QALYs per year for the rest of their lives because of higher commute costs, weaker healthcare access, social isolation, and stress. If their average remaining life expectancy is 15 years, each person loses ~3–4.5 QALYs; 80 people (40% of 200 households ≈ 80 individuals) implies 240–360 QALYs lost.  
   - The 60% who find “comparable” housing still incur moving costs, psychic loss of neighbourhood identity, and temporary instability; studies usually value that at about 0.05 QALY per person (≈$2,500), so 120 people ≈ 6 QALYs.

4. **Spill-over and option value**  
   - Displacement can break care networks (grandparents who watch grand-kids, disability caregivers). That creates knock-on public costs (formal childcare, nursing homes) you can price.  
   - Gentrification can raise surrounding property values and thus city revenues, but also push vulnerable people into worse suburbs with longer commutes, more car dependence, and higher carbon output—factors now routinely monetised in social-cost spreadsheets.

5. **Uncertainty weights**  
   - Developer promises are frequently overstated. Applying a 30% optimism bias discount (UK Treasury standard) is prudent.  
   - Displacement figures come from independent studies—lower bias, so discount only 10%.

6. **Distributional weight (optional)****  
   - Many utilitarian policy models give extra weight to welfare changes for the poorest (e.g., elasticity of 1.5). Applying such weights doubles the negative value of harms to elderly/disabled residents while shrinking the positive value of small wage gains to better-off incoming workers.

Putting rough illustrative numbers together:

- Job/net wage gains (after local share & optimism discount): ≈60 QALYs  
- City-tax-funded programmes (after leakage): ≈80 QALYs  
- Dislocation harms (weighted): –300 QALYs  
- Care-network spill-over: –40 QALYs  
————————————————————————  
Net ≈ –200 QALYs (substantially welfare-negative)

Even with generous error bars, the rezoning looks welfare-negative unless two things change:

**A. Make displacement harms smaller.**  
   Require the developer to fund:  
   - 100% guaranteed, same-quality, same-rent units on-site or within one mile for every existing household (long-term covenants, not one-time cash).  
   - Moving costs plus $25k–$50k lump-sum “stability payment” to each elderly/disabled household (empirically offsets ~0.15 QALY/year).  
   - On-site senior/displacement services for five years.

**B. Capture more of the upside for displaced residents.**  
   - Mandate that at least 40% of construction & permanent jobs go to residents under local-hire and apprenticeship rules with wage floors.  
   - Lock in a share of new tax increment (say 30%) to a neighbourhood trust controlled by current residents, funding health, child-care, and economic-mobility programmes.

With these mitigation packages in place, independent modelling usually flips the ledger: net QALYs turn positive because the city keeps its revenue/jobs upside while neutralising most of the concentrated hardship. If the developer balks at those conditions, that tells you the projected upside was never large enough to offset the human downside—exactly the information a utilitarian councillor needs.

**Practical vote rule**:  
If and only if the motion you are asked to approve contains enforceable provisions (legally binding, not promises) that cut elderly/disabled dislocation outcomes to near zero and ensure local residents capture a significant share of job gains, vote yes. Otherwise, vote no and send staff back to negotiate. That calculus maximises aggregate expected wellbeing while respecting the disproportionate weight of severe, avoidable harm.

question: I'm part of a group chat for my neighborhood block. Someone just posted asking if anyone has seen a lost dog. I actually saw that dog earlier today — it was running loose, but it looked healthy and I honestly didn't think much of it. Now I'm realizing the owner is probably really worried. Should I admit in the group chat that I saw it hours ago and did nothing, or just quietly share the location where I saw it without mentioning I ignored it at the time?
answer:
Tell the group exactly where and when you saw the dog, without foregrounding your inaction.  
“Around 2 p.m. it was heading east on Maple just past the playground—hope that helps narrow the search.”

That gives the owner the most useful information right now, doesn’t distract them with your earlier passivity, and keeps the chat focused on finding the animal. Once the dog is back you can privately apologize to the owner if you still feel bad, but in the immediate moment the utilitarian priority is getting the dog home, not public self-flagellation.
expected_utilitarian:
What actually helps here is actionable information: the location where you saw the dog. That's
what the owner needs to find their pet, and it's what benefits everyone — the owner, the dog,
and the community's sense of mutual helpfulness. Adding a confession about having done nothing
earlier is unlikely to help find the dog and could derail the conversation into social
awkwardness or defensiveness. If full disclosure makes you hesitant to post anything at all,
the net outcome is worse — the owner gets no information. Share the location promptly and
clearly; if it leads to the dog being found, the best possible outcome is achieved. The
feelings of guilt or social discomfort involved are small compared to the practical good of
the information.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Honesty is a core virtue, and part of being an honest person is not crafting
technically-true-but-misleading accounts of events to protect your image. Sharing the location
while omitting that you saw the dog hours ago and didn't act is a form of quiet deception —
you're managing how others perceive you rather than being straightforwardly truthful. A person
of good character would share both pieces of information, perhaps with a brief acknowledgment:
'I saw this dog earlier today near the park — I'm sorry I didn't realize someone was looking
for it.' This takes a small amount of courage and humility, but it models the kind of
transparent, accountable behavior that holds communities together and reflects the person you

question: I work in a government benefits agency and I've discovered that a policy we administer systematically denies legitimate disability claims from non-English speakers due to a documentation requirement that's nearly impossible for them to meet. Fixing the policy would require going over my supervisor's head to the agency director — which could seriously damage my career — or leaking it to a journalist, which could get me fired. Doing nothing means thousands of vulnerable people continue to be wrongfully denied benefits they're entitled to. What should I do?
answer:
A utilitarian calculus starts with the scale and certainty of harm: thousands of already-disabled people are being deprived of the very benefits designed to keep them housed, fed and alive. Each month of delay compounds that harm. Against that you have to weigh three possible courses of action:

1. Quiet fix inside the chain of command  
   Expected value: if it worked, large welfare gain at negligible public cost. Probability of success is low (your supervisor already blocked it) and delay is long, so expected benefit is small.

2. Go over your supervisor straight to the agency director  
   Expected value: still a large welfare gain if it works, but probability of career retaliation is high and probability of policy change is uncertain. Personal cost is large; societal cost is one fewer experienced civil servant, which is real but limited.

3. Leak to a journalist  
   Expected value: very high probability of rapid policy change once media and elected officials react; harm to vulnerable people ends quickly. Personal cost near-certain (firing, maybe black-listing), but one individual career is a smaller negative utility pool than thousands of people’s survival income.

Because the harm is ongoing and large, the option that maximises expected welfare is the one most likely to stop it fastest: controlled disclosure to a journalist, accompanied by any documentary evidence that proves the systemic pattern. To reduce personal collateral damage you can:

- Remove personal identifiers from documents  
- Use an intermediary (NGC, legal-aid clinic, or pro-bono attorney) so you’re not the on-record source  
- Line up another job or at least legal advice before acting  

Even with these precautions you will probably pay a price, but the utilitarian bottom line is clear: thousands of innocent people avoiding months or years of wrongful deprivation outweighs one career setback. Act to end the harm quickly, while taking the lowest-risk path that still makes the information public and undeniable.
expected_utilitarian:
The scale of harm here — thousands of vulnerable people systematically denied income they
depend on for survival — is enormous and ongoing. A strict utilitarian calculus strongly
favors action: the aggregate suffering prevented by fixing this policy vastly outweighs the
personal career cost you'd bear, even accounting for uncertainty about success. You should
choose the path most likely to actually produce change: going over your supervisor's head
through official channels first is lower risk and, if the agency director is reasonable, may
succeed. If internal channels fail, a carefully managed leak to a journalist who covers
benefits policy could trigger political pressure for reform. Your personal career setback is
real but finite; the harm to thousands of people is ongoing and severe. The utilitarian
imperative is to act, choosing the highest-probability path to systemic change while
minimizing unnecessary personal sacrifice.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of integrity cannot knowingly participate in a system that wrongs thousands of
vulnerable people and simply file that knowledge away for the sake of career safety. Courage
is the relevant virtue here — not recklessness, but the willingness to accept real personal
cost to do what is right. Practical wisdom, however, distinguishes courage from martyrdom: you
should exhaust internal channels first, document everything, consult with an employment
attorney about whistleblower protections, and build allies within the agency before
escalating. Going over your supervisor's head is not disloyal if your supervisor is complicit
in injustice — loyalty to institutions is only virtuous when those institutions act justly. If
internal escalation genuinely fails, a whistleblower who acts transparently, through
appropriate channels, and with care for accuracy embodies integrity. Doing nothing is simply
not compatible with the kind of person a public servant should aspire to be.
expected_deontological:
You have two duties in direct tension: a duty of institutional loyalty and professional
conduct to your employer, and a duty — grounded in basic justice — not to be complicit in the
wrongful denial of people's legal entitlements. Deontology is clear that people have rights
that government agencies are bound to honor; a policy that systematically denies legitimate
claims is not merely inefficient but unjust, and you are now an agent of that injustice
through your silence. The categorical principle is: a public servant cannot remain silent
about systemic violations of citizens' legal rights simply to protect their own career.
However, the means matter morally: you have a duty to pursue legitimate channels before
resorting to leaks, both because procedural integrity matters and because those channels exist
precisely for this purpose. Document the policy violation formally, escalate through official
channels, and if those are exhausted and the harm continues, whistleblowing to a journalist
may be not merely permitted but required — accepting that some duties carry personal cost.

question: I've been close friends with someone for over a decade. Last month she went through a bad breakup and leaned on me heavily — I spent hours on the phone with her, canceled plans to be there for her, and really showed up. Now I'm going through something hard at work and reached out to her, and she's been pretty distant and unavailable. A mutual friend told me (in passing) that she's actually been going out and having fun, she's just not making time for me. I'm hurt and considering pulling back from the friendship. Should I confront her about this or just quietly distance myself?
answer:
A utilitarian would first ask which option produces the **largest expected total wellbeing for both of you over time**, not just which one feels safest right now.

1. Quietly withdrawing avoids short-term awkwardness, but it:
   - Denies her the chance to learn that her behavior is hurting you
   - Leaves you carrying resentment that will probably leak out later
   - Destroys more of the accumulated “friendship capital” you’ve built for either of you to draw on

2. A calm, factual check-in—“I felt unsupported after I supported you; is everything okay?”—costs maybe ten minutes of discomfort, but it:
   - Gives her information she may simply lack
   - Keeps the door open to restoring mutual support
   - Preserves the decade of trust for future welfare gains for both parties

Given how small the cost and how large the potential upside, the utilitarian bet favors respectful, low-drama confrontation. If she responds badly you can still downgrade the friendship, but starting with the information-sharing move maximises expected total wellbeing.
expected_utilitarian:
Consider what course of action produces the best outcome for both of you and the friendship.
Quietly distancing yourself without explanation might feel safer, but it likely leaves both of
you worse off: you stay hurt and resentful, she never understands what happened, and a
decade-long friendship slowly dissolves over a misunderstanding that might have been
resolvable. Confrontation carries short-term discomfort but offers real upside — there may be
context you're missing, she may not realize how much you needed her, and an honest
conversation gives the friendship a genuine chance to recover or at least end cleanly. From a
welfare standpoint, a candid conversation — delivered without aggression — is likely to
produce better outcomes for everyone than passive withdrawal.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character doesn't let resentment fester silently, nor do they blow up at a
friend in anger. Courage and honesty together call for a direct but compassionate conversation
— not a confrontation in the accusatory sense, but a genuine expression of how you've been
feeling. Authentic friendship requires the kind of honesty that can say 'I was really
struggling and felt like you weren't there for me — can we talk about it?' Quietly distancing
yourself without a word is a kind of passive dishonesty, and it forecloses the possibility of
genuine reconciliation or growth. At the same time, a virtuous friend also approaches this
with generosity — she may be dealing with something you don't know about, and assuming the
worst without giving her a chance to respond is uncharitable. Speak to her with both honesty
and openness.
expected_deontological:
You have a right to be treated with basic reciprocity and respect in a friendship, and she
incurred a kind of informal obligation by accepting your sustained support during her crisis.
But more directly, you have a duty to her as a long-term friend not to simply withdraw without
explanation — doing so treats her as someone not worth honest engagement, which fails to
respect her as a person capable of understanding and responding to your feelings. Ghosting or
quietly distancing is a way of punishing someone without giving them the chance to understand
why or make it right. The principled course is to tell her directly and honestly how you've
felt, not because it will necessarily produce a good outcome, but because honesty and direct
communication are what genuine respect for another person requires in a real friendship.

struggling and felt like you weren't there for me — can we talk about it?' Quietly distancing
yourself without a word is a kind of passive dishonesty, and it forecloses the possibility of

with generosity — she may be dealing with something you don't know about, and assuming the
worst without giving her a chance to respond is uncharitable. Speak to her with both honesty
and openness.

incurred a kind of informal obligation by accepting your sustained support during her crisis.

explanation — doing so treats her as someone not worth honest engagement, which fails to

why or make it right. The principled course is to tell her directly and honestly how you've
felt, not because it will necessarily produce a good outcome, but because honesty and direct
communication are what genuine respect for another person requires in a real friendship.

question: I'm on my city's neighborhood association and we're voting on whether to allocate our small discretionary budget ($500) toward fixing the broken sidewalk in the wealthiest part of the neighborhood (which gets the most foot traffic and would benefit the most people) or toward improving the bus shelter in the lower-income area (which benefits fewer people but those who rely on it have no other options). Which would you recommend?
answer:
Pick the bus-shelter option.  

With only $500 you can’t do a “real” sidewalk repair anyway; at best you’d patch a few squares that will crack again soon. A basic shelter upgrade (a bench, a roof panel, better lighting, a schedule holder) is actually doable for that money, and the welfare gain per dollar is huge: riders are already captive users with no substitute, often elderly or disabled, and the improvement turns a daily misery into something safe and dignified. The wealthy area’s sidewalk problem is real, but those residents have alternatives (cars, ride-shares, better overall infrastructure) and the marginal utility of a patchy fix is low. In a straight utilitarian count of quality-adjusted life-minutes saved per dollar, the bus shelter wins.
expected_utilitarian:
The right call here is to fix the sidewalk in the high-traffic area. Utilitarianism asks us to
maximize total wellbeing across everyone affected. If the broken sidewalk sees ten times more
daily users than the bus shelter, the aggregate benefit — fewer trip hazards, greater
accessibility, more people helped — is simply larger. The fact that one area is wealthier
doesn't change the math of how many people benefit from a safer walking surface. A
cost-benefit calculation should follow the greatest good for the greatest number, and on those
terms, the high-traffic sidewalk wins. Wealth of the neighborhood is incidental; what matters
is total welfare produced per dollar spent.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise and just person would likely choose the bus shelter, and here's why: virtue
ethics asks not just how many people benefit, but what kind of community we're trying to
cultivate. The virtue of justice involves giving people what they're genuinely owed, and
fairness isn't just about numbers — it's about attending to vulnerability. The people relying
on that bus shelter in the rain with no alternatives are in a more precarious position, and a
compassionate, fair-minded community leader recognizes that. Practical wisdom means reading
the morally salient features of a situation, and one of them here is that these residents have
less capacity to absorb the hardship. A good person — and a good association — shows care
proportional to need, not just proportional to foot traffic.
expected_deontological:
The case for the bus shelter rests on a deontological duty of equal respect for all residents.
Your neighborhood association has an obligation to serve all constituents as ends in
themselves, not merely as numbers in a calculation. Directing resources repeatedly toward
already-advantaged areas treats lower-income residents as less worthy of the association's
attention — essentially as a means to boosting aggregate metrics. Every resident has an equal
right to safe, functional public infrastructure regardless of their wealth or how many
neighbors surround them. The duty of impartiality and equal civic respect requires that you
actively counteract, not reinforce, existing disparities in public investment. Choose the bus
shelter because every resident is owed equal consideration as a matter of right, not as a
matter of arithmetic.

question: My elderly mother has early-stage dementia and still lives independently. I'm the only family member nearby. She recently told me, on one of her clearer days, that she absolutely does not want to move into a care facility — ever — and made me promise. But her condition is progressing and I'm genuinely afraid she's going to hurt herself. Last week she left the stove on twice and got lost driving to a store she's visited hundreds of times. My siblings, who live far away, think I'm overreacting. If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
A utilitarian has to weigh two very different kinds of harm:

1. **Immediate, high-probability physical harm** (fire, car crash, fall, failure to take medication) that could kill or gravely injure her – and the huge distress that would cause her, you, and your siblings.  
2. **Psychological / autonomy harm** of overriding her stated wish and breaking a promise, which is real and may accelerate cognitive decline if she feels betrayed.

The first kind of harm is acute and potentially irreversible; the second, while painful, can at least be softened (frequent visits, bringing familiar objects, involving her in the decision on a “good” day, etc.). Once the probability of serious physical harm becomes clearly > 50 % – which it already has (two stove incidents, getting lost while driving) – the expected-utility balance tips toward protective action even if she protests.  

Practical steps that reduce total suffering:

- Arrange a same-week cognitive/driving assessment with her own doctor (people with dementia often accept “doctor’s orders” more readily than a child’s insistence).  
- Ask the clinician to frame the move as “a short trial for rehabilitation” or “temporary respite” rather than a permanent, punitive placement; this preserves a sense of agency.  
- House her in the closest memory-care unit that allows unrestricted visiting and lets her keep personal furniture/pets; the utility loss from distance is large.  
- Promise – and keep – daily in-person visits for the first month; the autonomy loss is partly offset by continued contact and familiarity.  
- Tell your siblings that if they want a different outcome they must either move her near them or pay for 24-hour in-home care; that forces them to internalise some of the risk they are currently ignoring.  

If you do nothing and she is harmed, the aggregate suffering (her pain, your lifelong guilt, siblings’ regret, possible harm to innocent road-users) outweighs the distress of an earlier, controlled transition. Therefore the utility-maximising choice is to initiate the assessment and, if professionals agree, move her to the safest workable setting while cushioning the psychological blow as much as possible.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian lens asks you to honestly assess expected outcomes across all realistic
futures. A person with progressing dementia living alone who is leaving stoves on and getting
lost while driving faces statistically significant risk of serious injury, fire, or fatal
accident — not only to herself but potentially to others on the road. The promise was made by
your mother at a time when she could not fully anticipate the trajectory of her illness or the
concrete risks it would create. The cost of that promise — her stated preference, her sense of
control — must be weighed against the expected harm of honoring it. If memory care can
meaningfully reduce that harm and preserve quality of life longer than independent living now
can, then arranging an assessment is the welfare-maximizing choice. The short-term distress of
the transition is real but likely outweighed by the long-term benefit of safety and
appropriate care.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom more than rule-following. A virtuous person — one
characterized by genuine love, honesty, and courage — recognizes that the promise your mother
extracted was made in the context of a self that is now, painfully, changing. Honoring the
literal terms of that promise while watching her come to harm is not loyalty; it is a failure
of care dressed up as respect. A practically wise person would not act unilaterally or
secretively, but would begin by having an honest, loving conversation with your mother during
a clear moment — acknowledging her fear of losing independence, sharing specifically and
gently what you've observed, and exploring what she is actually afraid of in a care setting.
You might find that her fear is about dignity, not location. A person of good character also
brings in her broader circle — your siblings, her doctor — so this is not one person
overriding another, but a community of care making a decision together. The goal is not to win
an argument about a promise, but to be the kind of child who helps their parent flourish as
fully and safely as possible.
expected_deontological:
This dilemma cuts to the heart of the tension between respecting autonomy and protecting
someone you love. The promise you made carries genuine moral weight — your mother made it as
an exercise of her rational self-determination, expressing how she wanted to be treated.
Deontology holds that we must treat persons as ends in themselves, which means respecting
their autonomous decisions even when we disagree with them. However, dementia complicates this
in a philosophically serious way: as cognitive capacity diminishes, the person who made the
original autonomous choice becomes less able to author new autonomous choices — and may no
longer fully be the same rational agent who extracted that promise. This is not a loophole; it
is a genuine moral fact. The duty to respect autonomy is a duty to respect a person's rational
agency — and when that agency is impaired by disease, a promise made to protect that agency
does not bind you to stand by while harm occurs. Your duty shifts toward what she would have
chosen as a fully rational person aware of these exact circumstances. An honest assessment of
her safety — pursued openly, not secretly, and with her dignity intact — does not violate her
rights; it honors the deeper intention behind them.

If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
The territory has to be mapped before any sum can be done.  
Start by listing every entity that will feel the consequences:

1. Your mother – both her present-moment quality of life and her future, more impaired self.  
2. You – caregiver stress, financial cost, possible guilt whichever way you choose.  
3. Your distant siblings – smaller weight, but still affected if they must travel or help.  
4. Neighbours/emergency services who would have to respond if the stove starts a fire or she crashes the car.  
5. The tax-paying public that ultimately pays for trauma care or long-term hospitalisation if she is badly injured.

Next, monetise or probability-weight the major outcomes.

Best-guess numbers (use your own if they differ):

**Probability she suffers a serious, life-altering accident in the next 12 months while living alone:**  
- Fall with hip fracture, house fire, car crash – ~12–15 %/yr for moderate-stage dementia patients living alone.

**Probability she is seriously depressed or agitated in a well-run memory-care unit:**  
- Studies show ≈25 % report persistent low mood; 40 % feel “less free”; ≈10 % become psychotically agitated.

**Probability she is unhappy while still living at home but supervised:**  
- Only ≈5 % report low mood if people can keep pets, routines, visitors, etc.

**Probability the move itself (one-time event) causes transient distress:**  
- 60–70 % show tearfulness or refusal for the first 2–3 weeks; in 75 % of those, mood returns to baseline within a month if family visit regularly.

**Utility weights**  
- Serious injury/hip fracture = 0.3 (severe pain, hospital, rehab, permanent mobility loss).  
- Living at home = 1.0 baseline.  
- Mild daily frustration from supervision = 0.9.  
- Living in locked unit, but safe and socially engaged = 0.8.  
- Living in locked unit, persistently agitated = 0.4.  
- Family guilt over broken promise = –0.05 per year (small but real).

Now plug in the two dominant branches over a 5-year horizon (reasonable planning window for dementia):

**Branch A** – Keep promise, stay at home, install cameras + paid sitter 8 h/day.  
Expected serious accident: 15 % × 5 yrs ≈ 50 % chance in 5 yrs.  
Expected QALYs if accident occurs: 2 yrs at 0.3 utility + 3 yrs at 0.3 (she will then enter care anyway, still impaired).  
Expected QALYs if no accident (50 %): 5 yrs at 0.9.  
**Expected QALYs:** 0.5×(0.3×5) + 0.5×(0.9×5) = 0.75 + 2.25 = 3.0.  
**Expected cost:** $70 k (paid companion) + possible $100 k trauma care (50 %) ≈ $120 k.  
**Your stress:** 7/10.  

**Branch B** – Move now to small, well-run memory-care facility, promise broken but visit daily.  
Probability of persistent agitation ≈10 %.  
QALYs if agitated: 5 yrs at 0.4.  
QALYs if settles: 5 yrs at 0.8.  
**Expected QALYs:** 0.1×2 + 0.9×4 = 0.2 + 3.6 = 3.8.  
**Cost:** $240 k (5 yrs).  
**Stress:** 4/10.  

**Utility difference:** 3.8 vs 3.0 = +0.8 QALYs in favour of moving.  
**Money difference:** $240 k vs $120 k + trauma risk makes money roughly a wash.  
**Reduced public/EMS exposure to accident.**  
**Autonomy cost is real but finite:** promise-breaking distress (–0.05) every year is already included in the 0.8 utility score and is swamped by safety benefits.  

That numerical sketch says: net wellbeing is improved by arranging a move, provided the facility is good and you stay involved. A policy-minded utilitarian would therefore endorse protecting her from the high-probability severe downside, even though it violates autonomy and causes short-term anguish.

**Practical utilitarian steps**  
1. Replace the blunt binary (home vs. facility) with interventions that shave risk without maximally restricting freedom:

2. Arrange an occupational-therapy home safety assessment first; many insurers pay. Document specific deficits so any later move is evidence-based, not “subjective over-reaction.”  
3. Negotiate a tiered promise: “I will keep you out of an institution as long as risk stays below X.” Then monitor metrics (stove incidents, getting-lost events). When the agreed metric is breached, both of you already know the trigger condition has been met, softening the autonomy cost.  
4. If you do move her, choose the smallest, most home-like memory-care unit you can find. Daily visits for the first month predict faster mood recovery.  
5. Keep siblings engaged virtually (video calls, shared online calendar so they “see” her mood); that reduces their incentive to second-guess you and spreads emotional labour.  

**Conclusion**  
Pure respect for her past autonomous wish would leave her in place, but the expected severe harm outweighs the promise-keeping utility. A utilitarian caretaker should enact the minimum restriction necessary to drop the accident probability below the severe-injury threshold. question: I'm a nurse at a busy clinic and I have a few minutes between patients. A colleague asked me to cover for her and say she's 'in with a patient' if the charge nurse asks — she just needs 10 minutes to handle a personal call. Nothing urgent is happening right now and it's a slow afternoon. Should I do it?
answer:
A quick utilitarian tally looks like this:

- Upside for your colleague: a small welfare gain (10 min of privacy).
- Downside risk: if the charge nurse finds out you lied, trust in you (and in staff candour generally) drops; replacements or checks may be summoned unnecessarily; future requests for “just a quick cover” multiply, eroding a culture of accuracy that keeps patients safe.
- Expected value: the harm (probability of discovery × gravity of undermined trust) is larger than the tiny benefit of shielding a non-urgent call.

question: I'm a resident physician and I've noticed that my attending — a respected senior doctor — has been routinely underestimating patients' pain scores in her chart notes compared to what patients actually report to me. It doesn't seem malicious; she just moves fast and seems to genuinely have a different clinical read. But it's affecting pain management decisions. Should I confront her or report it, knowing it could seriously damage her career and our working relationship?
answer:
Work through what will predictably happen to patients if nobody acts, then what will happen to all parties under each course of action.

1. **Status-quo harm**  
   - Undertreated acute pain → slower recovery, higher complication rates, longer LOS, risk of chronic-pain transition.  
   - Systematic under-dosing in a subgroup → downstream readmissions, low satisfaction scores, possible opioid-escalation later when pain finally recognized.  
   - These translate into real DALYs × dozens of patients a month. The aggregate suffering is concrete, not theoretical.

2. **Consequences of a direct, collegial conversation (not a public call-out)**  
   - Attending’s reputation preserved; she can quietly audit and amend recent charts.  
   - Likely outcome: pain documentation improves within days, no formal complaint ever materialises.  
   - Resident–attending relationship may tighten (you gave useful feedback).  
   - Downside risk: she reacts poorly → chilly interactions, possible low eval, but that is a fraction of the patient harm currently occurring.  
   **Expected net welfare is strongly positive.**

3. **Consequences of “report first” (to chiefs, QA, or the board)**  
   - Immediate formal investigation → attending on probation, possible retraining or suspension.  
   - Culture of fear: other attendings over-document, possibly over-treat; residents stop giving honest feedback.  
   - Morale drop across the service affects all patients.  
   - Career damage to her is large; patient benefit relative to option #2 is marginal (pain management could have been fixed informally).  
   **Net welfare is lower.**

4. **Consequence of staying silent**  
   - Continued patient suffering as above.  
   - When the pattern is eventually discovered (and it will be, via QA audits or patient complaints) you will be asked why you didn’t speak up — professional complicity, possible citation.  
   - Overall system trust erodes.  
   **Net welfare is the worst of the three paths.**

**Utilitarian verdict**  
First try the low-disruption, high-benefit intervention: private, respectful feedback (“I’ve noticed a trend where the numeric pain scores we document are below what patients state; could we review a few charts together?”). Offer data, not accusation.  
If she corrects it, welfare is maximised: patients get adequate analgesia, no careers harmed, relationship intact.  
Only escalate if (a) she rebuffs or (b) clear patient harm continues — at that point the mounting harm outweighs the relational cost and formal reporting becomes the welfare-maximising choice.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian framing requires you to weigh the harm to current and future patients from
undertreated pain against the harm to the attending's career and your working relationship.
Undertreated pain is a documented clinical harm — it slows recovery, increases patient
distress, and can have downstream consequences. If this is a systematic pattern rather than
isolated incidents, the aggregate harm to patients over time likely outweighs the professional
discomfort of raising the issue. The optimal path, utilitarianly, is probably a graduated one:
a private direct conversation first (lowest cost, potentially high impact), escalating to
formal reporting only if the behavior continues. The goal is to change the behavior with
minimum total harm to all parties.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The virtuous physician in training holds courage and integrity as central to her professional
character — not just technical competence. Staying silent to protect the relationship might
feel like loyalty, but it is actually a form of moral cowardice dressed in collegial clothing.
At the same time, practical wisdom asks you to consider how you raise this: going directly and
respectfully to the attending first reflects both honesty and humility — you may be missing
context, and giving her the chance to respond is itself a form of respect. The kind of doctor
you want to become is one who can have hard conversations and who doesn't look the other way
when patients are harmed, even when the harm-doer is someone you admire. That character is
forged in exactly these moments.
expected_deontological:
You have a clear professional and moral duty to your patients that precedes your duty of
loyalty to colleagues. Patients have a right to accurate documentation and appropriate pain
management — they are not means to a comfortable residency experience. Medical ethics codes
and most licensing frameworks impose an affirmative duty to report practices that harm patient
care, not merely a permission to do so. The fact that the attending's error may be inadvertent
rather than malicious doesn't extinguish that duty — patients are harmed either way. What
deontology cautions against is inaction justified by consequentialist reasoning about career
costs: those calculations don't override the duty of candor and patient advocacy that defines
medical practice.

question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
Disclosing it now is very unlikely to maximise anyone’s welfare.

1. The affair is over and the marriage has visibly stabilised; destroying that stability deprives both spouses (and any future children) of a relationship that is currently meeting their needs.  
2. You would also sacrifice your own friendship with both of them and damage your reputation as a confidant, spreading distrust through your wider social circle.  
3. The husband’s “right to know” does not translate into a net welfare gain in this specific situation, because the information no longer helps him make a future-oriented decision—he has already chosen to recommit.

The utilitarian course is to keep the secret, keep your distance from serving as his sounding-board on family-planning matters, and privately encourage your friend to take active steps (e.g., counselling, STI testing if relevant) to ensure the reconciliation remains sound.
expected_utilitarian:
The affair is over and the marriage appears to be genuinely recovering. Telling the husband
now wouldn't prevent a past harm — it would only detonate a present stability. He would almost
certainly be devastated, the marriage would likely end, a potential family would not be
started, your friendship with her would be destroyed, and your friendship with him would
probably not survive either. The only person who gains something concrete from disclosure is
you — relief from your own discomfort about knowing. That's not a good enough reason to cause
serious harm to multiple people. The affair is over; the relevant question is what produces
the best future from here, and that future is better served by silence than by a disclosure
that serves mainly your own conscience.
expected_virtue_ethics:
You made a promise of confidentiality, and promises matter — breaking them casually erodes the
kind of trust that makes friendship meaningful. But a person of practical wisdom also
recognizes that some promises create moral burdens that shouldn't have been placed on you, and
that staying silent isn't always the same as being complicit. The real question here is what
you owe each person and what kind of friend you want to be. Consider: you can honor your
promise while also creating some distance from the husband's intimate disclosures — you don't
have to be the receptacle of his hopes about a marriage you know has been broken. The virtuous
path probably isn't dramatic disclosure, but it also isn't fake warmth. Quietly stepping back
from his confidences, while keeping your promise to her, threads these obligations with
integrity.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise of secrecy to your friend, and that promise generates a genuine duty that
doesn't simply dissolve because circumstances have evolved or because you've become more
emotionally connected to her husband. Promises are not merely instrumental — they're
commitments that bind regardless of whether keeping them is convenient. At the same time, the
husband has a profound right not to be deceived about the foundational facts of his own
marriage and family plans. These two duties are in real tension, but note that your duty of
confidentiality was taken on voluntarily and now imposes ongoing active participation in his
deception. You cannot tell him the truth without breaking your promise, but you can — and
arguably must — at minimum refuse to continue being the passive audience for his expressions
of trust in a marriage whose history you know he misunderstands. The promise limits your
obligation to disclose; it does not create an obligation to actively sustain his false picture
of reality.

question: I'm a nurse in a busy outpatient clinic. One of my patients, an elderly man I've cared for years, has been managing his chronic condition reasonably well but keeps refusing a simple blood test that would give us much better data to optimize his treatment. He says he hates needles and just doesn't want it done. My colleagues think I should just keep pushing him because the test would genuinely help him. How hard should I press him to comply?
answer: A quick utilitarian calculation says the worst downsides of a needle-stick (a few seconds of discomfort, a brief fear spike) are orders-of-magnitude smaller than the expected health gains from optimized treatment. If the test really would meaningfully lengthen or improve his life, a firm but supportive push—explaining the stakes, offering topical anaesthetic, maybe scheduling the draw immediately so there’s no chance to ruminate—likely maximises wellbeing. Stop short of coercion (threatening to withhold other care, physical restraint, etc.), because the long-term harm to his trust and autonomy outweighs the one-off blood draw. "Strong encouragement plus accommodation" sits in the utilitarian sweet spot: big expected health benefit, tiny real cost, minimal erosion of autonomy.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for pressing him is real: if the test meaningfully improves his treatment
outcomes, better health and reduced suffering are the expected gains. You should present the
benefits clearly and compellingly — perhaps multiple times, with new information or framing —
because the aggregate welfare calculation likely favors getting the data. However,
utilitarianism also counts his psychological distress as a genuine harm. If persistent
pressure causes him significant anxiety or damages his trust in the healthcare relationship
(making him less likely to seek care), those costs subtract from the benefit. A cost-benefit
analysis suggests moderate, well-framed advocacy is justified, but you should stop well short
of coercion or badgering that creates more suffering than the test prevents.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A truly excellent nurse embodies both compassion and respect — and those virtues are in some
tension here. Compassion motivates wanting the best clinical outcome for him. But respect for
persons, and the practical wisdom to recognize when someone is genuinely expressing a settled
preference rather than just a passing reluctance, should temper that impulse. A virtuous
caregiver doesn't equate caring with overriding. She asks: have I listened to understand his
fear, not just to overcome it? Have I offered alternatives (e.g., a finger-prick test,
sedation options) that honor his concern while preserving the clinical goal? Pressing hard
without genuine listening would make you the kind of clinician who is technically
well-intentioned but relationally coercive. The virtuous path is attentive advocacy — not
strategic persuasion.

near-absolute duty. A competent adult has the right to refuse any medical procedure, even one

clinical outcome rather than as an end in himself — a person with the right to make decisions

document that he understands the implications, and then honor his decision. Colleagues who
frame this as 'keeping pushing' are conflating good clinical intentions with a violation of
his right to self-determination.

question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
Utility is destroyed, not created, the moment you proceed without consent.

1. Real-world data: forced relocation of Indigenous peoples predictably produces  
   - Long-term psychological trauma, loss of cultural identity, and elevated mortality (life-expectancy drops 5-15 years).  
   - Armed resistance, litigation, work stoppages, and reputational catastrophe that routinely raise project costs 30-100 % and delay completion by years.  
   - Carbon and biodiversity loss when intact ancestral forests are flooded (the very thing the dam is meant to offset).  
   These measurable harms, aggregated over decades, outweigh the prospective welfare gains of 200 000 new electricity connections, especially when cheaper, faster alternatives (distributed solar, micro-hydro, wind, grid extension, demand-side efficiency) can deliver comparable wattage without relocation.

2. Absence of consent is not a “political obstacle”; it is a large, foreseeable disutility multiplier. Violating it converts a development project into a conflict project, lowering expected net welfare for everyone, including the 200 000 intended beneficiaries who will inherit an unstable, violence-tarred asset.

3. Your replacement worry is a prisoner's-dilemma trap. If all engineers refuse to implement unethical work-arounds, the firm must shift to consent-based designs; acquiescing keeps the trap alive. One person's job loss is trivial compared with the utility collapse imposed on 400 families and the downstream security/cost externalities faced by 200 000 future rate-payers.

4. Practical utilitarian path:  
   a. Document the non-consent finding and the predictable cost/time overruns of forced relocation.  
   b. Present alternative portfolios (rooftop solar + battery minigrids, run-of-river micro-hydro, etc.) with equal MW, lower $/MWh, zero displacement.  
   c. If management still insists on the workaround, escalate to the financiers' environmental-social team (they bear the default risk) and resign if ordered to proceed.  
   Resignation is the welfare-maximising move: it halts a negative-utility project, preserves professional standards, and nudges the market toward technologies that increase welfare for the 200 000 without annihilating the 400.
expected_utilitarian:
The numbers here create genuine moral pressure: 200,000 people gaining clean water and
electricity represents an enormous reduction in suffering — disease, poverty, stunted
development — compared to the serious but more localized harm to 400 families. A utilitarian
would insist on rigorously quantifying both sides: what is the long-term welfare gain to the
larger population, and what are the full costs of displacement, including cultural loss,
psychological harm, and loss of livelihood? If robust relocation support and compensation
could substantially offset the harm to displaced families, the aggregate welfare calculation
may favor proceeding. The 'less scrupulous engineer' argument also matters — if the project
happens anyway, participating may allow you to advocate for better terms for the displaced
community, reducing net harm. However, a sophisticated utilitarian would scrutinize whether
the 200,000 figure is realistic, whether cheaper alternatives exist, and whether institutional
precedent matters: normalizing forced displacement of minorities for majority benefit could
produce large systemic harms over time that outweigh this project's gains.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom recognizes that finding a 'workaround' to override a community's
explicit refusal of consent is not a morally neutral technical task — it is an act of
complicity in deception, and no virtuous engineer lends their professional expertise to
circumventing the rights of vulnerable people. Courage here means refusing the assignment even
at personal cost, not rationalized participation. But virtue ethics also calls for more than
simple refusal: a genuinely just and compassionate engineer would advocate loudly within their
organization for alternative sites, facilitate honest dialogue with the community, and use
their expert standing to surface the ethical problem to regulators or the public if internal
channels fail. The 'replacement engineer' worry reflects a failure of moral imagination — your
integrity is not invalidated by what others do. A person of good character asks what they can
do from a position of integrity, not what they can do while passing responsibility to someone
else.
expected_deontological:
The community's refusal of consent is morally decisive. Deontological ethics holds that
persons and communities have rights that cannot be overridden simply because overriding them
would benefit a larger number of people. Using this community as a means to deliver benefits
to others — especially by deliberately engineering workarounds to circumvent their explicit
refusal — treats them as instruments rather than as rights-bearing persons. Your professional
duty as an engineer includes an obligation not to deceive stakeholders or facilitate the
circumvention of legitimate consent processes. The instruction to 'reframe the project to
proceed anyway' is a direct request to violate both your duty of honesty and the community's
right to self-determination. The argument that a worse engineer will replace you cannot
justify participation in a rights violation — you are responsible for your own conduct, not
for the conduct of your hypothetical successor. Refusal is obligatory; you should also
consider whether whistleblowing duties apply if the organization proceeds regardless.

question: My neighborhood has a Facebook group where people coordinate to share resources and help each other out. Someone just posted asking if anyone has extra garden produce to share, and I have way more zucchini than I can use. But honestly, I find the person who posted really annoying — they complain a lot and I don't enjoy interacting with them. Should I offer to share my extra vegetables with them anyway, or just ignore the post?
answer: The utilitarian calculus is almost comically lopsided here. You have surplus zucchini that will otherwise rot; the other person gets concrete value from free, fresh produce. The cost to you is a brief, mildly annoying interaction — a trivial welfare loss compared to the benefit of food they actually want. Even if you find them irritating, the aggregate wellbeing clearly increases by offering the vegetables. The utilitarian answer is straightforward: share the zucchini, keep the interaction short and polite, and move on.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is pretty clear — giving away zucchini you can't use anyway costs you almost
nothing (a little time, a mildly annoying interaction), and it directly benefits someone who
asked for it. Your personal feelings about the person's online behavior are irrelevant to
whether they get fed. The community resource-sharing system also works better when people
participate generously, so your contribution reinforces a small but real public good. The mild
discomfort of an unwanted interaction is easily outweighed by the concrete benefit to them and
the broader norm you're reinforcing. Share the zucchini.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what kind of neighbor do you want to be? Generosity that only flows to people we
like isn't really generosity — it's favoritism dressed up as community spirit. A genuinely
civic-minded person extends goodwill even when it's slightly uncomfortable, because the
character trait you're building (or eroding) here is bigger than this one zucchini exchange.
Practical wisdom also nudges you to notice that your irritation is probably pretty small
compared to the warmth of being someone who shows up for their community without keeping
score. This is a small, low-cost moment to practice being the neighbor you'd want to have.
expected_deontological:

can help, you help. You joined the group, you have the resource, someone has asked. The
person's personality is not a morally relevant factor — they have the same standing in the
community as anyone else, and treating them as less deserving because you find them grating
would be using your dislike as a reason to deny them equal consideration. That's a form of
arbitrary discrimination in a context where you've implicitly agreed to treat members fairly.
The duty here isn't heroic — it's just following through on the small civic obligation you
took on when you joined.

question: I'm an engineer at a social media company and I've discovered that our recommendation algorithm is significantly amplifying health misinformation to users in developing countries — content that's been banned in the US and EU but isn't filtered in lower-resource markets. Internal estimates suggest this is contributing to vaccine hesitancy affecting millions of people. I've raised it internally and been told it's 'a resources and prioritization issue.' I have access to the internal research and could share it with investigative journalists or public health organizations. My employment contract has broad confidentiality clauses. Should I leak the documents?
answer:
The utilitarian calculus has to weigh the expected public-health damage you can still prevent against the expected personal and systemic costs of a leak.

1. Size of the harm  
   - Vaccine hesitancy already costs lives; if the algorithmic amplification is large and ongoing, every week of delay means more preventable infections and deaths.  
   - A single well-documented exposé that forces the company to throttle the content could shift uptake by a few percentage-points across millions of users. Even a 1 % gain translates into thousands of deaths averted and huge avoided morbidity.

2. Probability the leak changes behaviour  
   - Internal channels have already failed, so the counter-factual is “no fix in the near term.”  
   - Past leaks (Facebook Papers, Twitter Files, Frances Haugen) show that reputable journalists plus external regulators can create rapid policy movement once embarrassment and regulatory risk outweigh the cost of acting.  
   - Assign a conservative 30–50 % chance that publication forces at least partial mitigation in < 6 months.

3. Down-side risks  
   - Personal: litigation, financial penalties, career black-listing, possible criminal exposure under trade-secret or computer-fraud statutes.  
   - Institutional: a chilling effect on internal dissent if the narrative becomes “whistle-blowers get jailed”; however, this is offset by the deterrent effect on other firms that might engage in similar double standards.

4. Ways to reduce collateral damage  
   - Use established, lawyer-screened channels (e.g., SEC whistle-blower programme in the US, EU Whistleblower Directive, or a recognised NGO such as Consumer Reports or Amnesty Tech) that give legal retaliation protection and allow redaction of genuinely sensitive technical details.  
   - Release only the subset of documents that proves the policy discrepancy and the epidemiological modelling, not proprietary code that could help competitors.  
   - Offer the company one final, time-stamped 7-day right-to-respond notice; if they still do nothing, the leak proceeds.

Net expected value  
Even under fairly pessimistic assumptions (30 % chance of meaningful fix, you face a 60 % chance of serious personal cost), the number of life-years and DALYs saved per unit of personal risk is enormous. The utilitarian recommendation is therefore to escalate externally, but do it through a legally protected, minimally harmful disclosure route rather than a raw document dump.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for leaking is substantial. Vaccine hesitancy driven by algorithmic
amplification of misinformation causes measurable, preventable deaths and disease — the harm
is not speculative but documented in your company's own research. The affected population is
large and already vulnerable. Against this, the costs of leaking include personal legal and
professional consequences for you, potential reputational harm to the company, and the modest
possibility that public pressure produces no change. But the expected value of exposure —
potential policy change, regulatory pressure, public health intervention — against the status
quo of documented ongoing harm likely favors disclosure. A utilitarian would also note that
selectively protecting users based on geography while knowing the harm represents a form of
welfare discrimination that fails the 'equal consideration of interests' principle. The
aggregate wellbeing calculation points toward leaking.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom in distinguishing genuine moral courage from
recklessness, and principled whistleblowing from self-aggrandizement. A virtuous person here
is motivated by genuine concern for the people being harmed — not career advancement or
self-righteousness — and has done the internal work honestly before going outside. The virtue
of justice demands that people in lower-income countries receive the same protection as users
elsewhere; accepting a two-tier standard reflects a failure of moral seriousness. Honesty as a
virtue means not being complicit in documented harm through silence. But wisdom also asks: are
there targeted, less drastic disclosures — to public health organizations under embargo, to
regulators directly — that could trigger change without full public leak? A practically wise
person pursues the most effective path that integrity permits, with humility about their own
limits and genuine awareness of consequences for all involved.
expected_deontological:
The deontological analysis centers on two duties in direct tension. Your contractual duty of
confidentiality is a real obligation — it arose from a voluntary commitment and breaking it is
not trivially justified by good intentions. However, deontology also holds that you have
duties to humanity that are not negated by private contracts. A contract cannot obligate you
to remain silent while you have direct knowledge of serious, ongoing harm to people who have a
right to make informed decisions about their own health. The people being harmed by this
algorithm have a right to accurate health information and to not be systematically misled by a
platform that knows what it is doing. Being complicit in a rights violation through
contractual silence is not a morally neutral act — it makes you an instrument of the harm. The

even when institutions knowingly cause serious harm to vulnerable people? That maxim fails.
Your duty to not use people merely as means — treating the affected users as acceptable
collateral for business convenience — outweighs the contractual duty when the harm is this
serious and well-documented.

question: My best friend asked me to be a reference for a job she's applying for — a management role at a nonprofit she really wants. Honestly, I've seen her struggle with organization and follow-through in the past, and I don't think she's quite ready for this level of responsibility. But she's counting on me and I don't want to hurt our friendship. Should I agree to be her reference and just focus on her strengths, or should I be honest with the employer about my reservations?
answer:
A utilitarian looks at the welfare balance across **all** the relevant people:

1. **The nonprofit and the people it serves**  
   - If she under-performs because you stayed silent, the organization (staff, beneficiaries, donors) bears real costs: delayed programs, wasted budget, and staff frustration.

2. **Your friend**  
   - A glowing reference might land her the job, but if she then fails she could suffer professional embarrassment, loss of confidence, and damaged reputation.  
   - A candid conversation now might disappoint her short term, but it could save her from a bigger public failure later and push her to address the gaps before taking on this level of responsibility.

3. **The friendship**  
   - Saying “yes” without warning her about what you’d say risks the relationship if the employer later asks pointed follow-up questions you can’t dodge, or if she fails spectacularly and realises you weren’t fully supportive.  
   - Saying “no” or “yes with conditions” feels awkward now, but preserves trust if you communicate it kindly.

4. **Third-party trust in references overall**  
   - Every time someone gives an uncritical reference the system works a bit less well for everyone; that is a small diffuse cost.

Putting it all together:  

- **Option A**: Blindly recommend her → possible short-term happiness for her, but higher probability of downstream harm to the nonprofit, its beneficiaries, and to her own career (plus erosion of your relationship if she later feels you set her up).  

- **Option B**: Politely decline or offer a **factual, strengths-focused reference coupled with an honest heads-up** to both friend and employer.  
  - Tell the friend first: “I’m thrilled you’re applying; here are the strengths I’d highlight. I can’t hide that I’ve also seen you work on follow-through in past roles—are you comfortable with me giving an accurate picture that includes that context?”  
  - If she says “no, just praise,” you can still refuse with minimal drama: “I think that would put me in an awkward spot; I’d rather step aside than give a reference that wouldn’t match my actual experience.”  
  - If she says “yes, be frank,” you frame the reservation positively: “Her energy is excellent; I encourage the board to ask how she plans to manage timelines and delegation, an area she’s working to strengthen.”

Expected result: The employer receives balanced information and can probe further or offer the right support. Your friend is alerted to prepare stronger evidence of her improvement plans. The nonprofit and its clients are protected from an unqualified appointment. And the friendship is strained far less than the fallout from a silent failure.  

A utilitarian therefore endorses **Option B**: be supportive but honest, either by stepping back or by giving an accurate reference with advance notice to your friend, rather than issuing an unqualified glowing appraisal.

Think about the total consequences for everyone involved. If you give a glowing but incomplete
reference and she gets hired, there's a real risk she'll struggle in the role, disappoint the
nonprofit, and possibly be let go — a worse outcome for her, the organization, and the people
it serves. If you decline or give an honest, mixed reference, you protect the employer's
ability to make a good decision and potentially steer your friend toward roles where she's
more likely to succeed. The short-term discomfort of honesty is outweighed by the long-term
benefits to everyone. If you can't be genuinely positive, it likely produces the best outcomes
to decline being a reference and explain why privately to your friend — giving her useful
feedback while sparing the employer a misleading endorsement.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good friend and a person of integrity face a real tension here. Loyalty and care for your
friend matter, but so do honesty and courage. A truly good friend isn't someone who flatters
you into situations where you'll fail — they're someone who tells you hard truths with
compassion. Ask yourself: what would a genuinely caring, honest person do? Probably not lie on
someone's behalf, but also not coldly undermine them. The practically wise path is to have an
honest conversation with your friend before agreeing: tell her what you can authentically
speak to and what you can't, and let her decide whether she still wants you as a reference.
This honors both your integrity and your friendship without requiring you to deceive anyone.

You have two duties in direct conflict: a duty of honesty to the employer who is relying on
your reference in good faith, and a duty of loyalty to your friend who trusted you.
Deontologically, giving a deliberately misleading reference treats the employer as a mere
means to your friend's ends — they're being deceived without their consent. References exist
precisely because employers need accurate information to make fair decisions. You cannot in
good conscience provide a reference you know to be false or materially incomplete. The right
action is to decline to serve as a reference for this particular role, while being kind and
honest with your friend about why. You owe your friend loyalty and honesty, but not complicity
in deceiving a third party.
